records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: A, an extremely talented digital artist, was employed by XYZ Creatives as a graphic designer. One day, A accidentally side-swiped the company president’s BMW car. From then on, the president had been verbally humiliating her in front of her co-employees. Traumatized, A resigned. She also immediately filed a complaint for constructive dismissal. In turn, XYZ Creatives contended that A voluntarily resigned. Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A was constructively dismissed.

Legal Basis: Under the Labor Code’s guarantee of security of tenure and Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc., constructive dismissal exists when continued employment becomes impossible, unreasonable, or unlikely, or when the employer’s discrimination, insensibility, or disdain becomes unbearable to a reasonable employee.

Application: After the accident involving the company president’s car, the president repeatedly humiliated A in front of her co-employees. The repeated public humiliation and resulting trauma made continued employment intolerable. Her immediate constructive-dismissal complaint is consistent with a resignation compelled by the employer’s conduct, not a genuinely voluntary resignation.

Conclusion: A’s resignation is treated as a constructive dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294 (security of tenure); Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69528
records.Controlling Doctrine: Constructive dismissal occurs when continued employment becomes impossible, unreasonable, or unlikely, or when the employer’s discrimination, insensibility, or disdain becomes unbearable; the test is whether a reasonable person in the employee’s position would feel compelled to resign.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: A filed a complaint against XYZ Corp. for unfair labor practice. A alleged that only workers who graduated from ABC University were given free breakfast and free lunch by the corporation. A, an alumnus of DEF University, was not entitled to this incentive. Is there unfair labor practice? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The facts do not establish unfair labor practice.

Legal Basis: Article 259(e) of the Labor Code treats discrimination as unfair labor practice when it is intended to encourage or discourage membership in a labor organization. In Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc., the Supreme Court explained that unfair labor practices are acts that violate workers’ right to self-organization or the observance of a collective bargaining agreement.

Application: The meal incentive is based on university affiliation, not union membership, union activity, or the exercise of the right to self-organization. Even if the distinction may be perceived as unfair, the facts do not supply the labor-relations element required for unfair labor practice.

Conclusion: XYZ Corporation did not commit unfair labor practice on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 259(e); Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67502
records.Controlling Doctrine: An act is not unfair labor practice merely because it is unfair; it must interfere with the right to self-organization, discriminate to encourage or discourage union membership, or violate the duty to bargain or observe the CBA.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Company was engaged in the construction of luxury multi-storey homes and midrise condominiums. One of its projects was a three-storey mansion of Senator A. XYZ Company was about to do concrete pouring of slab and beams on the second floor of the mansion, and this process would take at least 20 hours straight with no interruption or break; otherwise, the structural integrity of the second floor and beams would be compromised. More, the process would need 25 workers to finish.

B, one of the workers assigned to the project, refused to render overtime work, claiming that he cannot be compelled to do so. Is B correct? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. B may be required to render overtime work in this situation.

Legal Basis: Article 89(e) of the Labor Code permits compulsory overtime when completing or continuing work begun before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the employer’s business or operations. In Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc., the Supreme Court recognized that an overtime order justified by a statutory emergency or business-prejudice exception is a lawful work order. Statutory overtime premiums remain payable.

Application: Concrete pouring for the slab and beams must be continuous to avoid compromising the structure. Interrupting the work after eight hours would create serious prejudice to the project. The facts therefore fall within the statutory exception, subject to payment of the required overtime compensation.

Conclusion: B is not correct; XYZ Company may compel the overtime work and must pay the lawful overtime premium.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 89(e); Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book III, Rule I, Section 10; Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54784
records.Controlling Doctrine: An employee may be required to work overtime when continuation of work begun before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the employer’s business or operations, with the corresponding overtime premium.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: XYZ Gym engaged A, B, and C as fitness trainers. They were paid fixed monthly salaries, commissions, and other statutory benefits. After two years, XYZ Gym reclassified them as freelance trainers. While they were still paid monthly salaries and commissions, the other statutory benefits were discontinued. A, B, and C opposed their reclassification, claiming they are regular employees since their work is essential to the business of XYZ Gym. However, XYZ Gym maintained that as freelance trainers, they are deemed to be independent contractors and their engagement by the company was only in consideration of their skill and expertise. Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A, B, and C are regular employees, not independent contractors.

Legal Basis: Article 295 of the Labor Code treats employment as regular when the work is usually necessary or desirable in the employer’s business. Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc. holds that when employment status is disputed, the employer bears the burden of proving genuine independent-contractor status, including unique skills and freedom from control. Laurente v. Helenar Construction further recognizes the presumption of regular employment.

Application: The trainers performed the core service of a gym, received fixed monthly salaries and commissions, and initially received statutory benefits. Their work and compensation arrangement continued after the label changed. XYZ Gym presented no facts showing that the trainers operated independent businesses or controlled the means and methods of their work. The withdrawal of statutory benefits cannot convert regular employees into freelancers.

Conclusion: A, B, and C remain regular employees entitled to statutory benefits.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 295; Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep/2024/G.R.%20No.%20266552.pdf; Laurente v. Helenar Construction: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep/2021/G.R.%20No.%20243812.pdf
records.Controlling Doctrine: The employer bears the burden of proving that a person it pays for services is an independent contractor; labels do not defeat regular employment where the work is necessary or desirable and the worker is not shown to operate independently.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc.; Laurente v. Helenar Construction

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: XYZ International School, Inc. was a domestic educational institution established primarily for dependents of foreign diplomatic personnel and other temporary residents. It classified its teachers into two categories: (1) foreign hires; and (2) local hires. The salary of foreign hires was 25% higher than those of local hires. The local hires complained that this policy was allegedly discriminatory since both groups perform the same work. XYZ International School, Inc. countered that the policy was adopted to attract foreign hires and that the two groups are not similarly situated. Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The local hires’ complaint has merit.

Legal Basis: In International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, the Supreme Court held that persons who work with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions should receive similar pay. The constitutional policy against discrimination and the principle of equal pay for equal work prohibit a salary distinction based solely on foreign-hire status when no substantial work-related distinction is shown.

Application: The facts state that foreign and local teachers perform the same work. XYZ International School, Inc. identifies recruitment as its objective but supplies no material difference in qualifications, duties, responsibility, or working conditions that would justify paying foreign hires 25% more.

Conclusion: The salary classification is discriminatory, and the local hires are entitled to equal pay for substantially equal work.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53093
records.Controlling Doctrine: Persons who work with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions should receive similar salaries; nationality or foreign-hire status alone does not justify unequal pay.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: X, a cashier at ABC Mart, filed a complaint for illegal dismissal with prayer for reinstatement and payment of full backwages against ABC Mart. X alleged that one day, ABC Mart told her not to return to work anymore, thus, she was deemed to have been unlawfully dismissed. During the proceedings, ABC Mart countered that it was X who abandoned her post. Both the labor arbiter and the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) found, however, that what happened between X and ABC Mart was a mere misunderstanding and there was no dismissal or abandonment to speak of. Based on these findings, is X entitled to reinstatement and payment of full backwages? Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. X is not entitled to the remedies of reinstatement and backwages for illegal dismissal.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code grants reinstatement and backwages to an employee who was unjustly dismissed. Rodriguez v. Sintron Systems, Inc. explains that when no dismissal occurred, one cannot be reinstated to a position one still holds, and backwages do not accrue because the employment relationship was never severed.

Application: The labor tribunals found neither dismissal nor abandonment. X therefore continues to hold her employment. She may return to work, and ABC Mart must accept her, but this is not technical reinstatement following an illegal dismissal and does not carry an award of backwages.

Conclusion: X may resume work, but she is not entitled to reinstatement or full backwages as illegal-dismissal remedies.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294; Rodriguez v. Sintron Systems, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65491
records.Controlling Doctrine: When neither dismissal nor abandonment occurred, the employment relationship remains intact; the employee may return and the employer must accept the employee, but reinstatement and backwages as illegal-dismissal remedies are unavailable.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: ABC Corporation, a legitimate job contractor engaged in the construction business, hired X as a plumber. Under a service agreement, ABC Corporation undertook to provide workers for the construction project of XYZ Corporation, a company engaged in real estate development. X was among those assigned by ABC Corporation to the project. While the construction project was ongoing, X filed a complaint for underpayment of wages against both ABC Corporation and XYZ Corporation. XYZ Corporation denied liability, claiming that ABC Corporation, as the true employer of X, should be solely liable for the underpayment of wages of X. Is XYZ Corporation correct? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. XYZ Corporation is solidarily liable with ABC Corporation for X’s wage underpayment.

Legal Basis: Articles 106, 107, and 109 of the Labor Code make a principal jointly and severally liable with its contractor for unpaid wages to the extent of work performed under the contract. Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission confirms that this limited indirect-employer liability applies even when the contractor is legitimate.

Application: ABC Corporation directly employed X and assigned him to XYZ Corporation’s project. Because the claim is for underpayment of wages earned on that project, XYZ Corporation, as principal, cannot avoid the statutory solidary liability by pointing to ABC Corporation’s legitimate-contractor status.

Conclusion: ABC Corporation and XYZ Corporation are solidarily liable for the wage deficiency.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Articles 106, 107, and 109; Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44806
records.Controlling Doctrine: A principal is an indirect employer for the limited purpose of ensuring payment of the contractor’s employees’ wages and is solidarily liable with a legitimate contractor for wage underpayment attributable to work performed under the service contract.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Public Sector Labor Relations — Prohibited Mass Action
records.Essay Question: The workers of a government corporation went on a mass leave because of its refusal to increase their salaries. They invoked Article XIII, Section 3 of the Constitution which provides that the State “shall guarantee the rights of all workers to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities, including the right to strike in accordance with law[,]” as well as Section 2 of Executive Order No. 180, series of 1987, which provides that “[a]ll government employees can form, join or assist employees’ organizations of their own choosing for the furtherance and protection of their interests.” Is the mass leave lawful? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The mass leave is unlawful.

Legal Basis: Government employees possess the right to self-organization, but the right does not include a strike or concerted mass action that causes a work stoppage or service disruption. Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS applies this civil-service limitation and recognizes mass leave intended to force concessions as a prohibited concerted activity.

Application: The workers jointly stopped work through mass leave to pressure a government corporation into granting a salary increase. That conduct is a concerted service disruption designed to force an economic concession, not merely the formation or peaceful operation of an employees’ organization.

Conclusion: The workers’ right to self-organization does not make the mass leave lawful.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Constitution, Article IX-B and Article XIII, Section 3; Executive Order No. 180, Series of 1987; Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/40512
records.Controlling Doctrine: The right of government employees to self-organization does not include the right to strike or undertake concerted mass action, including mass leave, that causes or intends to cause a temporary work stoppage or service disruption to force concessions.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) of Region V issued Wage Order No. 16, providing an increase in the Cost-of-Living Allowance (COLA) for workers in the private sector. XYZ Corporation implemented the COLA increase in favor of its employees in its Naga Branch (Region V). ABC Union, as the exclusive bargaining agent of XYZ Corporation, demanded that the increase be extended to its employees outside Region V. According to the union, the implementation of the wage order created a wage distortion in the salary structure of rank-and-file employees in its Naga Branch vis-à-vis the other branches of XYZ Corporation. Is ABC Union correct? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. ABC Union is not correct.

Legal Basis: Article 124 of the Labor Code addresses wage distortion resulting from a prescribed wage increase. Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company identifies four elements, including the elimination or severe contraction of an existing wage distinction within the same region of the country.

Application: Wage Order No. 16 applies in Region V, and the comparison is between employees in the Naga Branch and employees in branches outside Region V. Because the alleged disparity crosses regional wage jurisdictions, the same-region element of statutory wage distortion is absent.

Conclusion: The regional COLA increase does not require its extension to employees outside Region V on the theory of wage distortion.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 124; Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29841
records.Controlling Doctrine: Wage distortion requires an existing hierarchy, a significant increase in a lower pay class without a corresponding increase in a higher class, elimination or severe contraction of the wage distinction, and a distortion occurring within the same region.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: In G.R. No. 123456, the Supreme Court declared ABC Company liable for illegal dismissal when it terminated the services of X without just or authorized cause. Following the finality of the decision, X filed a petition for computation of backwages and separation pay to be reckoned from the date he got illegally terminated until the finality of the decision in G.R. No. 123456. ABC Company, however, argued that the computation should be reckoned from the date of termination of employment until the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) rendered its judgment finding that X was illegally dismissed. Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: X’s position is correct; ABC Company’s proposed cut-off is not.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code provides the remedies for illegal dismissal. Bani Rural Bank, Inc. v. De Guzman holds that when separation pay is awarded in lieu of reinstatement, backwages are computed from dismissal until finality of the decision, while separation pay is reckoned through finality because the employment relationship is deemed severed only then.

Application: The illegal-dismissal ruling became final after the National Labor Relations Commission’s earlier decision. The NLRC ruling did not yet finally terminate the employment relationship. The proper terminal point for the monetary computation is therefore the finality of the controlling judgment, not the date of the NLRC’s initial finding.

Conclusion: Backwages and the relevant period for separation pay must be computed through finality of the decision.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294; Bani Rural Bank, Inc. v. De Guzman: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56480
records.Controlling Doctrine: When separation pay is awarded in lieu of reinstatement, backwages accrue from dismissal until finality of the decision, and separation pay is computed through finality because the employment relationship is severed only upon finality.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bani Rural Bank, Inc. v. De Guzman

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: A was engaged as a delivery personnel by a luxury optical store. In his two years of employment, he had twice served a one-month suspension for losing clients’ reading glasses. This time, he was tasked to deliver a pair of luxury eyeglasses worth PHP 250,000.00 to a client. On the way to the client’s address, A passed by his girlfriend’s house for coffee where he lost the eyeglasses. Consequently, the optical store dismissed A for gross and habitual neglect of duty. Is the dismissal of A valid? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, on the stated substantive facts, the dismissal is valid.

Legal Basis: Article 297(b) of the Labor Code permits dismissal for gross and habitual neglect of duties. Philippine National Bank v. Padao defines gross negligence as a want or absence of care and habitual neglect as repeated failure to perform one’s duties over time; repeated negligent failures causing serious loss may justify dismissal.

Application: A’s duty was to safeguard and deliver clients’ eyewear. He had already lost clients’ glasses twice and had been suspended for each incident. He then deviated from the delivery route for a personal stop and lost eyeglasses worth PHP 250,000.00. The third similar loss shows both serious want of care and repeated neglect despite prior discipline.

Conclusion: The employer had just cause to dismiss A for gross and habitual neglect, subject to compliance with procedural due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(b); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(c); Philippine National Bank v. Padao: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27251
records.Controlling Doctrine: Gross negligence is the want or absence of care in performing one’s duties; habitual neglect is repeated failure to perform those duties over time. Repeated negligent acts causing serious loss can constitute just cause for dismissal.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: X, Y, and Z, employees of ABC Security Agency, were security guards assigned in Sta. Clara, Lamitan, Basilan. On October 1, 2024, ABC Security Agency instructed them to report by October 15, 2024 to its head office in Manila for reassignment to its other clients. X, Y, and Z did not comply with the directive since they were not given sufficient time to prepare for this new assignment. Too, they were residents of Basilan, have families in Basilan, and ABC Security Agency did not even give them fare money. Consequently, ABC Security Agency dismissed them for insubordination and willful disobedience to lawful orders. Is the dismissal valid? Reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The dismissal is invalid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 297(a) of the Labor Code allows dismissal for willful disobedience only when the refusal is intentional and the violated order is reasonable, lawful, sufficiently known, and connected with the employee’s duties. Metro Psychiatry, Inc. v. Llorente applies these requisites and emphasizes that refusal alone is insufficient when the reasonableness of the directive is not established.

Application: The guards were based in Basilan with their families but were given only two weeks to report to Manila, without fare assistance or adequate time to arrange the transfer. In combination, these circumstances made the directive unreasonable. Their refusal therefore did not satisfy all requisites of willful disobedience.

Conclusion: ABC Security Agency lacked just cause to dismiss X, Y, and Z for insubordination.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(a); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(b); Metro Psychiatry, Inc. v. Llorente: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66149
records.Controlling Doctrine: Willful disobedience requires an intentional refusal to obey an order that is reasonable, lawful, sufficiently known to the employee, and connected with the employee’s duties; absence of any requisite defeats the just cause.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Zhi Go (Zhi) is a non-resident Chinese national who plans to live and establish a career in the Philippines. Zhi went to the Philippines and applied with the Tarlac Agricultural Products (TAP) as an ordinary farm worker. The TAP hired Zhi because of her diverse set of farming skills. The TAP assigned Zhi in its Bamban Farm. Did TAP lawfully hire Zhi Go as a farm worker? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Tarlac Agricultural Products did not lawfully hire Zhi Go on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 40 of the Labor Code requires the employer of an alien to obtain the required employment permit from the Department of Labor and Employment. Rouche v. French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines-Le Club likewise recognizes that a foreign national working in the Philippines must have the required alien employment permit and appropriate immigration authorization.

Application: Zhi Go is a nonresident alien hired to work in the Philippines, but the facts do not show that Tarlac Agricultural Products obtained an alien employment permit before engaging her. Her farming skills alone do not dispense with the statutory permit requirement.

Conclusion: Her employment was not lawful absent the required employment authorization.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 40; Rouche v. French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines-Le Club; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69141
records.Controlling Doctrine: A domestic or foreign employer that engages an alien for work in the Philippines must first obtain the legally required alien employment permit, together with the applicable immigration authorization.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Rouche v. French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines-Le Club

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Manila Yummy Restaurant (MYR) pays its receptionists PHP 500.00 a day. The receptionists contested the amount because the present minimum wage in the National Capital Region is PHP 645.00 for the non-agricultural sector. MYR countered that it is paying the receptionists a total of PHP 700.00 which is more than the required minimum wage. MYR explained that it provides the receptionists food and beverage worth PHP 200.00 per day in addition to the PHP 500.00 cash component of their wages. The food and beverage are given during lunch time to ensure that the receptionists will entertain guests instead of leaving their stations. Thus, the PHP 200.00 value of the food and beverage must be added to the PHP 500.00 cash component of their wage. May MYR lawfully add the value of the food and beverage as part of the wages of its receptionists? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The food and drinks may not be credited as part of the receptionists’ wages.

Legal Basis: Article 97(f) of the Labor Code and the implementing rules distinguish deductible facilities from supplements. Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian explains that a facility must be customarily furnished for the employee’s benefit, voluntarily accepted in writing, and charged at a fair and reasonable value; items primarily benefiting the employer are not deductible facilities.

Application: Manila Yummy Restaurant supplied the meals so that the receptionists would remain at their stations and attend to guests. The meals therefore primarily served the restaurant’s business convenience. The facts also show no written voluntary acceptance of their value as a wage deduction.

Conclusion: The PHP 200.00 value cannot be credited toward the minimum wage, leaving the PHP 500.00 cash wage deficient.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 97(f); Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book III, Rule VII-A, Sections 2 and 5; Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69683
records.Controlling Doctrine: For a benefit to be deductible as a facility, it must be primarily for the employee’s benefit, customarily furnished, voluntarily accepted in writing, and charged at a fair and reasonable value; an item supplied mainly for the employer’s convenience is a supplement.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Lexi Enterprises always made sure that the salary of its supervisory employees is 70% higher than the wage of its rank-and-file workers. Later, the management of Lexi Enterprises realized that its business is highly dependent on rank-and-file workers because they spend more time in providing services to the clients. Thus, Lexi Enterprises significantly increased the wages of its rank-and-file workers such that they are only 10% behind the salary of the supervisory employees. Consequently, the supervisory employees demanded an increase in their salaries and alleged that Lexi Enterprises must correct the wage distortion. May the supervisory employees validly demand an increase in their salaries? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The supervisors cannot compel a salary increase under the statutory wage-distortion mechanism on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 124 of the Labor Code requires correction when a prescribed wage increase under a law or wage order distorts an establishment’s wage structure. Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission holds that a voluntary, unilateral management increase does not create the statutory duty to rectify wage distortion, absent another legal or contractual source of obligation.

Application: Lexi Enterprises, not a law or regional wage order, voluntarily raised the rank-and-file employees’ wages. The facts identify no collective bargaining agreement or established company practice requiring a corresponding supervisory increase.

Conclusion: The supervisors may negotiate for an increase, but they cannot compel one under Article 124.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 124; Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/46976
records.Controlling Doctrine: A voluntary employer-initiated wage adjustment does not, by itself, trigger Article 124’s mandatory wage-distortion correction mechanism; another law, agreement, or established practice must supply the obligation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: The Philippines celebrates “Ninoy Aquino Day” every August 21 of the year as a special non-working holiday. Tyson Plastic Company (TPC) scheduled its machine shutdown on August 21, 2024 and informed the workers that the factory will be closed for maintenance. Later, the President of the Philippines issued Proclamation No. 665 moving the observance of “Ninoy Aquino Day” from August 21, 2024, Wednesday, to August 23, 2024, Friday, to promote domestic tourism in the country. The TPC announced that the machine shutdown will push through as scheduled and required the workers to report on August 23, 2024. Winslet is paid PHP 700.00 daily salary as a machine operator. Winslet reported for work on August 23, 2024 and claimed holiday premium pay. The TPC denied the claim and argued that Winslet already enjoyed the holiday on August 21, 2024 when the factory was closed. How much is Winslet entitled to for working on August 23, 2024? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Winslet should receive PHP 910.00.

Legal Basis: Article 93(c) of the Labor Code requires at least 30% additional compensation for work performed on a special nonworking day. Peñaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corporation expressly recognizes this special-day premium. Proclamation No. 665 designated August 23, 2024 as the special nonworking observance of Ninoy Aquino Day.

Application: Winslet worked on the officially designated special nonworking day. The August 21 closure was a maintenance shutdown, not payment for work on the transferred holiday. Her compensation is PHP 700.00 multiplied by 130%, or PHP 910.00.

Conclusion: Winslet is entitled to PHP 910.00 for August 23, 2024.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 93(c); Proclamation No. 665, Series of 2024; Peñaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44812
records.Controlling Doctrine: Work performed on a special nonworking day must be paid the employee’s regular daily wage plus a premium of at least 30%.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Brent Therapy Clinic (BTC) engaged Franklin as a probationary physical therapist for a period of five months. BTC informed Franklin that he must obtain satisfactory grades in these criteria: (a) diagnosis of movement dysfunction; (b) therapeutic exercise techniques; (c) stimulation and healing massage; and (d) proper use of machines and equipment. After three months, BTC observed that Franklin cannot meet the minimum criteria. Franklin was unfamiliar with therapeutic exercise techniques and was unable to remember the use of therapy machines. The following day, the owner of BTC left a note on Franklin’s desk which reads:

Hi Franklin. I tried to guide and train you in the past months but there has been no improvement. The management is unhappy with your work performance. Thus, your probationary employment is terminated one week from notice for failure to meet the minimum standards for regularization.

Aggrieved, Franklin questioned his termination for lack of procedural due process. Is BTC required to comply with the twin-notice rule before terminating Franklin’s employment? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The twin-notice rule for a just-cause dismissal is not required when termination rests solely on failure to meet disclosed probationary standards.

Legal Basis: Article 296 of the Labor Code permits termination of probationary employment for failure to qualify under reasonable standards made known at engagement. Section 2(d), Rule I, Book VI of the implementing rules requires written notice within a reasonable time from the effective date. Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz recognizes the employer’s authority to end probationary employment for failure to satisfy disclosed regularization standards.

Application: Brent Therapy Clinic disclosed the standards when Franklin was hired, evaluated him during the probationary period, and issued written notice one week before termination. The stated ground was failure to qualify, not a separate just-cause offense requiring notice to explain and a later notice of decision.

Conclusion: The single written termination notice required for failure to qualify was sufficient on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 296; Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book VI, Rule I, Section 2(d); Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69562
records.Controlling Doctrine: When a probationary employee is terminated solely for failure to meet reasonable standards disclosed at engagement, written notice within a reasonable time from the effective date is required; the twin-notice procedure applies when the ground is a just cause.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Preston Salon and Spa (PSS) hired Nixon as a senior stylist in its Manila branch. Nixon signed an employment contract which provides that “employees shall not engage in or set up within the same locality a business similar or related to the company during their course of employment and for a period of one year after their tenure.” Thereafter, PSS received information that Nixon assisted his sister in establishing a new salon in Manila. Nixon admitted lending PHP 300,000.00 to his sister as capital and that he shall be entitled to 10% yearly profits of the new salon. Nixon also referred two former PSS employees as applicants to the new salon. After the required notices, PSS dismissed Nixon for violation of his employment contract. Is Nixon’s dismissal valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Nixon’s dismissal was valid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 297(a) of the Labor Code permits dismissal for willful disobedience of a lawful, reasonable, known, and work-related order. Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines, Inc. recognizes that a restraint against competing business may be valid when reasonably limited as to time or place and necessary to protect a legitimate business interest.

Application: The clause was known to Nixon, limited to the same locality and one year after employment, and directly protected Preston Salon and Spa’s business from competition. While still employed, Nixon financed a competing Manila salon, acquired a profit interest, and helped recruit workers for it. These acts were deliberate and violated the work-related restriction.

Conclusion: Preston Salon and Spa had just cause to dismiss Nixon, assuming the required procedural notices were observed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(a); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(b); Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines, Inc.; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41269
records.Controlling Doctrine: A willful violation of a lawful, reasonable, known, and work-related noncompetition restriction may constitute just cause for dismissal; a restraint reasonably limited by time or place may be enforceable.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Ronin Airline Company (RAC) hired Orwell as a flight engineer. In January 2024, RAC and Orwell entered into a three-month overseas training agreement which reads: “the employer agrees to invest on the travel expenses and allowances of the employee abroad provided that he will remain in the company for two years after the training. Otherwise, the employee must reimburse the employer travel expenses and pay liquidated damages of PHP 30,000.00.” Orwell completed the training abroad and returned to the Philippines. In August 2024, Orwell tendered his irrevocable resignation. Aggrieved, RAC filed against Orwell a complaint for sum of money before the trial court. Orwell sought to dismiss the action for lack of jurisdiction and argued that it is the labor arbiter that has authority to decide money claims arising from employment relationship. Which between the trial court and labor arbiter has jurisdiction over the complaint? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The regular trial court has jurisdiction.

Legal Basis: Article 224(a)(6) of the Labor Code places within Labor Arbiter jurisdiction only those money claims arising from an employer-employee relationship in the legally relevant sense. Esico v. Alphaland Corporation holds that an employer’s action to recover flight-training expenses and contractual damages from a former employee belongs to the regular courts when the claim is resolved by civil law on contracts rather than labor law.

Application: Ronin Airline Company’s principal relief is enforcement of Orwell’s reimbursement and liquidated-damages undertaking after his early resignation. Resolving liability requires interpretation of the training agreement and the Civil Code, not determination of a labor standard or statutory employment benefit.

Conclusion: The regular trial court, not the Labor Arbiter, has jurisdiction.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 224(a)(6); Esico v. Alphaland Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67906
records.Controlling Doctrine: A contractual reimbursement claim for flight-training costs belongs to the regular courts when the principal relief depends on civil law and breach of contract, not on rights and obligations created by labor law.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Athena Coffee Company (ACC) hired 300 coffee roasters under similar employment terms and conditions. ACC assigned these employees to its three roasting factories in Manila, Laguna, and Cavite. In August 2024, the AAC Manila Workers Organization (AAC-MWO) filed a petition for certification election to represent all coffee roasters including those in the unorganized Laguna and Cavite factories. AAC opposed the petition and argued that the three factories do not constitute an appropriate bargaining unit on account of their different geographical locations. May the coffee roasters in the three factories constitute an appropriate bargaining unit? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The coffee roasters may form one appropriate bargaining unit.

Legal Basis: The community-of-interest test asks whether employees share substantial mutual interests in wages, hours, working conditions, and collective-bargaining subjects. Erson Ang Lee v. Samahang Manggagawa ng Super Lamination holds that geographical separation may be disregarded when it does not sacrifice the employees’ communal or mutual interests.

Application: All 300 employees work for Athena Coffee Company as coffee roasters under similar terms and conditions. Their common duties and employment interests outweigh the fact that they report to factories in Manila, Laguna, and Cavite.

Conclusion: The three groups may constitute one appropriate bargaining unit.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book V, Rule I, Section 1(e); Erson Ang Lee v. Samahang Manggagawa ng Super Lamination; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62659
records.Controlling Doctrine: Geographical location may be disregarded in defining an appropriate bargaining unit when the employees retain substantial mutual interests in wages, hours, duties, and working conditions.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Strike — No-Strike Clause and Seven-Day Ban
records.Essay Question: EXO Corporation, Inc. (ECI) and its exclusive bargaining agent Kami Labor Union (KLU) entered into a collective bargaining agreement effective from December 15, 2019 to December 14, 2024. The agreement prohibits KLU and its members from holding a strike and lockout. In May 2024, ECI and KLU negotiated the economic provisions of the agreement but ended in a deadlock. KLU filed a notice of strike. After the conciliation failed, KLU conducted a strike vote which obtained majority support. KLU reported the strike vote to the Department of Labor and Employment. KLU then went on strike after the mandatory cooling-off period. ECI questioned the validity of the strike for being contrary to the collective bargaining agreement. In contrast, KLU argued that it complied with the strict requirements for staging a strike. Is the strike legal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The strike was illegal.

Legal Basis: Article 278 of the Labor Code requires observance of both the cooling-off period and the separate seven-day period after submission of the strike-vote report. Independently, C. Alcantara & Sons, Inc. v. Court of Appeals holds that a strike is illegal even when statutory staging requirements are observed if it violates a valid no-strike clause in an existing collective bargaining agreement.

Application: Kami Labor Union struck while the collective bargaining agreement’s no-strike clause remained in force. That breach is independently decisive. In addition, the facts state only that the cooling-off period elapsed; they do not establish that the distinct seven-day period after the strike-vote report also elapsed.

Conclusion: The strike was illegal for violating the subsisting no-strike clause and for failure of the facts to establish compliance with the separate seven-day strike ban.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 278; C. Alcantara & Sons, Inc. v. Court of Appeals; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/26658
records.Controlling Doctrine: A strike may be illegal despite compliance with statutory staging requirements when it violates a valid no-strike clause; the seven-day period after submission of the strike-vote report is also distinct from the cooling-off period.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: C. Alcantara & Sons, Inc. v. Court of Appeals

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Thalia, the owner of Quinn Karaoke Club (QKC), hired Darrence as an accountant. On January 19, 2023, QKC’s owner verbally informed Darrence to look for another job and banned him from the club. Darrence filed against QKC a complaint for illegal dismissal. Meantime, Darrence was hired as an accountant in another company on February 14, 2023. In its answer, QKC countered that Darrence abandoned his work in favor of a better paying job. On June 22, 2024, QKC ceased business. In due course, the Labor Arbiter declared Darrence unjustly dismissed from work and awarded him full backwages computed from January 19, 2023, when he was verbally dismissed, until June 22, 2024, when QKC stopped operations. Thalia sought reconsideration and invoked the principles of “no work no pay” and “unjust enrichment.” Thalia argued that Darrence’s salaries earned from another employer should be deducted from the award of backwages. The Labor Arbiter granted the motion and recomputed backwages from January 19, 2023, Darrence’s date of illegal dismissal, until February 14, 2023, when another employer hired him. Is the Labor Arbiter correct in limiting the period for computing the award of backwages? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Labor Arbiter may not deduct or cut off backwages because Darrence found another job.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code grants full backwages to an illegally dismissed employee. Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission holds that “full backwages” are computed without deducting earnings obtained elsewhere during the period of illegal dismissal.

Application: Darrence’s new employment on February 14, 2023 did not cure Quinn Karaoke Club’s illegal dismissal or reduce the employer’s statutory liability. Because the club later ceased operations, the relevant period ends on June 22, 2024, when reinstatement became impossible due to the business closure.

Conclusion: Backwages should run from January 19, 2023 through June 22, 2024, without deducting Darrence’s outside earnings.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294; Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43023
records.Controlling Doctrine: Full backwages are not reduced by earnings that an illegally dismissed employee obtains from another employer while the dismissal case is pending.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Zoe Enterprises hired Celine as a machine operator. In January 2024, Celine was medically diagnosed with tuberculosis and declared “unfit to continue working.” Zoe Enterprises dismissed Celine because of serious illness and gave her separation pay of one month salary per year of service which she used for her hospitalization and medical expenses. In April 2024, Celine was cleared of tuberculosis and was issued a medical certificate that she is medically fit to work. Celine demanded reinstatement from Zoe Enterprises but was refused. Aggrieved, Celine filed a complaint for illegal dismissal. Zoe Enterprises countered that Celine was validly dismissed because she was suffering from a contagious disease. Is Zoe Enterprises liable for illegal dismissal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Zoe Enterprises was liable for illegal dismissal.

Legal Basis: Article 299 of the Labor Code permits disease-based termination only when continued employment is legally prohibited or prejudicial to health. The implementing rules additionally require certification by a competent public health authority that the disease cannot be cured within six months despite proper treatment. Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu applies these requirements strictly.

Application: Zoe Enterprises did not obtain the required public-health certification that Celine’s tuberculosis was incurable within six months. Her medical clearance after only three months confirms that the statutory condition was not established. Payment of separation pay cannot create an authorized cause that was absent when she was dismissed.

Conclusion: The dismissal was illegal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 299; DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.4(e); Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66998
records.Controlling Doctrine: Disease-based dismissal requires certification by a competent public health authority that the disease cannot be cured within six months despite proper treatment and that continued employment is prohibited or prejudicial to health.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Mabuhay Travels, Inc. (MTI), a local manning agency acting for its principal Carousel Cruise Corporation (CCC), deployed Elizabeth as waitress on board the vessel M/S Carnival Miracle. Elizabeth finished the contract and prepared for repatriation. Upon arrival in Manila, Elizabeth complained of episodic chest and neck pains. Elizabeth consulted a cardiologist and was diagnosed of “mitral regurgitation, allergic rhinitis, and thyroid pathology.” The chest and neck pains of Elizabeth persisted that rendered her unfit for sea service. Elizabeth then filed a complaint for disability benefits against MTI and CCC. The Labor Arbiter dismissed the complaint because Elizabeth did not undergo a post-employment medical examination with the company-designated physician within three working days from arrival in the Philippines. Is the Labor Arbiter correct in dismissing the complaint for failure of Elizabeth to comply with the mandatory three-day reportorial requirement? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Dismissal of Elizabeth’s claim was proper on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: The applicable POEA Standard Employment Contract requires a seafarer claiming disability benefits to submit to a post-employment examination by the company-designated physician within three working days after return, subject to narrow exceptions for physical incapacity and timely written notice. Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation holds that the requirement applies regardless of the reason for repatriation and that unjustified noncompliance forfeits the claim.

Application: Elizabeth completed her contract, returned to the Philippines, and consulted only her private cardiologist. The facts show neither examination by the company-designated physician within three working days nor physical incapacity, timely written notice, or another recognized exception.

Conclusion: Her failure to comply with the mandatory reportorial requirement barred the disability claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: POEA Standard Employment Contract, mandatory three-working-day post-employment medical examination requirement; Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68295
records.Controlling Doctrine: A seafarer must report to the company-designated physician for post-employment examination within three working days after return, regardless of the cause of repatriation, unless a recognized exception or timely written notice applies.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Fabio entered into a contract of overseas employment as a seafarer with Gibson Ship Management (GSM), a local manning agency acting in behalf of its principal Blythe Tankers Company (BTC). On board the vessel, Fabio suffered lower back pains while performing his assigned task. Despite therapy and medication, Fabio continued to suffer severe lower back pains. The company-designated physician diagnosed Fabio with “Lumbar Strain T/C Slipped Disc.” Fabio then filed a complaint for disability benefits before the Labor Arbiter. GSM and BTC countered that Fabio is disqualified from claiming disability benefits because he concealed his urinary tract infection and hypertension during his pre-employment medical examination. Is Fabio entitled to disability benefits even if he concealed pre-existing medical conditions? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes.

Legal Basis: Section 20(E) of the POEA Standard Employment Contract addresses knowing concealment of a pre-existing illness or condition. Under Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc., the concealment bar applies only when: (1) the seafarer had a qualifying pre-existing illness or injury; (2) the seafarer intentionally concealed it; and (3) the concealed condition has a causal or reasonable connection to the illness or injury for which disability is claimed.

Application: Fabio's claimed disability is lumbar strain or a possible slipped disc. The facts establish no causal or reasonable connection between that back condition and his concealed urinary-tract infection or hypertension.

Conclusion: Fabio is entitled to disability benefits; concealment of the unrelated conditions does not bar his claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: POEA Standard Employment Contract, Sections 20(A) and 20(E); Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc.; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68794
records.Controlling Doctrine: The concealment bar applies when the seafarer intentionally conceals a qualifying preexisting condition that has a causal or reasonable connection to the disability claimed; unrelated concealment does not defeat the claim.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Lottie, Mathie, and Cachie asked Homer if he is interested to work in Indonesia. Homer inquired about the available job and Lottie told him that he will work as a restaurant entertainer. Mathie said that Homer only needs a passport. Cachie added that a certain Mr. Park will finance Homer’s travel expenses. After a week, Cachie gave a ticket to Homer and informed him that he can now leave for Indonesia. Homer, together with Lottie and Mathie, boarded a boat which transported them to Miangas Island. Lottie and Mathie brought Homer to a restaurant and introduced him to Mr. Park. A vehicle fetched Homer and took him to a club. The driver said that the place is a prostitution den. Inside the club, Homer was forced to have sexual intercourse with customers every night. Later, the police authorities rescued Homer and repatriated him to the Philippines. Homer filed against Lottie, Mathie, and Cachie criminal complaints for illegal recruitment and human trafficking. In her counter-affidavit, Cachie claimed that she cannot be convicted of illegal recruitment and human trafficking because she was not part of the group that transported Homer to Miangas Island. Is Cachie criminally liable for both illegal recruitment and human trafficking? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Cachie may be criminally liable for both illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons.

Legal Basis: Section 6 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, broadly covers unlicensed recruitment and placement acts. Section 4(a) of Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, prohibits recruiting or facilitating a person for prostitution or sexual exploitation. People v. Lalli holds that even referral for overseas placement may constitute illegal recruitment and that conspiracy may be inferred from coordinated acts in which each participant performs a pivotal role in recruiting and trafficking the victim.

Application: Cachie joined the job offer, identified the supposed financier, supplied Homer’s ticket, and told him he could depart. Those acts materially advanced the common recruitment and trafficking scheme. Her absence from the boat does not negate participation or conspiracy; in People v. Lalli, a recruiter who did not board with the victim was still liable based on referral, ticketing, and concerted action.

Conclusion: Cachie’s purposeful participation supports liability for both illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons, subject to proof beyond reasonable doubt in the criminal case.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, Section 6; Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, Section 4(a); People v. Lalli; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/28489
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unlicensed referral or facilitation for overseas work may constitute illegal recruitment; a participant who knowingly performs a pivotal role in a concerted scheme to recruit and traffic a victim for sexual exploitation need not personally accompany the victim during every stage.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Maria met Ange, Louise, and Sam at a coffee shop one afternoon. Maria promised she could send the three of them to work as bartenders in Scotland in exchange for ₱100,000 each. Ange, Louise, and Sam immediately agreed and gave the money to Maria. Upon receipt of the placement fees, Maria used the money to buy a luxury bag and posted it on her Instagram page. Ange, Louise, and Sam followed up on their employment in Scotland, but Maria stopped replying to them. After six months of waiting, Ange, Louise, and Sam filed a complaint for Illegal Recruitment in Large Scale against Maria. During trial, Ange, Louise, and Sam testified and presented a certification from the Department of Migrant Workers stating that Maria was neither licensed nor authorized to recruit people for employment. On the other hand, Maria claimed that she was not the one who recruited them but a certain Rashid, the president of the placement agency where Maria supposedly worked. Is Maria guilty of Illegal Recruitment in Large Scale? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Maria is guilty of illegal recruitment in large scale.

Legal Basis: Under Section 6 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, illegal recruitment is committed when a person without the required license or authority undertakes recruitment activities. It is committed in large scale when the unlawful acts are committed against three or more persons, individually or as a group.

Application: Maria herself offered Ange, Louise, and Sam employment abroad for a fee, received their money, and lacked a license or authority, as shown by the Department of Migrant Workers certification. Her claim that Rashid was the recruiter or that she worked for a placement agency does not negate her own direct recruitment acts.

Conclusion: All elements of illegal recruitment in large scale are present.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 8042, Section 6, as amended; People v. Liwanag, G.R. No. 232245, March 2, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68333
records.Controlling Doctrine: Recruitment acts by an unlicensed person against at least three victims constitute illegal recruitment in large scale.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Lipad Pinoy (LP), a licensed local recruitment agency, deployed Mutya for its principal, Alab Construction (AC), for a two-year project in Dubai. Mutya had been on the job for one year when, for unknown reasons, AC and LP terminated their agency agreement. Thereafter, AC failed to pay the salary of Mutya. Upon her return to the Philippines, Mutya sued both LP and AC for unpaid salaries and damages. May LP be held liable together with AC? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Lipad Pinoy remains solidarily liable with Alab Construction.

Legal Basis: Section 10 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, makes the recruitment agency and the foreign principal jointly and solidarily liable for claims arising from the overseas employment contract. Sameer Overseas Placement Agency, Inc. v. Cabiles recognizes this statutory protection and the agency’s continuing responsibility for the recruited worker’s contractual claims.

Application: Mutya’s unpaid salary arose during the two-year overseas contract secured through Lipad Pinoy. The later termination of the agency agreement cannot defeat the statutory solidary liability attached to that deployment.

Conclusion: Mutya may recover the unpaid salary from either Lipad Pinoy, Alab Construction, or both.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Bangko Norte (BN) implemented an “Exogamy Policy”, which prohibits employees from marrying their co-employees. Specifically, the policy states that when two of its employees marry each other, one of them must sever his or her employment immediately. Clara, who was hired as an account specialist, married her co-worker Ibarra, a loan specialist. Subsequently, BN terminated the employment of Clara but retained Ibarra. Clara argued that the policy should not apply to her since she was employed prior to its effectivity, and that said policy violates the Labor Code. She also pointed out that BN did not explain why it was her, and not Ibarra, whose employment was terminated. Since BN refused to reinstate her, Clara filed a complaint for illegal dismissal. Will the complaint of Clara prosper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Clara was illegally dismissed.

Legal Basis: The Labor Code prohibits discrimination against a woman employee merely because of marriage. A workplace restriction that produces sex-based discrimination must be supported by a genuine business necessity or bona fide occupational qualification. Dela Cruz-Cagampan v. One Network Bank, Inc. rejects an exogamy policy when its application discriminatorily burdens the woman employee without adequate business justification.

Application: Bangko Norte applied the marriage policy only against Clara and retained Ibarra. Priority in hiring does not establish that being unmarried, or dismissing the woman rather than the man, was necessary to the job or the bank’s operations.

Conclusion: The discriminatory enforcement supplied no valid cause for Clara’s dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code provisions against discrimination by reason of marriage; Dela Cruz-Cagampan v. One Network Bank, Inc., G.R. No. 217414, June 22, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68409
records.Controlling Doctrine: An exogamy policy cannot be discriminatorily enforced against a woman employee without a valid business necessity or bona fide occupational qualification.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Dela Cruz-Cagampan v. One Network Bank, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Arnel, a 55-year-old seafarer who worked on board different foreign vessels, went to the office of the Social Security System (SSS) to avail of his retirement benefits. However, he found out that his contributions had not been paid by his principal employer, Pancho Lines (PL). When Arnel demanded an explanation from PL, the latter replied that it was not obligated to cover his SSS membership since he was hired abroad and covered by another insurance provider. Is PL correct? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Pancho Lines’ position is incorrect.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 11199 places sea-based overseas Filipino workers under compulsory Social Security System coverage and assigns contribution duties under the statutory arrangement. Joint Ship Manning Group, Inc. v. Social Security System sustained the compulsory coverage framework for sea-based overseas Filipino workers.

Application: Arnel’s overseas hiring and private insurance do not replace compulsory statutory coverage. As the responsible employer or manning principal under the law, Pancho Lines cannot use those circumstances to excuse non-remittance.

Conclusion: The required Social Security System contributions must be remitted for Arnel.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Private insurance and foreign hiring do not displace compulsory SSS coverage of sea-based overseas Filipino workers.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Federation Affiliation of Rank-and-File and Supervisory Unions
records.Essay Question: Araro Federation applied for registration as a federation in the agricultural sector. It has under its membership a mix of five rank-and-file unions and five supervisory unions. One of the rank-and-file unions and one of the supervisory unions both belong to the same establishment, Ani Corporation (AC). AC opposed the application for registration citing the legal prohibition against the commingling of rank-and-file and supervisory employees. Is the opposition of AC meritorious? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The opposition is not meritorious.

Legal Basis: Article 255 of the Labor Code prohibits supervisory employees from joining a rank-and-file bargaining unit, but it expressly allows rank-and-file and supervisory unions operating in the same establishment to join the same federation or national union. San Miguel Foods, Inc. v. San Miguel Corporation Supervisors and Exempt Union distinguishes prohibited bargaining-unit commingling from permissible common federation affiliation.

Application: The two Ani Corporation unions remain separate bargaining organizations; they merely share affiliation with Araro Federation. The facts do not show that supervisors became members of the rank-and-file union or vice versa.

Conclusion: Their common federation affiliation is lawful and does not justify denial of registration.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 255; San Miguel Foods, Inc. v. San Miguel Corporation Supervisors and Exempt Union, G.R. No. 146206, August 1, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/31013
records.Controlling Doctrine: Separate rank-and-file and supervisory unions in one establishment may affiliate with the same federation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: San Miguel Foods, Inc. v. San Miguel Corporation Supervisors and Exempt Union

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Certification Election Winner and CBA Renegotiation
records.Essay Question: Lazara Corporation (LC) and Lazara Employees Union (LEU) forged a collective bargaining agreement (CBA). During the freedom period, a certification election was conducted where LEU lost to Samahan ng Manggagawa sa Lazara (SML), a rival union in the same establishment. SML then sent a letter to LC demanding for renegotiation of the existing CBA. LC refused to renegotiate the CBA claiming its validity for two more years. SML filed a notice of strike against LC on the ground of Unfair Labor Practice for the alleged refusal of the latter to comply with its duty to bargain collectively. Is the notice of strike meritorious? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The notice of strike has a meritorious unfair-labor-practice ground, subject to compliance with statutory strike procedures.

Legal Basis: The certified bargaining agent chosen during the freedom period represents the employees and may demand bargaining over the negotiable provisions of the collective bargaining agreement. An employer’s refusal to bargain with the duly chosen representative may constitute unfair labor practice. Ren Transport Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission recognizes the duty to bargain with the employees’ legitimate representative.

Application: Samahan ng mga Manggagawa sa Lazara won the certification election during the proper period and replaced Lazara Employees Union as bargaining representative. Lazara Corporation’s blanket refusal based only on the remaining agreement term disregarded the new representative’s bargaining rights.

Conclusion: The asserted refusal to bargain supports the notice, although any actual strike must independently satisfy all procedural requirements.

National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. Nos. 188020 and 188252, June 27, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62084
records.Controlling Doctrine: A duly certified bargaining representative may demand bargaining, and an unjustified refusal may constitute unfair labor practice.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Ren Transport Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Procedural Requirements for an Economic Strike
records.Essay Question: Adarna Manufacturing Company (AMC) and Adarna Employees Union (AEU) entered into collective bargaining negotiations but reached an impasse. AEU then filed a notice of strike before the National Conciliation and Mediation Board, which immediately conducted conciliation meetings to avert the strike. Fifteen days after the filing of the notice, and despite the conciliation proceedings, AEU staged a strike with the participation of 50% of its members. Is the strike legal? Briefly explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The strike was illegal for failure to comply with mandatory statutory requirements.

Legal Basis: For a bargaining-deadlock strike, Article 278 of the Labor Code requires the applicable 30-day cooling-off period, approval by a majority of all employees in the bargaining unit through secret ballot, reporting of the strike-vote results, and observance of the seven-day waiting period after the report. Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission treats these requirements as mandatory.

Application: The union struck after only 15 days, and participation by exactly 50 percent did not establish approval by a majority of all bargaining-unit employees. The facts also do not establish compliance with the strike-vote report and seven-day waiting period.

Conclusion: The strike cannot be considered legal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 278(c) and (f); Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 147080, April 26, 2005: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43334
records.Controlling Doctrine: The cooling-off period, majority strike vote, report, and seven-day waiting period are mandatory for a lawful economic strike.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
In 2011, Amer and Raj worked as welders on board the barges of Magiting Shipping Company (MSC), which later changed its corporate name to Perlas Corporation (PC). In 2018, PC verbally dismissed Amer and Raj from employment. Thus, they jointly filed a complaint for illegal dismissal against PC, which countered that it already had a separate and distinct personality from MSC.

It also alleged that both complainants were not its regular employees as they were merely helpers brought in by its own regular employees on certain occasions when urgent repairs were required for its barges. The Labor Arbiter (LA) held that there was an employer-employee relationship between the parties based on Article 295 [280] of the Labor Code since Amer and Raj: 1) were engaged to perform activities which are usually necessary or desirable in the usual business or trade of PC; and 2) have rendered at least one year of service. Was the LA correct in using Article 295 [280] as the basis? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Article 295 cannot itself establish the existence of an employer-employee relationship.

Legal Basis: The four-fold test—selection and engagement, payment of wages, power of dismissal, and control over the means and methods of work—determines whether an employment relationship exists, with control generally the most important factor. Valeroso v. Sky Cable Corporation applies that framework. Article 295 classifies employment only after the relationship has first been established.

Application: The Labor Arbiter moved directly from the nature or duration of the welding work to regular-employee status without first resolving the four-fold factors and the alleged continuity between MSC and Perlas Corporation.

Conclusion: The relationship must first be proved under the proper employment test before Article 295 may classify it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 295; Valeroso v. Sky Cable Corporation, G.R. No. 202015, July 13, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62027
records.Controlling Doctrine: Article 295 classifies an existing employment relationship; it does not substitute for proof under the four-fold test.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: On May 15, 2022, Marina International Shipping (MIS) hired Felipe as a bosun on board its vessel for a period of nine months. On July 30, 2022, Felipe joined his vessel of assignment. On October 31, 2022, he was repatriated due to medical reasons and was immediately referred by MIS to its company-designated physician for treatment and monitoring. On May 31, 2023, the company-designated physician pronounced Felipe fit to resume sea duties. Is MIS obligated to rehire Felipe? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Marina International Shipping (MIS) is not obligated to rehire Felipe.

Legal Basis: Seafarers are contractual employees whose employment is governed by the fixed-term contracts they sign for each engagement. Their employment ends when the contract expires unless the parties mutually agree to renew or extend it.

Application: Felipe joined the vessel on July 30, 2022 under a nine-month contract. By the time the company-designated physician declared him fit on May 31, 2023, that fixed term had expired. A medical finding of fitness removed the medical impediment but did not revive the expired contract or create a new contract.

Conclusion: MIS cannot be compelled to rehire Felipe.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Standard Employment Contract for Seafarers; Covita v. SSM Maritime Services, Inc., G.R. No. 206600, December 7, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62553
records.Controlling Doctrine: A declaration of fitness does not revive an expired seafarer contract or create an automatic right to reemployment.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Covita v. SSM Maritime Services, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question: Eduardo owns a licensed company that supplies janitorial and messengerial aides to various businesses, including Gloria Restaurant (GR). The tools and supplies used by the janitors and messengers are supplied by the clients who also train the workers and monitor their performance. Their minimum wages are paid by the clients through Eduardo. After two years of working in GR, the janitors and messengers joined the union there to receive the same benefits as the directly hired employees of GR. Can the janitors and messengers legally join the union? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the stated facts establish labor-only contracting. The workers are then deemed employees of Gloria Restaurant for labor-law purposes.

Legal Basis: Article 106 of the Labor Code and the governing contracting rules treat the principal as the direct employer when the contractor lacks substantial capital or investment and the principal controls the workers’ performance. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary applies the indicators of labor-only contracting and the resulting direct-employment consequence.

Application: Eduardo merely supplied labor, while Gloria Restaurant furnished the tools, trained the workers, and controlled their work. Payment coursed through Eduardo does not outweigh those indicators. As deemed employees of Gloria Restaurant, the workers may exercise self-organization rights in the appropriate bargaining unit.

Conclusion: They may legally join the appropriate Gloria Restaurant employees’ union, subject to the union’s lawful membership rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Articles 106 and 253; Caballero v. Vikings Commissary, G.R. No. 238859, October 19, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68775
records.Controlling Doctrine: In labor-only contracting, the principal is deemed the direct employer, and the workers may exercise self-organization rights in the appropriate unit.
