records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Aggravating Circumstances — Chief Executive and Nighttime
records.Essay Question: During a concert at nighttime held in the Cultural Center of the Philippines, Chito physically assaulted another attendee, Butch. Chito slapped Butch several times in front of the President of the Philippines, who was also present. Are there any modifying circumstances affecting the criminal liability of Chito? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The offense is aggravated because it was committed in the presence of the Chief Executive; nighttime is not appreciable on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 14(5) of the Revised Penal Code lists commission of a crime in the presence of the Chief Executive as an aggravating circumstance. Article 14(6) treats nighttime as aggravating only when it facilitates the offense. People v. Abrazaldo explains that nighttime, by itself, is not aggravating and must have been purposely sought or used to facilitate the crime.

Application: Chito repeatedly slapped Butch in front of the President of the Philippines, satisfying the circumstance identified in Article 14(5). The concert’s occurrence at night, without proof that Chito sought or exploited darkness, does not establish nocturnity.

Conclusion: Presence of the Chief Executive aggravates the offense, but nighttime does not.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 14(5) and (6); People v. Abrazaldo, G.R. No. 124392, February 7, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/47695
records.Controlling Doctrine: Commission of a crime in the known presence of the Chief Executive is aggravating; nighttime is not aggravating unless deliberately sought or used to facilitate the crime or ensure impunity.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question: Pido, a private contractor, was convicted of Plunder in conspiracy with certain government officials. He was sentenced by the Sandiganbayan to serve the penalty of reclusion perpetua. Years later, his childhood friend, Benjamin, was appointed as Secretary of Justice and was able to convince the President to grant Pido a presidential pardon. Both the judgment of conviction and the presidential pardon were silent as to accessory penalties. Now a free man, Pido decided to give back to the community by running for public office as Mayor of his hometown in Bulacan. The incumbent Mayor sought your advice if he can challenge the candidacy of Pido. On what ground/s can the incumbent Mayor challenge the candidacy of Pido? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The candidacy may be challenged because Pido remains perpetually disqualified from public office.

Legal Basis: Articles 36, 41, and 73 of the Revised Penal Code provide that reclusion perpetua carries perpetual absolute disqualification, that accessory penalties are deemed imposed with the principal penalty, and that a pardon does not restore the right to hold public office unless the pardon expressly does so. Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections recognizes that the wording of the pardon controls whether political rights were expressly restored.

Application: Pido’s judgment need not separately state the accessory penalty because it follows reclusion perpetua by operation of law. His pardon was silent: it neither expressly remitted perpetual absolute disqualification nor restored his right to hold public office.

Conclusion: The incumbent mayor may challenge Pido’s candidacy on the ground of continuing perpetual absolute disqualification and non-restoration of the right to hold public office.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 36, 41, and 73; Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 206666, January 21, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/58837
records.Controlling Doctrine: An accessory disqualification follows the principal penalty by operation of law and survives a pardon unless the pardon expressly remits the disqualification or restores the right to hold public office.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question: Samuel, a Filipino citizen of Chinese descent, assisted the Chinese Government in surveying and determining the safest and most secure shores in the Philippines. He thought he was helping the Philippines in this endeavor since the geodetic maps he prepared would allegedly be transmitted to the Philippines for future use. Before the survey was completed, Chinese military vessels entered the Philippines’ Scarborough shores, set up a station secured by two warships, and populated two islets which the Chinese Government proclaimed as their own, all with the use of the geodetic maps. Samuel was then charged with Treason by the Philippine Government. The following testified against Samuel: 1) his helper, Therese, who saw Samuel in numerous meetings with the Chinese Government, though she did not understand their conversations since she does not know Chinese; and 2) his gardener, Rolando, who knows Chinese but has bad eyesight. Rolando was present in all these meetings and had a glimpse of the finished geodetic maps signed by Samuel. Is Samuel liable for Treason? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Samuel is not liable for treason on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 114 of the Revised Penal Code makes treason a wartime offense and requires either two witnesses to the same overt act or a confession in open court. Estrada v. Sandiganbayan describes treason and conspiracy to commit treason as offenses committed in time of war. Adherence also requires an intent to betray and must be accompanied by aid or comfort to an enemy.

Application: The facts do not establish a state of war between the Philippines and China. Samuel also believed the maps would benefit the Philippine Government, negating an intent to betray. Finally, Therese and Rolando did not both competently perceive the same overt act of giving the maps to an enemy.

Conclusion: The wartime, adherence, and two-witness requirements are not established; Samuel cannot be convicted of treason.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 114; Estrada v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 148965, February 26, 2002: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50350
records.Controlling Doctrine: Treason requires a wartime enemy, intent to adhere to that enemy coupled with aid or comfort, and proof by two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question: Rita asked Belen, a 14-year-old girl, to meet with her at DuoMart Supermarket for an errand. Upon meeting at the supermarket, however, Rita brought Belen to the nearby hotel and met Elmer. Rita left the other two in the room, where Elmer had carnal knowledge of Belen. When Rita returned, Elmer paid her ₱2,200, of which ₱700 was then given to Belen. Rita warned Belen not to tell anyone about what happened. Before they could all leave the hotel room, the police barged in and arrested Elmer and Rita. During the investigation, Rita argued that she did not force Belen to have sex with Elmer for a fee. Belen herself admitted that she consented to have sexual intercourse with Elmer. What crime, if any, is Rita liable for? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Rita is liable for qualified trafficking in persons involving a child.

Legal Basis: Sections 3, 4, and 6 of Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, punish recruiting, transporting, providing, or obtaining a person for prostitution or sexual exploitation and qualify the offense when the trafficked person is a child. People v. Leocadio holds that a child’s recruitment or transport for exploitation is trafficking even without proof of coercive means, and consent does not negate the offense.

Application: Rita deceived 14-year-old Belen about an errand, transported her to a hotel, provided her to Elmer for paid sexual intercourse, accepted payment, and demanded secrecy. Belen’s minority qualifies the trafficking, and her purported consent is immaterial.

Conclusion: Rita is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, Sections 3, 4, and 6; People v. Leocadio, G.R. No. 237697, July 15, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66293
records.Controlling Doctrine: Recruiting, transporting, providing, or obtaining a child for prostitution or sexual exploitation constitutes qualified trafficking; the child’s consent and the absence of coercive means do not defeat liability.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question: Jon and Pilar were in a dating relationship for a year but due to the abusive behavior of Jon, Pilar broke up with him. Jon pursued Pilar but she refused to reconcile with him. He then uploaded to his social media account the video of their sexual congress, as well as the nude pictures of Pilar, all of which he had recorded on his cellphone without the knowledge of the latter. Distraught, Pilar filed a complaint with the Office of the Prosecutor and submitted in evidence the video and pictures that Jon posted on social media. What offense, if any, did Jon commit? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Jon may be held liable for psychological violence under Republic Act No. 9262 and for violations of Republic Act No. 9995.

Legal Basis: Section 5(i) of Republic Act No. 9262 punishes conduct that causes mental or emotional anguish, public ridicule, or humiliation to a woman with whom the offender has or had a dating relationship. Acharon v. People explains that the prohibited act, the resulting anguish, and the statutory mental element must be proved. Sections 4(a) and 4(d) of Republic Act No. 9995 separately prohibit secretly recording a sexual act or private area where privacy is reasonably expected and publishing that material online. XXX261049 v. People identifies the elements of unauthorized recording under Section 4(a).

Application: Jon secretly recorded Pilar during sexual activity, then uploaded the intimate material after she refused reconciliation. The recording and publication satisfy the conduct prohibited by Republic Act No. 9995. The retaliatory disclosure to humiliate a former dating partner, together with Pilar’s distress, supports psychological violence under Republic Act No. 9262.

Conclusion: Jon may be prosecuted for the applicable acts of photo and video voyeurism and for psychological violence, subject to proof of each offense’s distinct elements.

No. 261049, June 26, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69510
records.Controlling Doctrine: Secretly recording and publishing intimate material may create separate liability under the Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act; retaliatory publication that causes a former dating partner mental or emotional anguish may also constitute psychological violence when its distinct elements are proved.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question: Soccoro owns and leases an apartment building where Rami is one of the tenants under a two-year lease. The first year went by with no issue as Rami paid his rent on time, if not earlier. However, when he lost his job after the pandemic, Rami failed to pay his rent beginning the third month of the second year of the lease. Soccoro repeatedly demanded payment from him but to no avail. Thus, she filed a case for ejectment against Rami. When Rami received the summons, he locked himself in the apartment unit. This infuriated Soccoro so much so that she padlocked the apartment unit and cut off its utilities when Rami momentarily left to go to the supermarket. What crime, if any, did Soccoro commit? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Socorro committed unjust vexation.

Legal Basis: Article 287 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended, covers conduct that unjustifiably annoys, irritates, torments, or disturbs another when no more specific offense applies. Maderazo v. People holds that a lessor who takes the law into his own hands by padlocking leased premises may commit unjust vexation. Alejandro v. Bernas further explains that padlocking premises and cutting utilities without violence, threats, or intimidation does not establish grave coercion but may establish unjust vexation.

Application: Socorro had already invoked the lawful ejectment process but nevertheless excluded Rami from his dwelling and disconnected utilities without a court order. The acts foreseeably annoyed and disturbed Rami, while the facts do not show violence, threats, or intimidation required for grave coercion.

Conclusion: Socorro is liable for unjust vexation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 287, as amended; Maderazo v. People, G.R. No. 165065, September 26, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43100; Alejandro v. Bernas, G.R. No. 179243, September 7, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27939
records.Controlling Doctrine: A lessor who bypasses pending ejectment proceedings by padlocking leased premises and cutting utilities may commit unjust vexation; without violence, threats, or intimidation, grave coercion is not established.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Maderazo v. People; Alejandro v. Bernas

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Legislative Inquiries — Contempt and Due Process
records.Essay Question: The Senate conducted investigations on how to strengthen the efforts of the government against fugitives from justice after prominent personalities covertly left the country to escape prosecution. The Senate invited Winston as a resource person. Winston is a notorious drug dealer who managed to avoid his warrants of arrest and hold departure orders. At the hearing, the Senators asked Winston about the modus operandi and the names of immigration officers who helped him escape. Yet, Winston responded: "I will leave it to the Senate to find out the information about these immigration officers." Dissatisfied, the Senators immediately cited Winston in contempt and ordered his detention until he answers the question. Did the Senate lawfully cite Winston in contempt? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The immediate contempt citation was unlawful.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 21 of the 1987 Constitution requires Congress to respect the rights of persons appearing in legislative inquiries. Ong v. Senate recognizes that a witness must be given a meaningful opportunity to explain before contempt is imposed.

Application: Winston was cited in contempt immediately after an unresponsive answer. The Senate did not first allow him to explain or otherwise accord the process required before detention.

Conclusion: The contempt citation and detention violated due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 21; Ong v. Senate, G.R. No. 257401, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69108
records.Controlling Doctrine: Congress has inherent contempt power in aid of legislation, but it must respect the witness’s rights and afford an opportunity to be heard before punitive detention.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Rocco, a lawyer, filed a petition for mandamus to compel the President of the Philippines to defend the West Philippine Sea against Chinese invasion. Rocco alleged that the President has a ministerial duty to protect the national territory. Rocco likewise asked the President to bring the territorial dispute before the United Nations Security Council after diplomatic protests proved futile. Will the petition for mandamus prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Mandamus will not lie.

Legal Basis: Mandamus compels only a clear ministerial duty, not an act involving judgment or discretion. Esmero v. Duterte treats decisions concerning the West Philippine Sea and recourse through foreign relations as matters entrusted to executive discretion.

Application: The choice of military, diplomatic, or multilateral measures requires policy judgment by the President as chief architect of foreign policy. Rocco has no clear legal right to one particular course.

Conclusion: The Court cannot compel the requested foreign-affairs actions by mandamus.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rule 65, Rules of Court; 1987 Constitution, Article VII; Esmero v. Duterte, G.R. No. 256288, July 29, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67553
records.Controlling Doctrine: Mandamus reaches only ministerial duties; courts cannot dictate discretionary presidential choices in foreign relations and national defense.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Omar, an Iranian national, was admitted in the Philippines as a refugee. After more than 10 years in the Philippines, Omar filed a petition for naturalization as a Filipino citizen. The trial court found that Omar possessed all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications to become a Filipino citizen. However, the Office of the Solicitor General opposed the petition because the laws of Iran do not grant reciprocal rights to Filipinos to become naturalized citizens. Will the lack of the reciprocity requirement bar Omar’s application for naturalization? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Reciprocity does not bar the petition of a recognized refugee.

Legal Basis: The 1951 Refugee Convention and the Rule on Facilitated Naturalization of Refugees and Stateless Persons remove reciprocity as an obstacle for qualified refugees. Republic v. Karbasi applied the refugee framework in naturalization.

Application: Omar was admitted as a refugee and was found qualified. Requiring protection from, or reciprocity by, the country from which he fled would defeat the protective rule.

Conclusion: Lack of Iranian reciprocity does not bar Omar’s naturalization.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Commonwealth Act No. 473; 1951 Refugee Convention, Article 34; A.M. No. 21-07-22-SC, Section 5(a); Republic v. Karbasi, G.R. No. 210412, July 29, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60816
records.Controlling Doctrine: A recognized refugee who otherwise qualifies may use facilitated naturalization without satisfying the ordinary reciprocity disqualification.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Andrew, a long-time advocate of women’s rights, is a bona fide member of the BINI-bini Party registered with the Commission on Elections under the party-list system. BINI-bini Party seeks to represent the women sector in the House of Representatives. In the 2022 elections, BINI-bini Party secured one seat, and its first nominee, Andrew, took his oath of office and started to serve his term as a Member of the House of Representatives. However, an electoral protest was filed against Andrew on the ground that he is not qualified to represent the women sector because he is a male. Is Andrew qualified to represent BINI-bini Party in the House of Representatives? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Andrew may qualify as nominee.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 7941 governs party-list nominees. Atong Paglaum v. COMELEC holds that a nominee of a sectoral party must either belong to the represented sector or possess a track record of advocacy for it.

Application: Andrew is a bona fide party member and a long-time advocate of women’s rights. His sex alone does not defeat the advocacy-based qualification.

Conclusion: Andrew is qualified on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7941, Section 9; Atong Paglaum, Inc. v. COMELEC, G.R. Nos. 203766 et al., April 2, 2013: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/55861
records.Controlling Doctrine: A sectoral-party nominee need not personally belong to the represented sector when the nominee has the required bona fide advocacy and party membership.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Fidel, a government official, was charged with and convicted of three separate crimes: (1) receiving a gift in connection with government contracts where he intervened in his official capacity under Section 3(b) of Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act; (2) acceptance of gift in connection with transactions affected by the functions of his office under Section 7(d) of Republic Act No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees; and (3) direct bribery under Article 210 of the Revised Penal Code. On appeal, Fidel invoked a violation of his right against double jeopardy when the trial court convicted him of three separate crimes. Is Fidel’s contention that his right against double jeopardy was violated correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The three convictions do not, by themselves, violate double jeopardy.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 of the Constitution and Rule 117, Section 7 apply the identity-of-offenses test. Merencillo v. People recognizes that prosecution under different laws is permissible when each offense requires proof of an element the others do not.

Application: The anti-graft offense, the ethical-standards offense, and direct bribery contain distinct statutory elements concerning the transaction, official intervention, and corrupt agreement. None is necessarily identical to or included in every other offense.

Conclusion: Separate convictions for the distinct offenses do not place Fidel twice in jeopardy for the same offense.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 21; Rule 117, Section 7; Merencillo v. People, G.R. Nos. 142369-70, April 13, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43394
records.Controlling Doctrine: Double jeopardy bars a second prosecution for the same or an included offense, not cumulative liability for legally distinct offenses with different elements.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Privacy — Public Officials and Matters of Public Interest
records.Essay Question: Politico Film Productions (PFP) conceptualized a mockumentary called “Covidubidapdap” which will detail the poor government response during the pandemic. The Department of Health (DOH) Secretary was scared that he would be portrayed as a lazy and incompetent public officer. Thus, the DOH Secretary warned PFP that he would not approve the use or exhibition of his name or image in the film. Nevertheless, PFP began the production of the mockumentary and used the name and image of the DOH Secretary. Aggrieved, the DOH Secretary applied for injunction against PFP invoking his right to privacy. Is there a violation of the DOH Secretary’s right to privacy? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III protects privacy, but public officials have a reduced expectation concerning official conduct and matters of legitimate public concern. Labargan v. People discusses the diminished privacy expectations of public figures in matters connected with public life.

Application: The work concerns the government’s pandemic response and the Secretary’s public performance, not an unrelated intimate matter. Use of his public identity in commentary on official conduct is protected expression absent additional unlawful facts.

Conclusion: The Secretary cannot enjoin the production solely on the asserted privacy claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 3 and 4; Labargan v. People, G.R. No. 246824, June 19, 2024: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69827
records.Controlling Doctrine: A public official cannot ordinarily invoke privacy to suppress discussion of official conduct and legitimate public concern.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: The members of the Barangay Council wanted to make the yuletide celebrations of their constituents more festive. Accordingly, the Barangay Council adopted a resolution authorizing the solicitation of funds from private individuals to build a seven-meter tall statue of “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” in the plaza in front of the basilica. The residents from other barangays questioned the resolution for alleged violation of Section 5, Article III of the 1987 Constitution which states that “[n]o law shall be made respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” Is the barangay resolution invalid for violation of the non-establishment of religion clause? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The resolution is not invalid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 5 bars establishment of religion. Peralta v. Philippine Postal Corporation applies the purpose, primary effect, and excessive-entanglement analysis.

Application: A Rudolph display has a secular holiday purpose; it neither advances nor inhibits a faith, and the facts show no continuing governmental entanglement with the basilica. Its location alone does not convert the display into religious establishment.

Conclusion: The resolution does not violate the non-establishment clause.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 5; Peralta v. Philippine Postal Corporation, G.R. No. 223395, December 4, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64851
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government act survives establishment-clause review when it has a secular purpose, does not principally advance or inhibit religion, and avoids excessive entanglement.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Under the 2020 Rules of the Senate Electoral Tribunal, any election protest against a Member of the Senate shall be filed “within thirty (30) days after assumption office of the protestee.” Subsequently, the Senate promulgated its Internal Rules of Proceedings which shortened the period of filing election protests “within fifteen (15) days” from assumption of office of the protestee. Is the Senate Internal Rules of Proceedings relative to election protest constitutional? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Senate cannot alter the SET’s protest rules.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 17 makes the SET the sole judge of contests involving senators. Fernandez v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal confirms the constitutional autonomy of an Electoral Tribunal from the legislative chamber.

Application: The protest deadline concerns the SET’s adjudicatory procedure. The Senate, as a separate body, cannot shorten a period fixed by the tribunal.

Conclusion: The conflicting Senate rule is unconstitutional.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 17; Fernandez v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, G.R. No. 187478, December 21, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53223
records.Controlling Doctrine: Each Electoral Tribunal is an independent constitutional body and the sole judge of election contests involving members of its chamber.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Fernandez v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: The Local Government Code allocated shares in revenue collections to local government units (LGUs) in the following manner: 23% for the provinces, 23% for the Cities, 34% for the Municipalities, and 20% for the Barangays. In 2023, the proposed General Appropriations Act (GAA) provided a different distribution scheme of revenue collections to LGUs, to wit: 25% for the provinces, 25% for the Cities, 35% for the Municipalities, and 15% for the Barangays. Congressman Macky assailed the constitutionality of this item in the proposed GAA. The House of Representatives Budget Committee countered that it is within the power of Congress to enact laws to increase or decrease the just share of the LGUs in the revenues. Is the new distribution scheme in the proposed GAA lawful? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A general appropriations act cannot amend the Local Government Code through an unrelated rider.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 25(2) limits provisions in a GAA to matters specifically related to an appropriation. Araullo v. Aquino explains the constitutional limits on appropriations and inappropriate provisions.

Application: Changing the statutory allocation formula is substantive general legislation. It is not merely a condition on a particular appropriation and should be enacted through an amendatory law.

Conclusion: The proposed distribution provision is an unconstitutional rider.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 25(2); Araullo v. Aquino III, G.R. No. 209287, July 1, 2014: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/57044
records.Controlling Doctrine: A GAA provision must relate specifically to a particular appropriation; substantive amendments to permanent law are prohibited riders.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Qualified Political Agency — Ex Officio Board Members
records.Essay Question: MVL, a government-owned corporation, has three Cabinet Secretaries as ex-officio members of its Board of Directors. In 2024, the MVL Board of Directors resolved to grant additional benefits to qualified corporate officers and employees. The Commission on Audit (COA) disallowed the grant of benefits because there was no prior approval of the President. However, the MVL Board of Directors invoked the alter ego principle and argued that the President deemed approved the benefits when the three Cabinet Secretaries, as ex-officio board members, voted in favor of the resolution. Is the COA correct in disallowing the grant of benefits? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. COA was correct.

Legal Basis: The qualified-political-agency doctrine applies to department acts performed as presidential alter egos, not automatically to separate corporate-board acts. National Power Corporation Board of Directors v. COA rejects the attribution of ex officio board votes to the President.

Application: The Cabinet Secretaries voted as MVL Board members by virtue of office. Their votes were corporate acts and did not substitute for the distinct presidential approval required by law.

Conclusion: The benefits lacked the required approval and were properly disallowed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: National Power Corporation Board of Directors v. Commission on Audit, G.R. No. 218052, January 26, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67069
records.Controlling Doctrine: A Cabinet secretary serving ex officio on a GOCC board does not act as the President’s alter ego for every corporate-board decision.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: National Power Corporation Board of Directors v. Commission on Audit

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Kenneth had a romantic relationship with Mabel, a 14-year-old minor. Kenneth and Mabel constantly exchanged pictures through online messaging applications. One day, Kenneth rented a laptop in a computer shop and had an online chat and videocall with Mabel. Kenneth left the shop but forgot to logout his social media account. The next customer read the sensual conversations between Kenneth and Mabel as well as their nude videos and photos. The customer reported the matter to the police. Accordingly, Kenneth was charged with violation of Republic Act No. 11930 or the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials. At the trial, Kenneth objected to the admissibility of the pictures and videos as evidence for having been obtained against his right to privacy. Are the pictures and videos admissible in evidence to prosecute Kenneth of the criminal offense? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The constitutional exclusionary rule does not apply to this private discovery.

Legal Basis: The Bill of Rights restricts governmental action. Cadajas v. People holds that evidence obtained by a private person, without police participation, is not excluded under the constitutional search-and-privacy guarantees.

Application: The next customer, not a police officer or state agent, encountered the open account and reported the material. The facts show no government instigation in obtaining it.

Conclusion: Kenneth’s constitutional objection fails, and the material is admissible subject to ordinary evidentiary rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Cadajas v. People, G.R. No. 247348, November 16, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68092
records.Controlling Doctrine: The constitutional exclusionary rule generally applies to state action, not evidence independently obtained by a private individual.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: The sovereign Republic of Handskaland, represented by Ambassador Hansen, entered into a five-year contract with Hardee Services Corporation (HSC) for the maintenance and repair of the electrical facilities of its embassy in the Philippines. Ambassador Hansen pre-terminated the agreement after discovering HSC’s faulty electrical works. Aggrieved, HSC filed against the Republic of Handskaland and Ambassador Hansen a complaint for damages. HSC argued that the Republic of Handskaland and Ambassador Hansen waived their immunity from suit when they entered into a contract. Did the Republic of Handskaland and Ambassador Hansen waive their immunity from suit? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The contract did not amount to an implied waiver.

Legal Basis: Under restrictive sovereign immunity, consent may be inferred from a commercial act but not from an act performed in sovereign capacity. Republic of Indonesia v. Vinzon treated contracts necessary to embassy operations as governmental in character.

Application: Maintaining embassy electrical facilities is essential to diplomatic functions. The Republic and Ambassador acted in a sovereign, not ordinary commercial, capacity.

Conclusion: They retained immunity from suit absent express consent.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Generally accepted principles of international law; Republic of Indonesia v. Vinzon, G.R. No. 154705, June 26, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48858
records.Controlling Doctrine: A foreign state does not impliedly waive immunity by entering a contract that is governmental and necessary to embassy operations.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Acquittal — Grave Abuse and Double Jeopardy
records.Essay Question:
The Regional Trial Court (RTC) convicted Luciano of illegal sale of dangerous drugs. Luciano sought reconsideration. The RTC reversed its judgment of conviction and acquitted Luciano of the crime, thus:

ORDER

For resolution is the accused’s motion for reconsideration assailing his conviction for the offense of illegal sale of dangerous drugs. The prosecution did not file any comment. Hence, the motion is now submitted for resolution.

After a perusal of the motion for reconsideration, the Court finds merit that the prosecution miserably failed to overcome the accused’s presumption of innocence.

For this reason, the motion for reconsideration is GRANTED. The accused is ACQUITTED in the criminal case for illegal sale of dangerous drugs.

SO ORDERED.

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) questioned the order of acquittal before the Court of Appeals. The OSG explained that the RTC failed to comply with the constitutional requirements in rendering a valid judgment amounting to grave abuse of discretion. On the other hand, Luciano invoked his right against double jeopardy and argued that the order of acquittal is already final and not subject to review. Is the RTC guilty of grave abuse of discretion when it rendered the order of acquittal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The conclusory order was constitutionally defective and may be annulled through certiorari.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 14 requires a decision to state clearly and distinctly its factual and legal bases. Austria v. AAA holds that an acquittal issued with grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction is void and does not trigger double-jeopardy protection.

Application: The RTC reversed a conviction without identifying the evidence, factual findings, or governing law. That failure prevented meaningful review and exceeded constitutional adjudicatory bounds.

Conclusion: The RTC gravely abused its discretion; certiorari may proceed without violating double jeopardy.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 14; Austria v. AAA, G.R. No. 205275, June 28, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68436
records.Controlling Doctrine: A void acquittal rendered with grave abuse of discretion is not an acquittal in the constitutional sense and may be challenged by Rule 65 certiorari.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Academic Freedom and Taking — Mandatory Tuition Waiver
records.Essay Question: As an incentive for Filipino nurses to remain or be employed in the Philippines, the “Ang Nars Incentives Act of 2023” was approved by the President. The law allows children of any nurse to be enrolled in any private tertiary institution without need of taking any entrance examination provided the child maintains the required passing average grade each year. A 70% tuition waiver for each child shall be extended by the institution and 50% of the tuition waiver may be creditable to any national taxes owed by the institution to the government. Is the law constitutional? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The law is unconstitutional.

Legal Basis: Article XIV, Section 5(2) protects institutional academic freedom, including determining who may be admitted. Article III, Section 9 also requires just compensation when private property is taken for public use. OSG v. Ayala distinguishes regulation from a compensable taking.

Application: Compelling schools to admit applicants without their admissions process invades academic freedom. Requiring a partly uncompensated tuition waiver also transfers the public program’s cost to private institutions.

Conclusion: The law violates institutional academic freedom and, to the extent of the uncompensated mandate, the just-compensation clause.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XIV, Section 5(2), and Article III, Section 9; Office of the Solicitor General v. Ayala Land, Inc., G.R. No. 177056, September 18, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49990
records.Controlling Doctrine: The State may regulate education, but it cannot dictate admissions in derogation of institutional academic freedom or appropriate private value for public use without compensation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Office of the Solicitor General v. Ayala Land, Inc.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Legislative Vacancy — Mandamus and Special Elections
records.Essay Question: Sulu Second District Representative Alfonso died during the second year of his term. House Speaker Rodil then designated Sulu First District Representative Midas as the legislative caretaker for the remaining period of the term of Alfonso. Upon the prodding of majority of the constituents of the Sulu Second District who are invoking their right to representation, the members of the party of Alfonso filed a petition before the Supreme Court for the issuance of a writ of mandamus to compel Rodil to call for a special election in their district. Will the petition prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The petition will not prosper.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 9 provides that a special election “may” be called in the manner provided by law. Mandamus compels a ministerial duty, not the exercise of legislative discretion. Marcos v. Robredo explains the ordinarily permissive effect of “may.”

Application: No law imposes on Speaker Rodil a clear, personal, ministerial duty to call the election. Calling and providing for a special election requires discretionary legislative action.

Conclusion: Mandamus cannot issue.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 9; Marcos v. Robredo, P.E.T. Case No. 005, October 15, 2019, as discussed in G.R. No. 244587: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68832
records.Controlling Doctrine: Mandamus cannot compel an act that the Constitution or statute leaves discretionary, particularly legislative action to provide for a special election.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Presidential Succession — Reelection and Four-Year Bar
records.Essay Question: In the 2022 elections, the formidable tandem of Priscilla and Teodoro ran for and won as President and Vice-President, respectively, of the Republic of the Philippines. On her 15th month in office, President Priscilla suddenly resigned due to health reasons, paving the way for Vice-President Teodoro to assume office as President. President Teodoro then nominated incumbent Senator Angel, who was President of the Philippines from 2010 to 2016, to take his place as Vice-President. Voting separately and by the vote of a majority of all the members of both Houses of the Congress, Senator Angel was confirmed, and henceforth assumed office as the Vice-President. In the coming 2028 elections, may both President Teodoro and Vice-President Angel legally run for President of the Philippines? Explain your answer briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Neither may run.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 4 bars any President from reelection and bars a successor who served as President for more than four years from later election to the same office. Pormento v. Estrada interprets the constitutional ban on presidential reelection.

Application: Teodoro will have served more than four years of Priscilla’s term. Angel was previously elected President, so another election would be reelection prohibited by the text.

Conclusion: Both are constitutionally disqualified.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 4; Pormento v. Estrada, G.R. No. 191988, August 31, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54308
records.Controlling Doctrine: A person elected President is barred from any reelection, while a successor who serves more than four years is barred from election to the same office.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Section 1, Article IV on Bangsamoro Parliament Electoral Tribunal of the Proposed Electoral Code of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region for Muslim Mindanao states: “Section 1. Creation and Jurisdiction. – The Bangsamoro

Parliament shall have an Electoral Tribunal which shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the members of the Parliament.” Is the proposed provision constitutional? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed tribunal would displace jurisdiction assigned by the Constitution to COMELEC.

Legal Basis: Article IX-C, Section 2(2) gives COMELEC exclusive original jurisdiction over contests involving elective regional officials. Sema v. COMELEC, as applied in later E-Library jurisprudence, confirms that autonomous arrangements remain subject to constitutional allocation of election jurisdiction.

Application: Bangsamoro parliament members are elective regional officials. A regional code cannot transfer their election contests from COMELEC to a newly created tribunal.

Conclusion: The proposed provision is unconstitutional.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article IX-C, Section 2(2); Sema v. COMELEC doctrine applied in Datu Michael Abas Kida v. Senate, G.R. No. 196271, October 18, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53925
records.Controlling Doctrine: Autonomous-region legislation cannot override COMELEC’s constitutionally exclusive original jurisdiction over contests involving elective regional officials.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Datu Michael Abas Kida v. Senate

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Hector, a government employee, asked Ignacio to take the Police Officer I Examination in his behalf. Upon investigation, the Civil Service Commission (CSC) observed that the picture of Hector and signature in the application form and seat plan were not identical with those found in his Personal Data Sheet. Thus, the CSC concluded that Hector conspired with Ignacio by allowing the latter to impersonate him and found him guilty of dishonesty, meting out the penalty of dismissal. Hector appealed his dismissal to the Court of Appeals. He argued that the CSC has been divested of its authority and jurisdiction to conduct investigations and render administrative decisions based on alleged anomalies in police entrance and promotional examinations after the effectivity of Republic Act No. 8551 or the Philippine National Police Reform and Reorganization Act. The law transferred the power to administer and conduct entrance and promotional examinations to police officers from the CSC to the National Police Commission based on the standards set by the latter. Is Hector correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The CSC retained disciplinary authority over civil-service examination fraud.

Legal Basis: Article IX-B makes the CSC the central personnel agency. San Felix v. Civil Service Commission holds that Republic Act No. 8551 did not completely divest the CSC of jurisdiction over anomalies and irregularities in civil-service examinations.

Application: Administering police examinations may be assigned to NAPOLCOM, but Hector’s dishonest impersonation remains a civil-service offense within CSC authority.

Conclusion: The CSC validly investigated and disciplined Hector.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article IX-B; Republic Act No. 8551; San Felix v. Civil Service Commission, G.R. No. 198404, October 14, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65775
records.Controlling Doctrine: Transfer of examination administration to NAPOLCOM does not eliminate the CSC’s constitutional authority to investigate and sanction civil-service examination fraud.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
For purposes of the investigation of work-related misconduct, the Presidential Management Staff (PMS), searched the office computer of its employee, Zenaida, without the consent of the latter and without a search warrant. The personal files of Zenaida stored in the computer, which were seized during the search, were eventually used by the PMS as evidence of misconduct. Zenaida was accordingly dismissed from service. Zenaida now comes to you for advice

claiming that the search was unconstitutional for being violative of her right to privacy and right against unreasonable searches and seizures. Provide your legal advice with reasons.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Her constitutional challenge is unlikely to succeed on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 prohibits unreasonable searches. Pollo v. Constantino-David applies the two-part reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test to a government workplace and permits a work-related search reasonable in inception and scope.

Application: The computer belonged to the government, the inquiry concerned work misconduct, and no facts show measures creating a recognized private sphere or an excessively broad search.

Conclusion: Zenaida had no reasonable expectation sufficient to invalidate the search on these facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Pollo v. Constantino-David, G.R. No. 181881, October 18, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/31015
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government employee’s workplace privacy claim depends on a reasonable expectation of privacy and the reasonableness of the employer’s work-related search.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Just Compensation — Delay, Inflation, and Interest
records.Essay Question: The property of Anne was expropriated by the government for public use more than ten years ago without proper expropriation proceedings and without payment of just compensation. Since then, the value of the Philippine peso has greatly depreciated, while the inflation rate has substantially increased. Anne now contends that in the interest of justice and fair play, the inflation rate and the depreciated value of the peso should be taken into consideration in the computation and payment of her long-delayed just compensation. Is Anne correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No as to valuation by inflation, but she is entitled to legal interest for delay.

Legal Basis: Just compensation is generally the property’s fair value at the time of taking. Land Bank v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association holds that inflation is not added to valuation because delay is compensated by interest.

Application: Repricing the property by later inflation would depart from the time-of-taking rule. The government must instead pay the proper principal compensation plus applicable interest for the period of delay.

Conclusion: Inflation and currency depreciation are not separate valuation components; interest supplies the delay compensation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 9; Land Bank of the Philippines v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association, G.R. No. 193987, March 13, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62903
records.Controlling Doctrine: Delayed just compensation is valued at the time of taking and made fully compensatory through legal interest, not later inflation indexing.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Land Bank of the Philippines v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Ricardo, a third-year law student, was subjected to custodial investigation for the crime of Rape. He was duly informed by the police of his right to remain silent and his right to have counsel of his choice if he could afford one, and if not, he could be provided with one. Ricardo proudly informed the arresting officer that he is perfectly aware of his rights, being a law student, and that he is voluntarily waiving them. He then proceeded to issue a written statement truthfully detailing his participation in the crime of Rape. During trial, his written statement was presented as the primary evidence of his guilt. Atty. Alexander, counsel for Ricardo, promptly and vociferously objected to the presentation and admissibility of his written statement on the ground that Ricardo executed it without assistance of counsel. Is the objection justified and tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The confession is inadmissible.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12 requires any waiver of custodial rights to be in writing and made in the presence of counsel. People v. Reyes restates that an extrajudicial confession must be voluntary, express, in writing, and made with competent independent counsel.

Application: Ricardo’s legal education did not substitute for counsel. His waiver was oral and occurred without a lawyer; the resulting statement was obtained in violation of constitutional requirements.

Conclusion: The objection should be sustained.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 12; People v. Reyes, G.R. No. 178300, March 17, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49004
records.Controlling Doctrine: Custodial rights may be waived only in writing and in the presence of counsel; legal knowledge does not excuse either requirement.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Maasikaso Water Company (MWC), a private concessionaire, entered into a 25-year concession agreement in 2009 with the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) for the delivery of water supply, wastewater, and sanitation services in the City of Manila. In 2019, residents of Manila filed a complaint against MWC with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources Pollution Adjudication Board for violation of the Clean Water Act (CWA). The residents alleged that the severe flooding in Manila and worsening pollution in Manila Bay had been due to the failure of MWC to provide for adequate sewage and/or septage treatment facilities, as mandated under the concession agreement. MWC countered that the primary duty to construct sewage and/or septage treatment facilities rests upon the local government unit (LGU) under Section 7 of the CWA, which states: “Each LGU shall appropriate

the necessary land, including rights-of-way/road access to the land for construction of the sewage and/or septage treatment facilities”. MWC thus maintained that it must be absolved from any form of liability considering that the City of Manila clearly failed to comply with Section 7 of the CWA. Is MWC correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The local government’s duty is not a condition precedent to the concessionaire’s own statutory obligations.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 9275 requires water concessionaires to provide adequate sewerage and septage systems. Maynilad Water Services v. DENR applies the public-trust doctrine and rejects the argument that local-government nonperformance under Section 7 excuses the concessionaires.

Application: MWC remains bound by its concession and the Clean Water Act. Manila’s alleged failure does not erase MWC’s independent duty to protect water resources and public health.

Conclusion: MWC cannot obtain absolution on that ground.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9275; Maynilad Water Services, Inc. v. Secretary of DENR, G.R. Nos. 202897, 206823, and 207969, August 6, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65416
records.Controlling Doctrine: A water concessionaire’s Clean Water Act obligations are independent; an LGU’s land-access duty is not a condition precedent that excuses noncompliance.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Maynilad Water Services, Inc. v. Secretary of DENR

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Lorenzo was re-elected as Mayor of Roxas City for his third consecutive term in the 2022 local elections. In 2023, Lorenzo was administratively charged before the Office of the Ombudsman (OMB) for acts committed during his second term. Lorenzo moved to dismiss the complaint before the OMB on the ground that his re-election to a third term effectively exonerated him from the administrative charge pursuant to the condonation doctrine. Is Lorenzo correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Reelection no longer condones prior-term administrative misconduct.

Legal Basis: Article XI, Section 1 declares public office a public trust. Carpio-Morales v. Court of Appeals abandoned the condonation doctrine for lacking constitutional or statutory basis, prospectively from finality of that ruling.

Application: Lorenzo’s alleged acts and reelection occurred years after the doctrine’s abandonment became effective. His new mandate did not erase administrative liability.

Conclusion: The OMB case may proceed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 1; Carpio-Morales v. Court of Appeals, G.R. Nos. 217126-27, November 10, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61377
records.Controlling Doctrine: Reelection is not a mode of extinguishing administrative liability; the condonation doctrine has been prospectively abandoned.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question: Filed before the House of Representatives were Articles of Impeachment against Chief Justice Urduja for corruption, betrayal of public trust, and culpable violation of the Constitution. After a heavily publicized trial, the Senate, sitting as Impeachment Court, rendered a judgment removing Urduja from her position, with the additional penalty of disqualification to hold any other public office. However, during the pendency of the criminal, administrative, and civil cases subsequently filed against her, Urduja died due to health complications. The heirs of Urduja filed a petition before the Supreme Court for the release of her accrued retirement benefits and other gratuities as a member of the Judiciary. Senate President Francisco opined that the petition of the heirs of Urduja should be denied in view of her removal by impeachment. Is Francisco correct? Decide with reasons.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Impeachment alone does not forfeit accrued retirement benefits.

Legal Basis: Article XI, Section 3(7) limits impeachment judgment to removal and disqualification, without adjudicating separate criminal, civil, or administrative liability. In re Letter of Mrs. Corona holds that benefits are not forfeited merely by impeachment where no separate liability and forfeiture were finally established before death.

Application: Urduja’s other cases remained pending when she died. The impeachment judgment did not itself impose forfeiture of retirement benefits.

Conclusion: Her heirs may receive the accrued benefits, subject to any independently established lawful deductions.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 3(7); In re Letter of Mrs. Ma. Cristina Roco Corona, A.M. No. 20-07-10-SC, January 12, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66776
records.Controlling Doctrine: Impeachment determines removal and disqualification only; forfeiture or other liability requires a separate final legal determination.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: In re Letter of Mrs. Ma. Cristina Roco Corona

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Congress enacted a law providing for mandatory biometrics voter registration. The Commission on Elections (COMELEC) then issued resolutions implementing said law and further providing that registered voters who fail to submit their biometrics for validation by the last day of filing of application for registration for the May 2025 elections shall be deactivated. Consequently, those who fail to be validated, those without biometrics data, or those who have incomplete biometrics data will be deactivated and shall not be allowed to vote. A petition for certiorari and prohibition was filed before the Supreme Court assailing the constitutionality of the law and the COMELEC resolutions, on the ground that biometrics validation constitutes an additional and substantial qualification not contemplated by the 1987 Constitution, because non-

compliance therewith results in voter deactivation. Will the petition prosper? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Biometrics validation regulates registration; it is not a prohibited substantive qualification.

Legal Basis: Article V, Section 1 allows statutory regulation of suffrage while forbidding literacy, property, or other substantive requirements. Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC sustained mandatory biometrics as a reasonable registration measure.

Application: The requirement verifies voter identity and cleans the registry. It does not add a literacy, property, or comparable qualification to citizenship, age, residence, or voter eligibility.

Conclusion: The constitutional challenge fails.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article V, Section 1; Republic Act No. 10367; Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 221318, December 16, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61471
records.Controlling Doctrine: Biometric validation is a permissible registration mechanism, not an additional substantive qualification for suffrage.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Search and Seizure — Arrest for Ordinance Violation
records.Essay Question:
A police officer saw Harvey urinating in public. A local ordinance imposes a Php 500.00 fine for urinating in public. The police officer shouted at Harvey: “That is against the law!” Harvey sarcastically answered: “No, this is against the wall!” Then and there, the police officer arrested him and brought him to the police station. At the police station, Harvey was frisked and was found in possession of an unlicensed .38 caliber revolver loaded with five live ammunition. He was subsequently charged with Qualified Illegal Possession of Firearms. When the prosecution offered in evidence the unlicensed firearm and ammunition, the defense objected on the ground that the pieces of evidence are products of an illegal search and seizure. The prosecution contended that the pieces of evidence were lawfully seized after a valid warrantless search incidental to a lawful arrest.

Was the search and seizure valid? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The search was not incident to a lawful arrest.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 protects against unreasonable searches. Rule 113, Section 5 permits warrantless arrest only in specified circumstances. Luz v. People holds that when an offense is punishable only by a fine and the arrest is unauthorized, a later search cannot be justified as incident to that arrest.

Application: The ordinance imposed only a fine, and the facts do not show another lawful ground for custodial arrest. The station frisk therefore rested on an invalid arrest.

Conclusion: The firearm and ammunition were illegally seized and are inadmissible under the exclusionary rule.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Rule 113, Section 5; Luz v. People, G.R. No. 197788, February 29, 2012: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33179
records.Controlling Doctrine: A search incident to arrest is valid only if the arrest itself is lawful; an unauthorized arrest for a fine-only ordinance violation cannot support the search.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
A city ordinance was passed providing for the removal, at the owner’s expense, of: (i) all outdoor advertising materials displayed or exposed to the public in designated regulated areas such as residential zones, bridges, and along main city streets; and (ii) billboards of substandard materials, or which obstruct road signs and traffic signals. Failure to comply with said ordinance authorizes the mayor, assisted by the police, to implement the removal of the non-compliant materials. ABC Ad Agency, owner of the billboards removed by the city, filed a complaint because, considering the nature of its business, the removal of its billboards amounted to taking of private property without just compensation.

Will the complaint prosper? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The removal described is a police-power regulation, not a compensable taking.

Legal Basis: Local governments may regulate property under the general-welfare clause. Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes discusses the distinction between legitimate land-use or aesthetic regulation and eminent domain, while recognizing the regulation of structures affecting public welfare.

Application: The ordinance targets location, structural safety, and obstruction of public traffic signs. These are public-safety and thoroughfare concerns, and the owner bears the cost of curing noncompliance.

Conclusion: On the stated facts, removal does not require just compensation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Sections 16 and 458; Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes, Inc., G.R. No. 213948, April 25, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63069
records.Controlling Doctrine: Reasonable regulation or removal of unsafe and obstructive billboards under police power is not a taking requiring compensation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes, Inc.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
[This item has two questions.] As a reaction to China’s occupation of the Spratly Islands, a rally was organized by various civil society aggrupations at a vacant private lot. Before the event could even start, the police ordered the organizers not to proceed with the program because of security reasons and the fact that the group did not have a mayor’s permit. When the organizers still proceeded with the rally, the police dispersed the crowd and arrested the leaders of the group.

(a) Did the actions of the police constitute a violation of the group’s constitutional right to peacefully assemble? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A public-assembly permit was not required for a rally on private property with the owner’s consent.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 4 protects peaceful assembly. Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4 requires only the owner’s consent for an assembly on private property. Chavez v. Gonzales, discussing Bayan v. Ermita, emphasizes that government cannot impose prior restraint without a constitutionally sufficient basis.

Application: The stated justification was general “security” and absence of a mayor’s permit, although the venue was private. No specific clear and present danger or unlawful conduct appears.

Conclusion: Dispersal and arrests on those grounds violated the right of peaceful assembly.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 4; Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4; Chavez v. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, February 15, 2008: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56004
records.Controlling Doctrine: An assembly on private property requires the owner’s consent, not a mayor’s public-place permit; vague security claims do not justify prior restraint.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
[This item has two questions.] As a reaction to China’s occupation of the Spratly Islands, a rally was organized by various civil society aggrupations at a vacant private lot. Before the event could even start, the police ordered the organizers not to proceed with the program because of security reasons and the fact that the group did not have a mayor’s permit. When the organizers still proceeded with the rally, the police dispersed the crowd and arrested the leaders of the group.

(b) Would your answer be the same if the rally was held at a freedom park? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The police actions would still violate the group's constitutional right to peaceably assemble if the rally were held in a freedom park.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution protects peaceful assembly. Sections 4 and 15 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 provide that no permit is required for an assembly in a duly established freedom park. Bayan v. Ermita sustained the statute's permit framework while confirming the freedom-park exception.

Application: Because a mayor's permit is unnecessary in a freedom park, lack of such a permit cannot by itself justify stopping and dispersing the peaceful rally. The facts state no violence or other lawful ground for dispersal.

Conclusion: Yes; the police would still violate the right to peaceably assemble.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 4; Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Sections 4 and 15; Bayan v. Ermita, G.R. records.Controlling Doctrine: No permit is required for a peaceful public assembly in a duly established freedom park; lack of a mayor's permit therefore cannot, by itself, justify dispersal there.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The K-12 Law was passed with the objective to enhance the Philippine educational system by strengthening its curriculum and adding two years of high school. Parents of students in a science high school sought to have the law declared unconstitutional citing the equal protection clause of the Constitution. As well, the parents averred that the law should not apply to their children because the latter belong to a distinct class, being gifted and advanced for their age, with the capability to learn better and faster compared to other high school students.

Is the contention of the parents tenable? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed exemption lacks a classification germane to the law’s nationwide educational purpose.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 permits reasonable classification that rests on substantial distinctions, is germane to the law, applies to all members of the class, and is not limited to existing conditions. British American Tobacco v. Camacho applies this test.

Application: Attendance at a science high school does not by itself establish a distinction requiring exemption from the national K-12 structure. The program uniformly regulates students similarly situated within basic education.

Conclusion: The equal-protection challenge fails.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 1; British American Tobacco v. Camacho, G.R. No. 163583, April 15, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49123
records.Controlling Doctrine: Equal protection allows uniform education regulation unless the proposed different treatment rests on a substantial distinction germane to the law’s purpose.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
President Hidalgo, who wanted the Philippines to be part of the International Criminal Court once again, signed the Philippines' ratification of the Rome Statute. A copy of the treaty, along with the ratification, was sent to the Senate for its concurrence. Senator Dalisay filed a proposed “Resolution” for the Senate to concur with the Philippines’ ratification. The proposed “Resolution” was read three times on three separate days. Three days before the third reading, printed copies of the proposed “Resolution” in its final form were distributed to all the Senators. The Senators then unanimously approved the “Resolution”, and the Senate expressed its concurrence with the treaty’s ratification. A civil society group filed a petition before the Supreme Court questioning the validity of the Senate’s concurrence on the ground that the “Resolution” was void because only a “bill” becomes a law.

Rule on the petition. Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The petition should be dismissed.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 21 requires concurrence by at least two-thirds of all senators but does not require enactment of a statute. Bayan Muna v. Romulo distinguishes treaty-making from ordinary legislation and recognizes the President’s ratification role subject to Senate concurrence.

Application: The Senate was not legislating a new statute; it was expressing the constitutional consent required for ratification. A resolution is the appropriate vehicle for that single-chamber act.

Conclusion: The concurrence is not void merely because it was expressed through a resolution.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 21; Bayan Muna v. Romulo, G.R. No. 159618, February 1, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/52149
records.Controlling Doctrine: Senate treaty concurrence is a constitutional consent function, not ordinary bicameral lawmaking, and may be expressed by resolution.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
After Martial Law was declared over Mindanao, police officers arrested Jose Maria without any warrant while shopping for groceries at a supermarket in Mindanao. Jose Maria questioned the validity of the arrest as he had no pending case and was not committing any crime at the time of his arrest. The police officers countered that the declaration of Martial Law suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus, and as a result, they could effect warrantless arrests.

Is the contention of the police officers correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Martial law does not itself authorize warrantless arrest.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 18 states that martial law does not suspend the Constitution or automatically suspend the writ privilege. Lagman v. Medialdea confirms that the Bill of Rights remains operative. Warrantless arrest must independently satisfy Rule 113, Section 5.

Application: Jose Maria was not caught committing an offense, was not the subject of a valid hot pursuit, and was not an escaped prisoner.

Conclusion: His warrantless arrest was illegal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 18; Rule 113, Section 5; Lagman v. Medialdea, G.R. Nos. 231658 et al., July 4, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63533
records.Controlling Doctrine: A declaration of martial law does not suspend the Bill of Rights or create a free-standing power of warrantless arrest.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
A law was passed exempting the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) from the payment of filing fees in collection cases on loans granted by LBP to its borrowers. The Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) of the Supreme Court issued a Memorandum requiring all courts to continue to collect filing fees in collection cases filed by LBP, stating that only the Supreme Court can decide on exemptions from payment of filing fees. LBP assails the OCA Memorandum, arguing that the exemption found in the law is within the plenary power of Congress to enact legislation. Moreover, the law was approved by the President. Thus, LBP argues that the act of the OCA violates the principle of separation of powers.

Is LBP correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Statutory interference with filing fees and court procedure cannot override the Supreme Court’s exclusive rule-making authority.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 5(5) vests the Supreme Court with authority over pleading, practice, and procedure. GIOS-SAMAR v. Department of Transportation discusses the exclusivity and constitutional protection of judicial rule-making.

Application: Filing fees are integral to court procedure and fiscal administration. A legislative exemption cannot bind courts contrary to the Court’s rules and administrative directive.

Conclusion: The OCA may require continued collection; separation of powers supports, rather than defeats, the directive.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 5(5); GIOS-SAMAR, Inc. v. Department of Transportation and Communications, G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64970
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Supreme Court’s constitutional authority over pleading, practice, and procedure includes control over court filing-fee rules and exemptions.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: GIOS-SAMAR, Inc. v. Department of Transportation and Communications

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
During a press conference, President Acosta explained that the Executive Department can temporarily take over the operation of any privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest to address the shortage of hospital beds occasioned by the COVID-19 pandemic. She invokes Article XII, Section 17 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which provides that: “In times of national emergency, when the public interest so requires, the State may, during the emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, temporarily take over or direct the operation of any privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest.”

Is President Acosta correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not without an enabling law prescribing the takeover’s terms.

Legal Basis: Article XII, Section 17 authorizes the State, during a national emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, to take over qualifying enterprises. David v. Macapagal-Arroyo holds that presidential emergency takeover power requires congressional authorization.

Application: The President may identify an emergency, but the facts supply no statute delegating takeover authority or prescribing reasonable terms.

Conclusion: The Executive Department cannot unilaterally exercise the asserted takeover power.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XII, Section 17, and Article VI, Section 23(2); David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, G.R. Nos. 171396 et al., May 3, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41473
records.Controlling Doctrine: A presidential takeover of privately owned public utilities or businesses during an emergency requires legislative authorization and prescribed reasonable terms.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Citizenship and Candidacy — Foreign Certificate and Passport
records.Essay Question:
Lemuel was born in 1988 to a Filipino mother and an American father, as shown in his birth certificate. His parents, however, were not married to each other. Subsequently, his father petitioned for him, as a result of which Lemuel received a certificate of American citizenship and an American passport. In 2022, Lemuel filed a certificate of candidacy to run as Representative of the lone district of Batanes. Ayla, a Filipino citizen and resident of Batanes, filed a petition for disqualification with the Commission on Elections alleging that Lemuel is ineligible to run for public office in the Philippines as Lemuel is an American citizen.

Is Ayla correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts alone.

Legal Basis: Article IV, Section 1 makes those whose fathers or mothers are Filipino citizens of the Philippines. Albania v. COMELEC, applying Arnado and related dual-citizenship doctrine, distinguishes possession of foreign status documents from the acts legally required to renounce or lose Philippine citizenship.

Application: Lemuel acquired Philippine citizenship at birth through his Filipino mother. The facts show receipt, but not use, of the American passport and no effective renunciation of Philippine citizenship.

Conclusion: Ayla’s allegation does not establish ineligibility.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article IV, Section 1; Republic Act No. 9225; Albania v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 226792, June 8, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63084
records.Controlling Doctrine: A dual citizen’s foreign certificate or unused passport does not by itself prove loss or renunciation of Philippine citizenship for candidacy purposes.
