records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Academic Freedom — Removal of Library Materials
records.Essay Question:
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) directed higher education institutions to remove materials “that contain pervasive ideologies of Communist-Terrorist Groups” from their libraries. According to the CHED, the materials need to be removed because these would radicalize students against the government.

Is the CHED directive a violation of the institutions’ academic freedom? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article XIV, Section 5(2) protects academic freedom in institutions of higher learning. Miriam College Foundation v. Court of Appeals recognizes institutional autonomy in determining what may be taught and how academic objectives are pursued, subject only to valid overriding regulation.

Application: CHED’s directive compels removal based on ideology and rests only on a speculative fear of radicalization. No narrowly supported, overriding public-welfare basis is shown.

Conclusion: The blanket removal directive violates academic freedom.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XIV, Section 5(2); Miriam College Foundation, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 127930, December 15, 2000: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/36200
records.Controlling Doctrine: Institutional academic freedom includes control of educational content and resources; ideological censorship requires a constitutionally sufficient overriding justification.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The Congress passed a law prohibiting the sale and distribution of alcoholic drinks within 100 meters from religious and educational institutions. A city enacted an ordinance increasing the coverage of the prohibition to 150 meters from any religious and educational institution.

Is the city ordinance valid? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if enacted within delegated police power and otherwise reasonable.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code authorizes local governments to enact measures for general welfare. Batangas CATV, Inc. v. Court of Appeals recognizes that local regulation may supplement national law when it does not contradict or prohibit what the statute permits.

Application: The ordinance retains the national policy and imposes a stricter local buffer; it does not legalize a prohibited act or ban alcohol sales everywhere. The facts show a regulatory, geographically limited measure.

Conclusion: The ordinance is valid on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Sections 16 and 458; Batangas CATV, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 138810, September 29, 2004: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48194
records.Controlling Doctrine: An LGU may adopt a reasonable supplemental regulation stricter than national law when the measure is within delegated power and does not contradict the statute.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Pursuant to a law ordering the fixing of “just and reasonable standards, classifications, regulations, practices, or services to be furnished, observed and imposed by operators of public utility vehicles,” the Land Transportation Franchise and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) promulgated and published a regulation that “no car beyond six years shall be operated as a taxi.” Taxi operators assailed the validity of the regulation contending that procedural due process was violated because position papers were not asked of them and no notice was given to them prior to the issuance of the regulation.

Were the taxi operators denied procedural due process? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Trial-type notice and hearing were not required for this generally applicable rule.

Legal Basis: Administrative agencies acting quasi-legislatively may issue rules after compliance with statutory publication and filing requirements; individual adjudicatory hearings are ordinarily unnecessary. Sangguniang Panlungsod ng Baguio City v. Jadewell Parking Systems discusses Taxicab Operators and procedural due process in regulatory rule-making.

Application: The rule was promulgated and published for all taxi operators rather than issued to decide a contested case against particular operators. No statute requiring pre-issuance position papers is identified.

Conclusion: The operators were not denied procedural due process.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Generally applicable quasi-legislative rules require statutory publication and filing, not the individual notice and trial-type hearing required in adjudication.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Law of the Sea — Contiguous-Zone Enforcement
records.Essay Question:
A foreign commercial ship was spotted by the Philippine Coast Guard dumping garbage and toxic waste 20 nautical miles from Nasugbu, Batangas, the nearest coastline of the Philippines. The officers of the ship were arrested and charged in the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Batangas for violation of environmental laws of the Philippines. The officers of the ship filed a motion to dismiss the case on the ground that Philippine courts do not have territorial jurisdiction over the case since the vessel was sailing outside the territorial sea of the Philippines when the arrest was made.

Is the ground to dismiss correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Being outside the twelve-nautical-mile territorial sea does not end the inquiry; the vessel was within the twenty-four-nautical-mile contiguous zone.

Legal Basis: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Article 33, permits necessary control in the contiguous zone to prevent or punish infringement of specified coastal-state laws. Republic Act No. 9522 aligns Philippine maritime zones with UNCLOS. Magallona v. Ermita upholds that statutory framework.

Application: At twenty nautical miles, the ship was within the contiguous zone. Dumping toxic waste implicates coastal sanitary and environmental protection, allowing Philippine enforcement under applicable domestic law and treaty limits.

Conclusion: The motion cannot succeed solely because the ship was beyond the territorial sea.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: UNCLOS, Article 33; Republic Act No. 9522; Magallona v. Ermita, G.R. No. 187167, August 16, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29267
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Philippines may exercise treaty-authorized control in its contiguous zone; location beyond the territorial sea does not automatically defeat enforcement jurisdiction.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
[This item has two questions.] Philippine Medical Center (PMC) is a government hospital created by law to provide healthcare to the general public, especially the less fortunate. To enable PMC to perform its mandate, the national government provided the initial capital, land, buildings, and equipment to PMC. PMC’s charter also authorized it, acting through its Board of Trustees: to acquire property; to enter into contracts; to mortgage, encumber, lease, sell, convey, or dispose of its properties; and to do other acts necessary to accomplish its purposes and objectives.

Among the properties of PMC are five lands and buildings located in Quezon City. The Quezon City assessor issued notices of assessment for real property taxes (RPT) against PMC’s properties that are being leased to private concessionaires. According to the city assessor, PMC’s properties leased to private entities are subject to RPT because these properties are not being exclusively used for charitable purposes. PMC, on the other hand, claims that, as a government instrumentality imbued with corporate powers, it is exempt from RPT.

(a) Is PMC liable for the assessed RPT over the leased properties? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. PMC, as a government instrumentality, is not itself liable for the real property tax, although the taxable beneficial users may be assessed as the law permits.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code exempts Republic-owned property but withdraws the exemption when beneficial use is granted to a taxable person. Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City holds that the instrumentality retains immunity while the private beneficial user bears the tax consequence.

Application: Leasing does not convert PMC into a taxable private owner. The assessor must direct any lawful assessment concerning beneficial use to the private concessionaires rather than PMC.

Conclusion: PMC is not liable for the assessment against it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Section 234(a); Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City, G.R. No. 225409, March 11, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66268
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government instrumentality remains exempt from real property tax; when beneficial use is granted to a taxable private entity, liability attaches to that beneficial user.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Samson Manufacturing, Inc. insured its own goods with Delilah Insurance for Php 2,000,000.00. The same goods were insured by Alibaba Shipping Co. with Assured Corp. for the same amount pursuant to its contract of carriage with Samson Manufacturing, Inc. Both policies warranted that no other insurance exists, and in case another insurance does exist, such would not void either policy, but in no case should the claim exceed the total amount of Php 2,000,000.00 at the time of loss.

Is this a case of double insurance? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The two policies do not constitute double insurance.

Legal Basis: Section 95 of the Insurance Code requires identity of the insured person, subject matter, interest, and risk. Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. v. Philippines First Insurance Co., Inc. recognizes that an owner and a carrier may hold distinct insurable interests over the same goods.

Application: Samson Manufacturing, Inc. insured its ownership interest. Alibaba Shipping Co. insured its exposure as carrier. Although the goods and peril overlap, the insured persons and interests do not.

Conclusion: There is no double insurance, although the policies may still limit aggregate recovery according to their terms and the indemnity principle.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Sections 13, 15, and 95; Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. v. Philippines First Insurance Co., Inc., G.R. No. 184300, July 11, 2012: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/55013
records.Controlling Doctrine: Double insurance requires identity of the insured person and insurable interest; an owner’s property interest differs from a carrier’s liability interest.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. v. Philippines First Insurance Co., Inc.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
At around 4:00 p.m. of December 25, 2020, Christmas Day, Queenie and her child, Paeng, boarded a jeepney being operated by Emil and driven by Amor. Queenie was made to sit on an empty beer case at the edge of the rear entrance/exit of the jeepney with her sleeping child on her lap. When they reached an uphill incline on the road, the jeepney slid backwards. Queenie pushed both her feet against the step board to prevent herself and her child from being thrown out of the exit, but because the step board was wet, her left foot slipped and was crushed between the step board and the coconut tree which halted the jeepney’s backward motion. As a result, Queenie’s leg was badly injured and had to be amputated.

Queenie then sued Emil and Amor for breach of contract of carriage. Emil and Amor countered that the injuries Queenie sustained were due to her own fault since Amor had instructed everyone not to panic, but Queenie nevertheless tried to disembark which caused her foot to be crushed.

If you were the judge, would you hold Emil and Amor solidarily liable? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On a claim solely for breach of contract of carriage, the operator is directly liable, while the driver is not a contracting party.

Legal Basis: Articles 1733 and 1755 of the Civil Code require extraordinary diligence from common carriers. Sanico v. Colipano holds that the passenger’s contractual action lies against the carrier or operator; the driver may instead incur quasi-delictual or criminal liability if negligence is established.

Application: The transport contract was between Queenie and operator Emil. Amor drove the vehicle but was not a party to that contract.

Conclusion: Emil, not Amor, is answerable on the pleaded contractual cause of action; separate non-contractual claims against the driver remain possible.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1733 and 1755; Sanico v. Colipano, G.R. No. 209969, September 27, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63496
records.Controlling Doctrine: A breach-of-carriage action is contractual against the carrier or operator; the driver’s personal exposure rests on a different cause of action.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Juan, acting as president of Maharlika Car Dealers Incorporated (MCDI), entered into a contract of long-term lease with Antonino over a large commercial property along Pasong Tamo Avenue owned by the latter. When Antonino received a better offer for the commercial property, and having learned that MCDI was not formally incorporated with the Securities and Exchange Commission, he sought to have the contract of lease nullified on the ground that it was void for lack of the essential element of consent, since the lessee was not a juridical person with capacity to contract. May Juan, acting on behalf of MCDI, which is in the process of incorporation, legally insist on the enforceability and binding effect of the contract of lease as against Antonino? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Antonino may be held to the transaction under corporation by estoppel.

Legal Basis: Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code prevents one who assumes an obligation to an ostensible corporation from avoiding it by denying the corporation’s existence. Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona applies this principle to a person who transacted with a not-yet-incorporated entity.

Application: Antonino knowingly contracted with MCDI as the lessee and invoked its non-incorporation only after receiving a better offer.

Conclusion: Juan, acting for MCDI, may enforce the lease against Antonino, subject to the corporation’s adoption and the agents’ statutory liabilities.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 20; Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona, G.R. No. 224307, August 6, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64484
records.Controlling Doctrine: A party who contracts with an ostensible corporation may be estopped from denying its existence to escape the assumed obligation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Datu Commercial Corporation (DCC), a publicly-listed company with the Philippine Stock Exchange, incorporated Kidlat Close Corporation (KCC), investing into 91% of its outstanding capital. The chairman, president, and executive vice-president of DCC are incorporators of KCC, each holding 3% of the outstanding capital stock. The articles of incorporation of KCC provided: 1) a limit on the number of shareholders, which shall never exceed five; 2) a right of first refusal; and 3) a prohibition on the shares from being listed or being publicly offered. Pending the issuance by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the Certificate of Registration, the vice-president of KCC entered into a long-term contract of lease on behalf of KCC, which was declared therein as undergoing incorporation with the SEC. Is DCC qualified to be an incorporator of KCC although it is a juridical entity? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A corporation may now be an incorporator.

Legal Basis: Section 10 of the Revised Corporation Code allows any person, partnership, association, or corporation, singly or jointly with others but not more than fifteen in number, to organize a corporation for a lawful purpose. The statutory text is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: DCC is a corporation and therefore falls within the classes expressly permitted to incorporate KCC. The stated close-corporation restrictions do not disqualify DCC as an incorporator.

Conclusion: DCC is qualified to be an incorporator, assuming compliance with the remaining statutory requirements.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 10 and 95; Republic Act No. 11232: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/86463
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Revised Corporation Code expressly permits corporations and other juridical entities to act as incorporators.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: The Board of Directors of Mabini Corporation (MC) unanimously adopted a resolution directing its management to issue as fully paid 10,000 common shares to Atty. Apolinario for successfully prosecuting in favor of MC the derivative suit filed by a minority stockholder over mismanagement of corporate affairs. If the issuance of the 10,000 common shares in the name of Atty. Apolinario is by way of stock dividends to be credited from the unrestricted retained earnings of MC, would such issuance be valid? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Stock dividends cannot be used to compensate a non-stockholder for legal services.

Legal Basis: Section 42 of the Revised Corporation Code permits stock dividends only with the required stockholder approval and as a distribution to stockholders. Lao v. Lim discusses the statutory requisites and proportional character of stock dividends.

Application: Atty. Apolinario is described as counsel, not as an MC stockholder entitled to a dividend. Legal services may support issuance of shares as consideration under Section 61, but not under the guise of a stock dividend.

Conclusion: The proposed issuance as stock dividends is invalid; any lawful share compensation must follow the rules on valid consideration and corporate approvals.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 42 and 61; Lao v. Lim, G.R. No. 201306, August 9, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63497
records.Controlling Doctrine: Stock dividends are distributions to stockholders and cannot be issued as compensation to a non-stockholder.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: The articles of incorporation of Dakila Incorporated (DI) provides for a seven-member Board of Directors. Florante, the chairperson of the Board, resigned barely two months into office while Laura, another director, died in a vehicular accident on her sixth month in office, thereby leaving only five members in the Board. The one-year term of office of the remaining directors had just ended without an annual stockholders’ meeting being held since Laura was actually the majority stockholder of DI and her estate was still being settled. May the remaining five directors, acting as the Board, fill in the vacancies in the Board? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Once their one-year terms ended, the remaining directors held over only by tenure and could not use that status to fill the vacancies.

Legal Basis: Section 28 of the Revised Corporation Code distinguishes vacancies that the remaining board may fill from those caused by expiration of term. Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. v. Africa holds that holdover tenure does not extend the statutory term and that stockholders must fill vacancies after term expiration.

Application: The five directors acted only after their own terms had expired. At that point, the board lacked authority to fill seats for which no unexpired term remained.

Conclusion: The vacancies must be filled through the stockholders in the manner prescribed by law.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 28; Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. v. Africa, G.R. No. 151969, September 4, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49676
records.Controlling Doctrine: A holdover period is tenure, not an extension of the director’s term; stockholders fill vacancies after term expiration.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Singha Corporation (SC), a corporation organized and existing under Singapore laws, filed a complaint for a sum of money and damages against Muni Corporation (MC), a Philippine-incorporated company, before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Manila. SC alleged in its complaint that it was neither doing business nor licensed to do business in the Philippines and that it was suing MC on an isolated transaction involving a contract for design consultation and

drawing development. MC allegedly failed to pay the remaining 50% of the contract price despite repeated demands by SC. During trial, SC admitted filing a prior collection suit against another company in the RTC. Hence, MC filed a motion to dismiss the case on the ground that contrary to its allegation, SC was in fact doing business in the Philippines without a license and thus had no legal capacity to sue. Will the motion of MC prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts. A prior lawsuit alone does not prove that SC was continuously doing business in the Philippines.

Legal Basis: Section 150 of the Revised Corporation Code bars an unlicensed foreign corporation from maintaining an action only when it is transacting business here. Steelcase, Inc. v. Design International Selections, Inc. requires continuity of commercial dealings and evaluates the attendant circumstances; isolated transactions remain outside the bar.

Application: SC’s present design contract and one earlier collection suit do not, without facts about recurring local commercial operations, establish continuity of business. MC, having contracted with SC, also cannot use the licensing rule as an instrument of injustice.

Conclusion: The motion should be denied absent competent proof that SC was doing business locally without a license.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 150; Steelcase, Inc. v. Design International Selections, Inc., G.R. No. 171995, April 18, 2012: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54683
records.Controlling Doctrine: An unlicensed foreign corporation may sue on an isolated transaction; doing business requires continuity shown by the attendant facts.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Steelcase, Inc. v. Design International Selections, Inc.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Procopio owns the controlling interest in Ginto Bank (GB). Due to the promising potential of lending with real estate collateral, the bank is primarily focused on said transactions. After the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) conducted its examination of GB, the bank was placed under receivership due to illiquidity, as well as unsafe and unsound banking practices. Procopio contends that the actions of the BSP were arbitrary and denied GB its right to due process. He said that GB should have been given due notice and prior hearing, where the bank could have explained the reasons for its illiquidity. Is the contention of Procopio correct? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Prior notice and hearing are not indispensable before a bank is summarily placed under receivership on statutory grounds.

Legal Basis: Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act authorizes the Monetary Board to forbid a bank from doing business and appoint a receiver when the statutory conditions exist. Apex Bancrights Holdings, Inc. v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas recognizes the summary nature of the action, subject to judicial review for grave abuse.

Application: BSP’s examination found illiquidity and unsafe or unsound practices. GB may challenge the Monetary Board’s action in the statutory proceeding, but the absence of a pre-receivership hearing does not itself invalidate it.

Conclusion: Procopio’s due-process objection fails.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7653, Section 30; Apex Bancrights Holdings, Inc. v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, G.R. No. 214866, October 2, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63649
records.Controlling Doctrine: Bank receivership may be imposed summarily to protect depositors and the banking system, with post-action judicial review available.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Jacinto, the Governor of Sorsogon, maintains United States (US) dollar deposits in various offshore banks at the Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, and Switzerland. In an exposé by Balita Magazine called “Pandora Papers”, the writer detailed the offshore deposits of Jacinto amounting to US$60 million as well as his other investments and holding companies. Aggrieved, Jacinto filed a criminal complaint against Balita Magazine for violation of bank secrecy laws, alleging that his US dollar bank deposits were illegally disclosed even though they were neither involved in any civil or criminal case against him nor subjected to any investigation by the Anti-Money Laundering Council. Will the complaint of Jacinto prosper? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The stated offshore deposits and magazine publication do not fall within the penal coverage alleged.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 6426 protects foreign-currency deposits authorized in Philippine banks and restricts unauthorized inquiry or disclosure by persons connected with those deposits. China Banking Corporation v. Ortega discusses the statute’s confidentiality protection within the Philippine banking system.

Application: The accounts were maintained in foreign offshore banks, not Philippine banks governed by Republic Act No. 6426. The facts also identify a magazine publisher, not a Philippine bank official or employee who disclosed a protected local deposit.

Conclusion: Jacinto’s complaint under Philippine foreign-currency deposit secrecy law should not prosper on these facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 6426, Section 8; China Banking Corporation v. Ortega, G.R. No. 140687, December 18, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/40482

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Atty. Diwa is the lawyer of Tala in a criminal case for Estafa before the Regional Trial Court of Manila. After one of their hearings, Tala gave Atty. Diwa ₱10 million for safekeeping, which Tala admitted in confidence that it was part of the proceeds of her swindling activities. The husband of Atty. Diwa found out about this and reported it to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC). The AMLC demanded Atty. Diwa to disclose the details of her transaction with Tala, but she refused. Can Atty. Diwa validly refuse to report her transaction with Tala? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, under the suggested-answer treatment of the statutory exclusion, insofar as disclosure would reveal protected client information obtained in the professional relationship.

Legal Basis: Section 3(a) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, excludes lawyers acting as independent legal professionals in relation to client information when disclosure would compromise client confidences or the attorney-client relationship. Regala v. Sandiganbayan recognizes the breadth of attorney-client confidentiality, subject to established exceptions.

Application: Tala’s disclosure was made to her counsel during an ongoing estafa case and concerned the source of funds entrusted to counsel. The demand therefore directly implicates confidential client information. This does not immunize Atty. Diwa from liability if she knowingly transacts criminal proceeds or assists a continuing crime.

Conclusion: She may refuse the reporting demand on privilege grounds, without prejudice to lawful investigation and the crime-fraud exception on a sufficient factual basis.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9160, Section 3(a), as amended; Regala v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 105938, September 20, 1996: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/34080
records.Controlling Doctrine: AMLA reporting does not automatically override protected attorney-client confidences, but privilege does not shield a lawyer’s own participation in crime.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Insurance — Insurable Interest in Secured Property
records.Essay Question: Emilio owns a car which he purchased from Gregorio. Emilio agreed to pay Gregorio the balance of the purchase price in the amount of ₱500,000 within one year. To secure the payment of the balance, Emilio and Gregorio executed a security agreement that complies with the requirements of the Personal Property Security Act (PPSA). The security interest was also perfected in accordance with the PPSA. Who has insurable interest over the car? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Both Emilio and Gregorio have insurable interests, but of different extents.

Legal Basis: Sections 13 and 14 of the Insurance Code recognize insurable interest arising from an existing interest or a relation under which the insured may be damnified. The PPSA recognizes Gregorio’s perfected security interest. Gaisano Cagayan, Inc. v. Insurance Company of North America explains that different parties may insure distinct economic interests in the same property.

Application: Emilio, as owner, would suffer the loss of the car. Gregorio, as secured creditor, would be prejudiced by destruction of the collateral to the extent of the unpaid secured obligation.

Conclusion: Emilio may insure the ownership value; Gregorio may insure up to the amount of his secured exposure.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Sections 13 and 14; Personal Property Security Act; Gaisano Cagayan, Inc. v. Insurance Company of North America, G.R. No. 147839, June 8, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41412
records.Controlling Doctrine: An owner and a secured creditor may simultaneously hold separate insurable interests in the same property.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Gaisano Cagayan, Inc. v. Insurance Company of North America

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Diego, a cancer survivor, filed an application for a life insurance policy with Garantiya Insurance Company (GIC). He delivered his application and insurance premium to Gabriela, the officer of GIC in charge of approving life insurance policies. Gabriela then approved the application of Diego on June 1, 2020. On

January 30, 2023, Diego died in a vehicular accident. When the heirs of Diego claimed the insurance proceeds, GIC denied the claim on the ground that Diego had concealed the fact of his illness. Moreover, Gabriela knew about the illness of Diego but also concealed it from GIC. Is the denial of the insurance claim by GIC proper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The policy had been in force for more than two years during Diego’s lifetime, and GIC is barred from rescinding it for health-related concealment.

Legal Basis: Section 48 of the Insurance Code establishes the two-year incontestability period. Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban holds that, after the statutory period, concealment or misrepresentation concerning health no longer defeats the policy.

Application: More than two years and seven months elapsed between approval and Diego’s death. Moreover, Gabriela’s knowledge as the approving officer is attributable to GIC within the scope of her authority.

Conclusion: GIC’s denial on the stated concealment ground is improper.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Section 48; Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban, G.R. No. 175666, July 29, 2013: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56125
records.Controlling Doctrine: After a life policy has been in force for two years during the insured’s lifetime, health-related concealment generally becomes incontestable.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Transportation — Resort Ferry as Common Carrier
records.Essay Question: Hari and Reyna booked a honeymoon package at Anya Resort (AR) in Palawan which included transportation from Batangas to Palawan, and vice versa, via M/B Prinsesa owned and operated by AR. Despite PAGASA storm warning bulletins, M/B Prinsesa proceeded to ferry Hari and Reyna from the port of Batangas to Palawan. While in open seas, the boat was hit by big waves and eventually capsized, drowning Hari and Reyna. When sued by the heirs of the couple, AR denied liability on the ground that it is not a common carrier, as M/B Prinsesa is not available to the general public or other tourists, and exclusively ferries resort guests and crew members. AR further argued that they did not charge Hari and Reyna separate fees to board M/B Prinsesa. Are the arguments of AR correct? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. AR operated a common carrier and remained bound to extraordinary diligence.

Legal Basis: Articles 1732 and 1733 of the Civil Code cover transportation offered for compensation to general or limited clientele. Spouses Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. holds that a resort ferry bundled into a tour package is a common carrier even without a separately stated fare.

Application: AR’s ferry regularly transported paying resort guests, and its compensation was embedded in the package price. Sailing despite PAGASA warnings is inconsistent with extraordinary diligence.

Conclusion: AR’s limited-clientele and no-separate-fare defenses fail.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1732 and 1733; Spouses Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc., G.R. No. 186312, June 29, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54049
records.Controlling Doctrine: A resort ferry may be a common carrier when transport is regularly offered to paying guests as part of a package.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Spouses Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Kagandahan Corporation (KC) has been manufacturing medicated facial creams with the brand name “Kutis” since 2010. The facial creams are contained in pink, oval-shaped containers. However, KC did not secure a trademark registration for the brand name and the packaging. Later, upon discovering that there is no existing trademark registration in favor of KC, Bighani Corporation (BC) manufactured its own facial creams using different ingredients and procedure but under the trademark “Kutis” and sold the facial creams in pink, oval-shaped containers similar to those sold by KC. However, the label of BC specifically indicates that it is manufactured by BC. Is BC liable for Unfair Competition? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Trademark registration is not indispensable to an unfair-competition action based on passing off.

Legal Basis: Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code protects the goodwill of goods identified by their general appearance. Kho v. Summerville General Merchandising Co. explains that confusing imitation of the appearance or packaging may constitute unfair competition when calculated to deceive buyers.

Application: BC copied both KC’s “Kutis” name and the distinctive pink, oval packaging. A manufacturer label does not necessarily dispel the likely confusion created at the point of sale.

Conclusion: BC is liable for unfair competition if the proven overall presentation is likely to pass its creams off as KC’s goods.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Section 168; Kho v. Summerville General Merchandising Co., G.R. No. 213400, August 4, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67454
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unfair competition protects goodwill against deceptive passing off even when the imitated mark or trade dress is unregistered.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Kho v. Summerville General Merchandising Co.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Atty. Matalas prepared a deed of sale which contains all the elements necessary to perfect the contract, particularly a statement of the agreement to transfer in an absolute manner the parcel of land that was specifically described as well as the price certain. Impressed by his own draft deed of sale, Atty. Matalas wants to use the deed that he prepared as a template and to secure a copyright registration for the same. Can Atty. Matalas secure a copyright registration for the template? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not for the legal transaction or standard form as such.

Legal Basis: Sections 172 and 175 of the Intellectual Property Code protect original expression but not ideas, procedures, systems, or methods of operation. Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc. applies the idea-expression distinction and merger principle where protecting the expression would effectively monopolize the underlying method or functional form.

Application: The deed’s operative clauses express the legal requirements of a sale of land. Because those functional concepts can be expressed only in a limited number of conventional ways, copyright cannot be used to monopolize the template’s legal function.

Conclusion: The deed template is not protectable as claimed, although independently original non-functional literary expression may receive only its ordinary, narrow protection.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 172 and 175; Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., discussed in Juan v. Juan, G.R. No. 221732, August 23, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63340
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright protects expression, not a functional legal method; where idea and expression merge, protection cannot monopolize the idea.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Intellectual Property — Copyright and Useful Articles
records.Essay Question: Julio secured a copyright registration for a drawing of a light box. Julio used the drawing for his advertisements indicating the new internal electronic design features of the light box. Ten years after the registration of the copyright, Julian decided to manufacture and sell a light box with the same internal electric design features as the light box drawing created by Julio. However, the physical appearance of the light box manufactured by Julian is different. Julio objected to the manufacture by Julian of the light box on the ground that he (Julio) is the inventor of the light box design. Is the objection of Julio valid? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Copyright in the drawing does not confer a patent-like monopoly over the functional light-box design.

Legal Basis: Sections 172 and 175 of the Intellectual Property Code distinguish copyrightable pictorial expression from ideas, systems, and useful mechanisms. Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., as reiterated in Ching v. Salinas, holds that copyright in technical drawings does not protect the useful article depicted.

Application: Julian made a light box with a different external appearance but similar internal functionality. Julio’s copyright protects copying of his drawing, not manufacture of the unpatented device.

Conclusion: The copyright objection fails; exclusive rights over the functional invention would require valid patent protection.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 172 and 175; Ching v. Salinas, G.R. No. 161295, June 29, 2005: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43469
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright in a technical drawing does not extend to the manufacture of the useful article represented in the drawing.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
China Telecommunication Company (CTC), a Chinese state-owned enterprise, sought to acquire 40% equity in Duon Telecommunication Corporation (DTC), a telecommunications company in the Philippines. When questioned by the two

major telecommunication companies in the Philippines, Cheng, the president of DTC, defended the proposed acquisition by saying that CTC is allowed to own 40% equity pursuant to the nationality requirement under the 1987 Constitution. Is the argument of Cheng correct? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The general 40% foreign-equity ceiling does not override the statutory prohibition applicable to a foreign state-owned enterprise investing in critical infrastructure.

Legal Basis: Section 25 of the Public Service Act, as amended by Republic Act No. 11659, prohibits a foreign state-owned enterprise from owning capital stock in a public service classified as critical infrastructure, subject to statutory exceptions. The Act and its implementing rules classify telecommunications as critical infrastructure.

Application: CTC is state-owned, and DTC provides telecommunications. The proposed acquisition therefore triggers the special prohibition regardless of its 40% size.

Conclusion: Cheng’s constitutional-percentage argument is incomplete, and the acquisition is barred absent a statutory exception.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Public Service Act, Section 25, as amended by Republic Act No. 11659; official Supreme Court E-Library text: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/94539
records.Controlling Doctrine: Foreign state-owned enterprises are specially barred from owning capital in public services classified as critical infrastructure.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Upon seeing the global popularity of Korean culture, the President of the Philippines wanted to export Philippine culture as well. Thus, he met with both the Secretary of Tourism and the Chairperson of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts to come up with a plan to make Philippine culture the next big thing. After a series of meetings with industry stakeholders and with a resolution of support from Congress, the President issued a presidential proclamation granting tax exemptions to members of the Philippine entertainment and culinary industries who export 70% of their products and services. The proclamation also grants additional tax incentives (such as an income tax holiday) to artists, directors, chefs, studios (both TV and music), and authors who gain international acclaim. Is the proclamation constitutional? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A presidential proclamation cannot create tax exemptions without a clear statutory grant.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 28(4) of the Constitution requires the concurrence of a majority of all members of Congress for a law granting a tax exemption. John Hay Peoples Alternative Coalition v. Lim invalidated tax exemptions extended by presidential proclamation beyond the authority granted by statute.

Application: A resolution of support is not a tax-exemption law enacted with the constitutionally required concurrence. No statute expressly delegates the exemptions described.

Conclusion: The proclamation’s tax exemptions and incentives are unconstitutional.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 28(4); John Hay Peoples Alternative Coalition v. Lim, G.R. No. 119775, October 24, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/47416
records.Controlling Doctrine: Tax exemptions must rest on an unmistakable constitutional or statutory grant and cannot be created solely by presidential proclamation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: John Hay Peoples Alternative Coalition v. Lim

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Pedro ran a gambling den in the basement of a bar called Apolaki in Intramuros, Manila. His gambling operations consisted of a pastime from the late 1700’s called “Ratting”, where barrels of rats would be released in a fenced-off area for a cat to eat. Bettors would then wager on how many rats would be killed by the cat in a certain given time. As can be easily gathered, this is highly illegal. The apparent illegality did not stop Pedro from making millions of pesos from onsite and online bettors. Needless to say, Pedro did not file an income tax return to report his income. Based on the complaint of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, the Department of Justice filed an information against Pedro for Failure to File Income Tax Return under Section 255 of the National Internal Revenue Code. In his defense, Pedro argued that the profits from the gambling operations are not income in the first place because declaring such would violate his right against self-incrimination. Hence, he is not required to file any income tax return. Is the argument of Pedro tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Illegal gains are taxable income, and the privilege against self-incrimination does not create a blanket exemption from filing a return.

Legal Basis: Sections 23, 32, and 255 of the NIRC tax income from whatever source and penalize willful failure to file. People v. Mendez explains the independent legal obligation to pay tax and the elements of a Section 255 prosecution.

Application: Pedro realized economic gain from gambling operations. He could comply with the tax law without supplying unnecessary incriminating detail and invoke the privilege only against specific compelled disclosures presenting a real danger of prosecution.

Conclusion: His illegal profits are taxable, and his asserted blanket excuse for non-filing is untenable.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 23, 32, and 255; People v. Mendez, G.R. Nos. 208310-11 and 208662, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69095
records.Controlling Doctrine: Illegality of the income source does not remove the tax obligation; self-incrimination is not a blanket defense to filing.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Marites is the chief executive officer and sole shareholder of Tsismis Ngayon OPC (TNO), a One Person Corporation that runs a popular blog about showbiz news and juicy gossip. From March to April 2023, Marites asked her daughter, Laya, to work as an intern in the corporation and help around the press room. Her main duties were brewing coffee for the editorial staff and printing out hard copies of TNO blog posts for filing purposes. Laya did a decent (but not excellent) job as an intern in her two-month stint with TNO, except for the one time when she added two packets of sugar to the cup of coffee of a diabetic senior officer. Proud of the performance of Laya, Marites issued a TNO resolution granting a ₱2 million bonus to Laya. Laya used the ₱2 million bonus to buy a new car. Can TNO claim the ₱2 million bonus as a deduction? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The amount is not shown to be reasonable compensation or an ordinary and necessary business expense.

Legal Basis: Section 34(A)(1) of the NIRC allows ordinary and necessary expenses, including reasonable compensation for services actually rendered. ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue emphasizes that deductions are strictly construed and must be substantiated, while compensation must be reasonable in relation to the services.

Application: Laya’s brief internship and routine tasks bear no reasonable relationship to a ₱2 million bonus. Her close relationship to the sole shareholder further requires careful proof that the payment was genuine compensation rather than a personal benefit.

Conclusion: TNO cannot deduct the bonus on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 34(A)(1); ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 167679, July 22, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60762
records.Controlling Doctrine: Deductible compensation must be for services actually rendered, reasonable in amount, ordinary and necessary, and properly substantiated.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Ikapati Corporation (IC) is a value-added tax (VAT)-registered corporation that sells various kinds of instant noodles. It is recognized as the industry leader, especially after its spicy bulalo flavor gained immense popularity in December 2021. The success of IC has been attributed to its tax lawyer, Atty. Mahal, who helps IC understand the National Internal Revenue Code to its advantage. To show its appreciation, IC sent Atty. Mahal 1,000 boxes of spicy bulalo instant noodles. Is the transfer of 1,000 boxes of instant noodles to Atty. Mahal subject to VAT? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The gratuitous transfer is a transaction deemed sale.

Legal Basis: Section 106(B)(1) of the NIRC treats as a sale the transfer, use, or consumption, outside the ordinary course of business, of goods originally intended for sale or business use. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc. discusses the statutory deemed-sale rule.

Application: The noodles were inventory held for sale. IC withdrew and transferred them to its lawyer as a gratuitous benefit rather than selling them in the regular course.

Conclusion: The transfer is subject to VAT as a deemed sale, measured under the applicable valuation rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 106(B)(1); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc., G.R. No. 146984, July 28, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41526
records.Controlling Doctrine: Business goods withdrawn and transferred outside the ordinary course are subject to VAT as transactions deemed sale.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Quezon City assessed the Light Rail Transit Authority (LRTA) of real property taxes on its properties consisting of lands, buildings, machineries, and terminal stations. Despite repeated demands from Quezon City, LRTA failed to pay its outstanding obligations, prompting the city to issue a notice of delinquency with warrants of levy. LRTA questioned the assessments of Quezon City, claiming that it is exempt from real property tax. LRTA argues that it is operating a light rail transit system for the Philippines, which is the true owner of the subject real properties. Is LRTA exempt from real property tax? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, for property owned by the Republic of the Philippines and devoted to public use, subject to the beneficial-use exception.

Legal Basis: Section 234(a) of the Local Government Code exempts real property owned by the Republic, unless beneficial use is granted to a taxable person. Light Rail Transit Authority v. Quezon City holds that LRTA is a government instrumentality and that its public-use properties belong to the Republic.

Application: The assessed rail lands, stations, and machinery are held for the national light-rail system. No taxable private beneficial user is identified in the facts.

Conclusion: LRTA is exempt from the assessment as stated.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Section 234(a); Light Rail Transit Authority v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 221626, October 9, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66014
records.Controlling Doctrine: Real property of a government instrumentality owned by the Republic and used for public purposes is exempt, unless beneficial use is granted to a taxable person.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Nympha, a famous author, collaborated with Tobias, a novice illustrator, to create a children’s book. Tobias offered his services for free. Nympha gave Tobias the manuscript and discussed with him the inspiration for the characters. Nympha envisioned a story about two best friends who had a huge fight but later realized the value of forgiveness. Tobias drew the characters based on Nympha’s specifications and instructions. Nympha then published the book and claimed sole copyright ownership. Nympha argued that she is the author not only of the text but also the images in the book since Tobias exactly adopted her idea. Is Nympha the copyright owner of the images or drawings in the book? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Tobias, not Nympha, is the author of the illustrations.

Legal Basis: Section 175 of the Intellectual Property Code excludes ideas and concepts from copyright protection. Republic v. Heirs of Tupaz IV holds that authorship belongs to the person who uses skill and labor to give concrete expression to an idea.

Application: Nympha supplied concepts and directions, but Tobias created the visual expression. His gratuitous service does not transfer authorship or copyright absent a valid legal basis for transfer.

Conclusion: Nympha owns the text, while Tobias owns the copyright in the drawings, subject to any proven agreement.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 171.1 and 175; Republic v. Heirs of Tupaz IV, G.R. No. 197335, September 7, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/23/69955
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright protects concrete expression, and authorship belongs to the person who creates that expression rather than merely supplies the underlying idea.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Republic v. Heirs of Tupaz IV

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: In 1984, the Nova Family established the North Nova, Inc. (NNI), a pharmaceutical company. On August 31, 1984, NNI was issued its certificate of incorporation with corporate term of 40 years. On August 31, 2024, the corporate term of NNI expired without the board of directors renewing its corporate existence. However, the Nova Family continued NNI’s business operations. South Moon, Inc. (SMI), a rival company, questioned the Nova Family’s action. SMI argued that the Nova Family cannot continue to operate NNI without reviving its corporate existence. Is the Nova Family’s continued operations of NNI valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. NNI’s term was converted to perpetual existence by operation of law.

Legal Basis: Section 11 of the Revised Corporation Code provides perpetual existence and deems corporations existing before its effectivity to have perpetual terms unless they timely elect to retain a specific term. The official statute is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: Nothing indicates that NNI’s stockholders elected to retain the forty-year term within the statutory transition period. No articles amendment was needed for the automatic conversion.

Conclusion: NNI continued to exist beyond August 31, 2024, and its operations were valid.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 11; Republic Act No. 11232: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/86463
records.Controlling Doctrine: Pre-existing corporations acquired perpetual existence automatically unless they timely elected to retain their fixed term.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Ernest Bicycle Corporation (EBC) and Max Speed Corporation (MSC) are the leading manufacturers and sellers of electric bicycles in the country. EBC and MSC offer their bestselling models at PHP 25,000.00 per unit. In 2023, Gryffin Pedals, Inc. (GPI) entered the market and sold electric bicycles with features similar to EBC and MSC’s bestselling models for only PHP 20,000.00. GPI has no physical stores and offers its products in digital marketplaces. After a year, GPI had 75% share of the market leaving EBC and MSC at 15% and 10% shares, respectively. EBC and MSC filed a complaint before the Philippine Competition Commission and alleged that GPI is fast monopolizing the electric bicycles market because of its dominant position. Will the complaint against GPI for violation of the competition laws prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Dominance by itself is not unlawful; abuse must be proved.

Legal Basis: Section 15 of the Philippine Competition Act prohibits abuse of dominant position, not the legitimate acquisition of market share through superior efficiency or business acumen. Philippine Contractors Accreditation Board v. Manila Water Company, Inc. distinguishes market power from unlawful exclusionary conduct.

Application: GPI’s lower overhead, digital distribution, and lower price explain its market share. The facts do not establish below-cost predatory pricing, exclusionary contracts, or another prohibited abuse.

Conclusion: The complaint cannot prosper solely from GPI’s 75% share and lower price.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Philippine Competition Act, Section 15; Philippine Contractors Accreditation Board v. Manila Water Company, Inc., G.R. No. 217590, March 10, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66190
records.Controlling Doctrine: A dominant position is not illegal unless maintained or exercised through conduct that substantially prevents, restricts, or lessens competition.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Philippine Contractors Accreditation Board v. Manila Water Company, Inc.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Audrey read the 24-hour rush sale from Easy Shopping, a known digital marketplace, which offers free shipping plus 50% cash back for purchases worth at least PHP 10,000.00. Audrey checked out several items and placed the orders pursuant to the promotion. Easy Shopping accepted the orders and marked them “pending payment.” However, Audrey’s digital wallet had insufficient funds and was reloaded only the following day. At that time, the cashback and free shipping promotions were no longer available. Audrey then demanded from Easy Shopping to honor their transaction based on the promotion and presented a screenshot of her orders as supporting evidence. On the other hand, Easy Shopping countered that the transaction is unenforceable absent a written contract and that Audrey must pay the regular price and normal shipping rate. Is the transaction enforceable on the basis of the screenshot of Audrey’s orders with Easy Shopping? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The electronic transaction and its terms may be proved by an authenticated screenshot, but Audrey cannot compel benefits conditioned on timely payment that she failed to make.

Legal Basis: Sections 7 and 16 of the Electronic Commerce Act give electronic documents legal effect and allow offer, acceptance, and contract formation to be proved electronically. MCC Industrial Sales Corporation v. Ssangyong Corporation recognizes the evidentiary and contractual effect of electronic communications.

Application: The screenshot may establish the order and acceptance subject to “pending payment.” Audrey’s insufficient funds prevented performance of the payment condition during the sale period.

Conclusion: The screenshot defeats the no-writing objection, but it does not entitle Audrey to expired promotional benefits after her nonpayment.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Electronic Commerce Act, Sections 7 and 16; MCC Industrial Sales Corporation v. Ssangyong Corporation, G.R. No. 170633, October 17, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/45248
records.Controlling Doctrine: Electronic records can prove a contract, but their enforceability remains subject to the parties’ conditions and performance.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: MCC Industrial Sales Corporation v. Ssangyong Corporation

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Corporation by Estoppel — Donation Before Incorporation
records.Essay Question: In 2022, Annie, Brenda, Clara, Donna, and Enola formed Nurturing Family Organization (NFO), a corporation with the principal purpose of helping single parents. Gregory, a wealthy philanthropist, donated to NFO a parcel of land through a public document. Clara accepted the donation in the same public instrument because NFO was not yet registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). In 2023, the SEC issued a certificate of incorporation in favor of NFO. In 2024, Clara died and her heirs included the donated land in the settlement of her estate. The heirs of Clara argued that she owned the real property and not NFO which lacked legal personality at the time of the donation. Is the donation of real property in favor NFO valid despite its lack of legal personality? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The donor is estopped from denying the donee’s existence, and NFO’s later incorporation and affirmation cured the pre-incorporation defect.

Legal Basis: Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code embodies corporation by estoppel. Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona holds that one who assumes an obligation in favor of an ostensible corporation cannot evade it by denying the corporation’s existence after later incorporation and ratification.

Application: Gregory executed a public donation expressly in NFO’s favor. NFO later acquired juridical personality and accepted the benefit through the authority previously exercised for it.

Conclusion: The donation is enforceable for NFO, and Clara’s heirs cannot treat the land as her personal property.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 20; Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona, G.R. No. 224307, August 6, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64484
records.Controlling Doctrine: Later incorporation and ratification, together with corporation by estoppel, can sustain an obligation undertaken for an ostensible corporation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Pierre and Fonzi derived money from the illegal trade of Philippine wildlife like pangolins, tarsiers, and palm civets. Pierre and Fonzi collected PHP 2,000,000.00 each month which they delivered to Phoebe, an art collector. Phoebe used the funds to buy high-value paintings which she auctioned off in art galleries. The police officers tracked down the unlawful wildlife trading and arrested Phoebe. The operatives charged Phoebe with money laundering. At the trial, Phoebe argued that she should be acquitted of the charge because she did not participate in the illegal wildlife trading. Is Phoebe criminally liable for money laundering? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Not on the facts as stated, because her knowledge that the funds were criminal proceeds is not established.

Legal Basis: Section 4 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act requires that the accused know that the monetary instrument or property represents, involves, or relates to proceeds of unlawful activity. Lingad v. People applies the statutory elements of money laundering and the required proof of knowledge.

Application: Phoebe transacted the money by converting it into paintings, but the question supplies no fact showing that she knew its wildlife-trafficking source. Participation in the predicate offense is unnecessary, yet knowledge of the proceeds remains essential.

Conclusion: Absent proof of knowledge beyond reasonable doubt, Phoebe cannot be convicted.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Anti-Money Laundering Act, Section 4; Lingad v. People, G.R. No. 224945, October 11, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68639
records.Controlling Doctrine: Money laundering does not require participation in the predicate crime, but it requires knowledge that the property is connected to unlawful activity.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Nina and Roxanne are shareholders of Essean & Essaiah Corporation (EEC) engaged in the pet supplies business. In 2023, the Board of Directors declared surplus profits and distributed dividends to the shareholders. The Board of Directors likewise released the shareholders with unpaid subscriptions from their obligations. Accordingly, Nina and Roxanne no longer settled the unpaid balance of their subscriptions. Upon inspection of corporate books, however, it was revealed that EEC has been experiencing insolvency for the last three years. In 2024, the directors and shareholders dissolved EEC during their annual meeting and divided corporate properties and assets among themselves. Aggrieved, the creditors of EEC filed an action against Nina and Roxanne to collect corporate debts. In their answer, Nina and Roxanne invoked the distinct personality of EEC from its shareholders. Nina and Roxanne added that they are not privy to the transactions between EEC and its creditors. May the creditors of EEC run after Nina and Roxanne to satisfy their claims? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, to recover unpaid subscriptions and improperly distributed corporate assets within the limits of what they received or owe.

Legal Basis: The trust fund doctrine treats subscribed capital and corporate assets as a fund for creditors, especially upon insolvency or dissolution. Enano-Bote v. Alvarez recognizes a creditor’s direct action against unpaid subscribers when the corporation is insolvent, dissolved, or has condoned subscriptions.

Application: EEC condoned unpaid subscriptions, distributed dividends while insolvent, and transferred assets on dissolution. Nina and Roxanne cannot use separate personality to retain value belonging to the creditor fund.

Conclusion: The creditors may proceed against them for unpaid subscriptions and recoverable distributions.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 42, 66, and 139; Enano-Bote v. Alvarez, G.R. No. 223572, November 10, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66972
records.Controlling Doctrine: Under the trust fund doctrine, corporate creditors may reach unpaid subscriptions and assets improperly distributed during insolvency or dissolution.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Felix, Ivan, and Ruth formed a partnership to operate a coffee shop. Felix and Ivan provided the capital while Ruth contributed her labor and industry. Within the coffee shop, Felix opened his own plant kiosk and Ruth put up her own souvenir shop. Whereas Ivan set up a coffee stall two blocks away from the coffee shop. May the partners Felix, Ivan, and Ruth lawfully engage in their separate businesses? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Felix may operate the non-competing plant kiosk; Ruth and Ivan may not operate their stated businesses without the required permission or contrary stipulation.

Legal Basis: Article 1789 of the Civil Code bars an industrial partner from engaging in business for herself without express partnership permission. Article 1808 bars a capitalist partner from engaging for his own account in the same kind of business, absent a stipulation to the contrary. The Civil Code is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: Felix’s plant kiosk does not compete with coffee sales. Ruth, as industrial partner, opened another business without permission. Ivan’s coffee stall directly competes with the partnership.

Conclusion: Only Felix’s separate business is lawful on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1789 and 1808; official Supreme Court E-Library text: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/53360
records.Controlling Doctrine: Industrial partners need express permission for a separate business; capitalist partners may not compete in the partnership’s line absent a contrary stipulation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Express Innovation Corporation (EIC) applied for registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The EIC submitted its proposed Articles of Incorporation which reads:

First: That the name of the corporation shall be, “Express Innovation Corporation” …. Third: That the principal office of the corporation is located in Sakurajima, Konohana Ward, Osaka, Japan. …. Ninth: That Haru Nikko, a resident of Japan, has been elected by the subscribers as the Treasurer of the Corporation to act as such until after the successor is duly elected and qualified in accordance with the by-laws, that as Treasurer, authority has been given to receive in the name and for the benefit of the corporation, all subscriptions, contributions or donations paid or given by the subscribers or members, who certifies the information set forth in the seventh and eighth clauses above, and that the paid-up portion of the subscription in cash and/or property for the benefit and credit of the corporation has been duly received.

If you are the SEC Examiner, will you recommend the approval of the Articles of Incorporation? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed articles contain statutory defects.

Legal Basis: Sections 14 and 24 of the Revised Corporation Code require the principal office to be located in the Philippines and the treasurer to be a resident. The official statute is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: EIC’s stated principal office is in Japan, and its proposed treasurer is also a Japanese resident. Both provisions conflict with mandatory corporate requirements.

Conclusion: The examiner should withhold approval until the articles are corrected.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A domestic corporation’s principal office must be in the Philippines, and its treasurer must be a resident.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Blaine Builders Corporation (BBC) has a total of 200,000 outstanding shares which are all entitled to vote. However, 10,000 of the shares are under dispute or subject matter of pending litigations. Harold and Joaquin are BBC’s major stockholders. Harold called a meeting where stockholders representing 98,400 shares attended and voted for new members of the board of directors. Joaquin filed an election protest and claimed that there was no quorum in the meeting which shall consist of the stockholders representing a majority of the outstanding capital stock. Harold insisted that there is a quorum after excluding the 10,000 disputed shares. Is there a required quorum in the stockholders’ meeting that elected the new members of the board of directors? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The disputed shares remained outstanding and counted in the quorum base.

Legal Basis: Sections 6 and 51 of the Revised Corporation Code base quorum on a majority of outstanding capital stock unless law or the bylaws provide otherwise. Villongco v. Yabut holds that shares do not cease to be outstanding merely because their ownership is litigated.

Application: A majority of 200,000 is more than 100,000 shares. Only 98,400 were represented. Excluding the disputed 10,000 shares has no statutory basis.

Conclusion: The meeting lacked quorum, so the director election was invalid.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 6 and 51; Villongco v. Yabut, G.R. No. 225022, February 5, 2018, discussed in Gamboa v. Finance Secretary: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69360
records.Controlling Doctrine: Shares under ownership dispute remain outstanding and are included in computing the stockholders’ quorum.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Justin opened a peso savings account with the Ozzy Pay Bank (OPB) where he deposited his earnings. In 2024, Justin went to OPB to verify his account. The OPB showed to Justin the transaction history and informed that he had only PHP 100.00 remaining balance after a series of withdrawals. Justin denied the transactions and claimed that his signatures appearing on the withdrawal slips in the sum of PHP 3,000.000.00 were forged. The investigation revealed that an impostor forged the signature on the withdrawal slips and delivered the amounts to his conspirator who opened a peso savings account with OPB using the funds as initial deposit. Aggrieved, Justin filed a complaint for sum of money against OPB and alleged that it was negligent in allowing the unauthorized withdrawals. Meantime, the trial court directed the OPB to produce the bank records of the conspirator. The OPB refused contending that the conspirator’s bank account is not the subject of litigation. Did the OPB validly refuse to disclose the conspirator’s bank records? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, where the pleaded and traced money deposited in the conspirator’s account is itself the subject matter of the action.

Legal Basis: Section 2 of Republic Act No. 1405 permits inquiry pursuant to a court order when the money deposited or invested is the subject matter of litigation. Republic v. Rabusa applies the exception where allegedly illegally acquired money is placed in the account sought to be examined.

Application: The investigation traced Justin’s specific unauthorized withdrawals into the conspirator’s newly opened account. The order seeks the whereabouts and recovery of that money, not a general examination of unrelated deposits.

Conclusion: OPB may not invoke bank secrecy to refuse the narrowly directed court order.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Bank secrecy yields to a court-ordered inquiry when the deposited money itself is the subject matter of litigation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Insurance — Premium Paid to Authorized Agent
records.Essay Question: Flavio obtained from Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC), through its agent Laureen, a fire insurance policy over his residential house for a period of one year from August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025. Flavio delivered on August 26, 2024 a check representing premium payment to Laureen who then issued an acknowledgment receipt. On August 27, 2024, a fire completely razed Flavio’s house. Oblivious of the incident, Laureen deposited the check on August 28, 2024 to SAC’s bank account and was credited on the same day. Thereafter, Flavio filed against SAC an insurance claim. However, SAC denied the claim and argued that there was no payment of premium yet to make the insurance policy effective at the time of the loss. SAC explained that it received the premium payment only on August 28, 2024 or after the fire occurred on August 27, 2024. Is there a valid and binding insurance contract between SAC and Flavio? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Payment to SAC’s authorized agent before the loss bound the insurer.

Legal Basis: Sections 77, 79, and 315 of the Insurance Code govern premium payment and deem an insurer’s agent authorized to receive premiums when the policy is delivered through that agent. South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals recognizes the effect of payment through the insurer’s authorized representative.

Application: Flavio delivered the check and received Laureen’s acknowledgment one day before the fire. Laureen’s later deposit was an internal act that did not postpone receipt by SAC.

Conclusion: The policy was valid and binding when the loss occurred.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Sections 77, 79, and 315; South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 102253, June 2, 1995: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33779
records.Controlling Doctrine: Premium paid to an insurer’s authorized agent before loss is payment to the insurer despite the agent’s later deposit of the check.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question: Sierra Electronics Inc. (SEI) has an outstanding capital stock consisting of 100 common shares and 100 non-voting preferred shares. The common shares are held by Filipino citizens while the preferred shares are held by foreigners. SEI planned to buy real property and establish a manufacturing plant in the Philippines. May the SEI own land in the Philippines? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Filipino ownership covers only 50% of SEI’s total outstanding capital stock.

Legal Basis: Article XII, Section 7, in relation to Section 2, of the Constitution permits land acquisition by corporations at least 60% Filipino-owned. Roy v. Herbosa requires 60% Filipino ownership both of voting shares and of total outstanding capital stock with full beneficial ownership.

Application: Filipinos own all voting common shares but only 100 of the 200 total outstanding shares. The foreign-held preferred shares remain part of outstanding capital despite being non-voting.

Conclusion: SEI does not meet the 60% total-capital requirement and may not acquire the land.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XII, Sections 2 and 7; Roy v. Herbosa, G.R. No. 207246, April 18, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63014
records.Controlling Doctrine: For constitutionally restricted ownership, Filipino nationals must hold at least 60% of voting shares and 60% of total outstanding capital stock.
