records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Klaus was drinking in front of his rented apartment when he suddenly heard a gunshot which came from inside the apartment owned by Luther. Klaus then saw Igor, a neighbor, going down the stairs and leaving the scene holding a gun. Klaus also witnessed Luther fall from the stairs with blood oozing from his chest. Vanya, Luther’s daughter, also rushed to Luther when he fell.

During Igor’s trial for Murder, Vanya testified and presented a flash drive containing the closed-circuit television (CCTV) footages of the scene. Said footages showed a man appearing to be Igor, armed with a gun, proceeding up the stairs and entering Luther’s apartment. In the video, the same man was seen hastily leaving the premises. Vanya further testified that she was the one who transferred to the flash drive the video footages from the barangay-owned CCTV that was located outside their apartment.

When the footages were played in court and an enlarged screenshot was presented, Vanya identified the shooter as Igor. The defense objected on the ground that Vanya was not the recorder of the video footages.

Are the CCTV footages admissible as electronic evidence? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Authentication does not invariably require the technician or person who pressed the record button; a competent witness who can establish the recording’s identity and accuracy may suffice.

Legal Basis: Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 5 requires proof of authenticity through evidence of integrity and reliability. People v. Manansala recognizes authentication through a witness with personal knowledge of the recording, its retrieval, or the events depicted.

Application: The proposed witness can explain the scene, custody, retrieval, and accurate depiction. Those facts may establish authenticity, while any weakness affects weight unless integrity remains genuinely unproved.

Conclusion: The CCTV recording may be admitted after an adequate foundation from the competent witness.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 5; People v. Manansala, G.R. No. 229092, September 16, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66508
records.Controlling Doctrine: A CCTV recording may be authenticated by any competent witness who establishes its identity, integrity, and accurate depiction.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
In a case for Estafa, the prosecution offered the photocopy of the acknowledgment receipt signed by the accused showing personal receipt of the sum of money from the private complainant to prove the amount of damage. Accused objected to the offer of the photocopy on the sole ground that it is a mere reproduction of the original in violation of the original document rule. The court overruled the accused’s objection and admitted in evidence the photocopy of the acknowledgment receipt.

Did the court err in admitting the photocopy? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Under Rule 130, Section 4(b), a photocopy that accurately reproduces the original is a duplicate. Section 4(c) makes a duplicate admissible to the same extent as the original unless a genuine question is raised about the original's authenticity or admission of the duplicate would be unjust or inequitable.

Application: The accused objected solely because the exhibit was a reproduction. That objection does not raise either statutory exception.

Conclusion: The court did not err in admitting the photocopy.

No. 19-08-15-SC, Rule 130, Section 4(b)–(c), effective May 1, 2020: https://lawphil.net/courts/rules/am_19-08-15-sc_2019.html; Kuwait Airways Corp. v. Tokio Marine, G.R. No. 213931, November 17, 2021 (pre-examination majority authority applying the amended duplicate rule): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/21/67979
records.Controlling Doctrine: A photocopy that accurately reproduces the original is a duplicate and is admissible to the same extent as the original unless authenticity is genuinely questioned or admission would be unjust or inequitable.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
[This item has five questions.] Assume that you received an adverse decision and filed a motion for reconsideration which was denied.

Give the reglementary periods for filing the following:

(a) Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeals
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Fifteen (15) days from notice of the order denying the timely motion for reconsideration.

Legal Basis: Rule 41, Section 3 provides the ordinary appeal period. Under the fresh-period rule in Neypes v. Court of Appeals, a party who timely moves for reconsideration receives a fresh fifteen-day period to file the notice of appeal, counted from receipt of the order denying the motion.

Application: The motion for reconsideration was denied, so the fifteen-day period is counted from notice of that denial.

Conclusion: The notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals must be filed within fifteen days from notice of denial.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 41, Section 3; Neypes v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 141524, September 14, 2005: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43280
records.Controlling Doctrine: A timely motion for new trial or reconsideration triggers a fresh fifteen-day appeal period, subject to the special habeas-corpus period.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
[This item has five questions.] Assume that you received an adverse decision and filed a motion for reconsideration which was denied.

Give the reglementary periods for filing the following:

(b) Petition for Certiorari under Rule 65
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The petition must be filed not later than sixty days from notice of the order denying the motion for reconsideration.

Legal Basis: Rule 65, Section 4 expressly reckons the sixty-day period from notice of denial when a timely motion for reconsideration or new trial is filed. Thenamaris Philippines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals applies that text and distinguishes certiorari from an appeal.

Application: The aggrieved party receives no new appeal period under Rule 65; the rule itself supplies a sixty-day outer limit counted from receipt of the denial.

Conclusion: The governing period is sixty days from notice of denial, subject only to a justified extension under the rule.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A Rule 65 petition is due within sixty days from notice of denial of a timely reconsideration or new-trial motion.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Define the following terms:

(a) Trust fund doctrine (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The trust fund doctrine treats subscribed capital and other assets available for creditors as a fund that may not be distributed to stockholders to the prejudice of corporate creditors.

Legal Basis: The Revised Corporation Code and Philippine Long Distance Telephone Company v. National Telecommunications Commission recognize that subscribed capital is held for the payment of corporate debts.

Application: Because the item asks for the doctrine’s meaning, the controlling point is that creditors may look to the corporation’s capital and assets for satisfaction before those assets are returned or diverted to stockholders.

Conclusion: Corporate capital is impressed with a trust in favor of corporate creditors.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Subscribed capital is treated as a trust fund for payment of corporate debts and cannot be distributed to stockholders to creditors’ prejudice.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Define the following terms:

(b) Unfair competition (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Unfair competition is the use of deception or means contrary to good faith to pass off one’s goods, business, or services as those of another who has established goodwill.

Legal Basis: Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code and Coca-Cola Bottlers, Phils., Inc. v. Gomez require deception, passing off, and fraud upon the public.

Application: The definition covers conduct calculated to make ordinary purchasers believe that one trader’s goods or services are those of another; a merely unfair business act without deception or passing off is insufficient.

Conclusion: Unfair competition protects established goodwill against deceptive passing off.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Define the following terms:

(c) Insurable interest in property (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Insurable interest in property is an interest arising from a relation to the property such that the insured benefits from its preservation or suffers pecuniary loss from its destruction or injury.

Legal Basis: The Insurance Code and Lalican v. Insular Life Assurance Company Limited recognize a legally protectable pecuniary interest in the subject of insurance.

Application: The test is economic exposure: preservation must produce benefit or advantage, while the insured peril’s occurrence must cause loss or damage.

Conclusion: A person has insurable interest in property when the person stands to gain from its preservation or lose from its impairment.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Define the following terms:

(d) Splitting of deposits (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Splitting of deposits is the breakup and transfer of a deposit exceeding the maximum insured amount into two or more accounts of persons without beneficial ownership, within the statutory period surrounding a bank holiday or closure, to obtain increased deposit-insurance coverage.

Legal Basis: The Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation Charter, as amended, and Linsangan v. Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation identify the source account, breakup and transfer, absence of beneficial ownership, timing, and insurance-coverage purpose as controlling elements.

Application: The prohibition targets artificial transfers made shortly before or during bank distress so that one beneficial owner appears to hold several separately insured deposits.

Conclusion: Deposit splitting is a prohibited artificial breakup designed to multiply insurance coverage.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
In May 2018, ABC Corp. entered into a merchandising contract which terms and conditions were totally lopsided in favor of the counterparty, XYZ, Inc. As a result, ABC Corp. suffered tremendous financial losses.

A year after, or in May 2019, Mr. X became a stockholder of ABC Corp. Learning about the circumstances surrounding the merchandising contract, Mr. X filed a derivative suit against ABC Corp. 's directors to claim damages on behalf of ABC Corp. due to their mismanagement.

(a) What is a derivative suit? (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A derivative suit is an action brought by a stockholder in the corporation’s name to enforce a corporate cause of action when those who ordinarily should sue refuse, are unable to act, or are themselves the alleged wrongdoers.

Legal Basis: Rule 8 of the Interim Rules of Procedure Governing Intra-Corporate Controversies and Yu v. Yukayguan treat the corporation as the real party in interest and the suing stockholder as a nominal representative.

Application: The action vindicates an injury to the corporation, not a personal injury unique to the stockholder; any recovery therefore belongs to the corporation.

Conclusion: A derivative suit is the stockholder’s procedural vehicle for enforcing a corporate right that corporate management will not enforce.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Interim Rules of Procedure Governing Intra-Corporate Controversies, Rule 8; Yu v. Yukayguan: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49329

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
In May 2018, ABC Corp. entered into a merchandising contract which terms and conditions were totally lopsided in favor of the counterparty, XYZ, Inc. As a result, ABC Corp. suffered tremendous financial losses.

A year after, or in May 2019, Mr. X became a stockholder of ABC Corp. Learning about the circumstances surrounding the merchandising contract, Mr. X filed a derivative suit against ABC Corp. 's directors to claim damages on behalf of ABC Corp. due to their mismanagement.

(b) Was Mr. X's filing of a derivative suit proper? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Mr. X lacked the contemporaneous stock ownership required for a derivative suit.

Legal Basis: Rule 8 of the Interim Rules of Procedure Governing Intra-Corporate Controversies and Yu v. Yukayguan require the plaintiff to have been a stockholder when the challenged act occurred and when the action was filed, subject to the rules governing shares devolved by operation of law.

Application: The challenged merchandising contract was made in May 2018, but Mr. X acquired his shares only in May 2019. He was not a stockholder when the transaction occurred.

Conclusion: Mr. X’s derivative suit was not properly filed.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
In June 2018, DEF Corp. sent notices to its stockholders informing them of the corporation's issuance of new shares of stock. The notice included a reminder that, pursuant to DEF Corp.' s Articles of Incorporation, any stockholder who fails to exercise his or her pre-emptive right within three (3) weeks from receipt of notice would be considered to have waived the same.

Ms. Z, a stockholder of DEF Corp., failed to exercise her pre-emptive right within the said period. However, she claimed that she did not validly waive her right to do so because a waiver must be expressed in writing.

(a) Explain the concept of pre-emptive right under the Corporation Code. (2 %)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Pre-emptive right is a stockholder’s right to subscribe to new issues or dispositions of shares in proportion to existing ownership, so the stockholder may preserve proportionate voting and proprietary interests.

Legal Basis: Section 38 of the Revised Corporation Code and Majority Stockholders of Ruby Industrial Corporation v. Lim recognize the right, subject to lawful denial in the articles and statutory exceptions.

Application: When a corporation issues additional shares, each stockholder must ordinarily receive a proportionate opportunity to subscribe before the shares are offered elsewhere.

Conclusion: Pre-emptive right protects a stockholder against involuntary dilution, subject to the Code and the articles.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
In June 2018, DEF Corp. sent notices to its stockholders informing them of the corporation's issuance of new shares of stock. The notice included a reminder that, pursuant to DEF Corp.' s Articles of Incorporation, any stockholder who fails to exercise his or her pre-emptive right within three (3) weeks from receipt of notice would be considered to have waived the same.

Ms. Z, a stockholder of DEF Corp., failed to exercise her pre-emptive right within the said period. However, she claimed that she did not validly waive her right to do so because a waiver must be expressed in writing.

(b) Is Ms. Z's contention correct? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A stockholder may waive the pre-emptive right by failing to exercise it within a reasonable period after notice.

Legal Basis: Section 38 of the Revised Corporation Code and Majority Stockholders of Ruby Industrial Corporation v. Lim recognize that the corporation may set a reasonable exercise period and treat inaction after its expiry as waiver.

Application: DEF Corp. gave notice and three weeks to exercise the right. Nothing in the stated facts makes that period unreasonable, and Ms. Z allowed it to lapse.

Conclusion: Ms. Z is deemed to have waived the pre-emptive right.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
In 2016, X Corp. obtained a loan worth ₱50,000,000.00 from J Bank, which was secured by a third-party mortgage executed by Y, Inc. in favor of X Corp. Since X Corp. was not able to settle its loan obligation to J Bank when it fell due, and despite numerous demands, J Bank foreclosed the mortgaged properties. The properties were sold in a foreclosure sale for ₱35,000,000.00, thereby leaving a ₱15,000,000.00 deficiency. For failure of X Corp. to pay said deficiency, J Bank filed a complaint for sum of money against X Corp., its President, Mr. P, and Y, Inc.

With respect to Mr. P, J Bank argued that he should be held solidarily liable together with X Corp. because he signed the loan document on behalf of X Corp. in his capacity as President. On the other hand, J Bank contended that Y, Inc. should also be held solidarily liable because the shareholdings of both corporations are identically owned and their operations are controlled by the same people; hence, Y, Inc. is a mere alter ego of X Corp.

(a) Should Mr. P be held liable? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, absent a separate legal ground for personal liability.

Legal Basis: The Revised Corporation Code and Bustos v. Millians Shoe, Inc. recognize that a corporation has a juridical personality separate from its officers and stockholders; corporate debts are not automatically their personal debts.

Application: Mr. P signed expressly in his representative capacity as president of X Corp.. The facts do not show that he personally guaranteed the loan, acted in bad faith, or agreed to be solidarily bound.

Conclusion: Mr. P is not personally liable for the corporate deficiency on the stated facts.

In 2016, X Corp. obtained a loan worth ₱50,000,000.00 from J Bank, which was secured by a third-party mortgage executed by Y, Inc. in favor of X Corp. Since X Corp. was not able to settle its loan obligation to J Bank when it fell due, and despite numerous demands, J Bank foreclosed the mortgaged properties. The properties were sold in a foreclosure sale for ₱35,000,000.00, thereby leaving a ₱15,000,000.00 deficiency. For failure of X Corp. to pay said deficiency, J Bank filed a complaint for sum of money against X Corp., its President, Mr. P, and Y, Inc.

records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Common ownership and control alone do not justify piercing the corporate veil.

Legal Basis: Pacific Rehouse Corporation v. Court of Appeals requires control amounting to domination of finances, policy, and business practice, use of that control to commit fraud or wrong, and proximate causation of the claimant’s injury.

Application: The facts show identical ownership and overlapping control but do not show that Y, Inc. had no separate will, that the corporate form was used to perpetrate fraud, or that such misuse caused J Bank’s deficiency.

Conclusion: Y, Inc. cannot be held solidarily liable on the stated facts.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
ABC Homeowners Association, Inc. sued Mr. X before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) for collection of unpaid association dues. Mr. X filed a motion to dismiss solely on the ground of lack of jurisdiction, asserting that the Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes among homeowners and their associations. The RTC denied Mr. X's motion, maintaining that it has jurisdiction over the case. This prompted Mr. X to file a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court before the Supreme Court, alleging grave abuse of discretion on the part of the RTC in denying his motion to dismiss.

(a) Is Mr. X's chosen remedy of certiorari and direct recourse to the Supreme Court proper? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Certiorari may be an available remedy against a denial attended by grave abuse of discretion, but direct recourse to the Supreme Court was improper.

Legal Basis: Rule 65 and Pacaña-Contreras v. Rovila Water Supply, Inc. recognize certiorari when no plain, speedy, and adequate remedy exists. The hierarchy-of-courts doctrine ordinarily requires filing in the Court of Appeals (CA), despite concurrent jurisdiction.

Application: The denial did not finally dispose of the case, so ordinary appeal was unavailable at that point. However, Mr. X alleged no exceptional and compelling reason to bypass the CA.

Conclusion: The Rule 65 remedy was potentially proper, but the direct filing in the Supreme Court was not.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Concurrent jurisdiction does not excuse disregard of the hierarchy of courts; direct Supreme Court recourse requires exceptional reasons.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
ABC Homeowners Association, Inc. sued Mr. X before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) for collection of unpaid association dues. Mr. X filed a motion to dismiss solely on the ground of lack of jurisdiction, asserting that the Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes among homeowners and their associations. The RTC denied Mr. X's motion, maintaining that it has jurisdiction over the case. This prompted Mr. X to file a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court before the Supreme Court, alleging grave abuse of discretion on the part of the RTC in denying his motion to dismiss.

(b) Assuming that Mr. X's motion was instead granted by the RTC, what is the proper remedy of ABC Homeowners Association, Inc. to challenge the RTC ruling? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: It should first seek reconsideration and, if the dismissal is without prejudice and therefore nonappealable, file a Rule 65 petition for certiorari in the Court of Appeals (CA).

Legal Basis: Rule 41 bars an appeal from an order dismissing an action without prejudice, while Rule 65 supplies the remedy against a nonappealable order issued with grave abuse of discretion. Pacaña-Contreras v. Rovila Water Supply, Inc. applies these remedial distinctions.

Application: A dismissal solely for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction does not adjudicate the claim on the merits and ordinarily permits refiling. An ordinary appeal is therefore unavailable, making Rule 65 the proper corrective remedy after reconsideration.

Conclusion: The association should pursue reconsideration, then certiorari in the CA if necessary.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Judgment on the Pleadings — Negative Pregnant
records.Essay Question:
Ms. A filed a complaint for damages against Ms. B, alleging that Ms. B negligently caused the demolition of her house's concrete fence, the top half of which fell on the front portion of Ms. A's car and permanently damaged its engine. In her answer, Ms. B denied any personal liability for the damage caused to Ms. A's car, averring that she merely acquiesced to the advice of her contractor, XYZ Construction Co., to have the concrete fence demolished. Thus, damages, if any, should be collected from it.

Thereafter, Ms. A filed a motion for judgment on the pleadings, alleging that Ms. B's statement in her answer is actually a negative pregnant. Ms. B opposed the motion, reiterating her defense in her answer which purportedly rendered judgment on the pleadings improper. Ms. B also moved for the dismissal of the case on the ground of non-joinder of XYZ Construction Co., which she alleged is an indispensable party to the case.

(a) Is Ms. A's motion for judgment on the pleadings proper? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The answer did not genuinely deny the material occurrence and instead avoided personal liability by pointing to the contractor.

Legal Basis: Rule 34 permits judgment on the pleadings when the answer fails to tender an issue or admits the material allegations. Republic v. Sandiganbayan explains that a negative pregnant is a denial carrying an admission of the substantial facts alleged.

Application: Ms. B effectively admitted the demolition and resulting damage while asserting that another party should bear liability. That qualified denial did not controvert the material facts supporting Ms. A’s claim.

Conclusion: Judgment on the pleadings was proper, subject to proof of unliquidated damages if required.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 34; Republic v. Sandiganbayan: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48708
records.Controlling Doctrine: A negative pregnant admits the substantial facts while denying only a qualification; an answer that tenders no real issue may support judgment on the pleadings.

(b) Is XYZ Construction Co. an indispensable or a necessary party? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: XYZ Construction Co. is a necessary party, not an indispensable party.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Sections 7 and 8 distinguish an indispensable party, without whom no final determination can be had, from a necessary party whose presence allows complete relief or complete settlement. Boston Equity Resources, Inc. v. Court of Appeals applies this distinction.

Application: The court can determine Ms. B’s liability to Ms. A without the contractor, so the contractor is not indispensable. Its joinder is nevertheless desirable because Ms. B’s asserted claim against it may permit complete settlement of related liability.

Conclusion: XYZ Construction Co. is a necessary party.

records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Non-joinder of an indispensable party does not by itself require immediate dismissal.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 11 and Lotte Philippines Co., Inc. v. Dela Cruz direct the court to order joinder of the absent party. Dismissal becomes proper only if the plaintiff refuses to comply with the joinder order.

Application: The trial court should require Ms. A to implead XYZ Construction Co. so that a binding and complete adjudication can be made. Only disobedience of that lawful order would justify dismissal.

Conclusion: The proper initial remedy is joinder, not dismissal.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Mrs. G defaulted in the payment of her loan obligation with Z Bank. As such, Z Bank extra-judicially foreclosed Mrs. G's mortgaged property and sold it at public auction where it emerged as the highest bidder. Eventually, a certificate of sale was issued in Z Bank's favor, and title to the property was later consolidated under the bank's name.

Claiming that Z Bank used fraudulent machinations in increasing the interest and penalty charges on the loan, thereby making it impossible for her to pay, Mrs. G filed before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) a complaint for cancellation of consolidation of ownership over a real property with prayer for the issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction against Z Bank. Immediately thereafter, the RTC issued an ex parte writ of preliminary injunction enjoining Z Bank from disposing of the foreclosed property or taking possession thereof.

Did the RTC err in issuing the writ of preliminary injunction ex parte? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A writ of preliminary injunction cannot be issued ex parte.

Legal Basis: Rule 58, Section 5 and Spouses Tan Lee v. Philippine Bank of Communications require prior notice and hearing before a preliminary injunction is granted. Only a temporary restraining order may issue ex parte under the rule’s emergency conditions and limited duration.

Application: The RTC immediately granted the preliminary injunction without giving Z Bank notice and an opportunity to oppose it. The order was not merely a temporary restraining order.

Conclusion: The ex parte preliminary injunction was procedurally invalid.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
On October 5, 2016, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) sent KLM Corp. a Final Assessment Notice (FAN), stating that after its audit pursuant to a Letter of Authority duly issued therefor, KLM Corp. had deficiency value-added and withholding taxes. Subsequently, a warrant of distraint and/or levy was issued against KLM Corp. KLM Corp. opposed the actions of the BIR on the ground that it was not accorded due process because it did not even receive a Preliminary Assessment Notice (PAN) after the BIR' s investigation, which the BIR admitted.:

(a) Distinguish a PAN from a FAN.(2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A PAN states the BIR’s initial findings and proposed assessment; a FAN fixes the tax liability and demands payment.

Legal Basis: Section 228 of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC) and Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Transitions Optical Philippines, Inc. distinguish the preliminary notice from the final assessment and demand.

Application: The PAN gives KLM Corporation an opportunity to answer the proposed factual and legal bases before finalization. The FAN states the computed deficiency, demands payment, triggers applicable additions, and starts the period for an administrative protest.

Conclusion: A PAN is preliminary and generally part of due process; a FAN is the final assessment and demand for payment.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
On October 5, 2016, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) sent KLM Corp. a Final Assessment Notice (FAN), stating that after its audit pursuant to a Letter of Authority duly issued therefor, KLM Corp. had deficiency value-added and withholding taxes. Subsequently, a warrant of distraint and/or levy was issued against KLM Corp. KLM Corp. opposed the actions of the BIR on the ground that it was not accorded due process because it did not even receive a Preliminary Assessment Notice (PAN) after the BIR' s investigation, which the BIR admitted.:

(b) Are the deficiency tax assessment and warrant of distraint and/or levy issued against KLM Corp. valid? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Section 228 of the NIRC generally requires a PAN before a FAN, except in the specifically enumerated statutory cases. Transitions Optical holds that the PAN is part of procedural due process.

Application: The facts do not show a mathematical error on the return, a withholding-remittance discrepancy, a prohibited carryover of a refund claim, unpaid excise tax, or a transfer from an exempt to a nonexempt person. Because no exception applies, the FAN was issued without the required preliminary notice.

Conclusion: The deficiency assessment is void for denial of due process, and the collection warrant based on it cannot stand.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Unless a statutory exception applies, omission of the PAN violates the taxpayer’s right to procedural due process and voids the assessment.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: VAT — Input Tax versus Output Tax
records.Essay Question:
For purposes of value-added tax, define, explain or distinguish the following terms:

(a) Input tax and output tax (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Input tax is VAT due from or paid by a VAT-registered person on taxable importations or local purchases used in trade or business; output tax is VAT due on that person’s taxable sales, leases, or services.

Legal Basis: Sections 110 and 236 of the NIRC, as discussed in Panasonic Communications Imaging Corporation of the Philippines v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, recognize the invoice-based VAT mechanism in which allowable input tax is credited against output tax.

Application: VAT paid on business purchases is an input credit. VAT imposed on the taxpayer’s own taxable sale is output tax. The excess of output tax over allowable input tax is ordinarily payable.

Conclusion: Input tax arises on acquisitions; output tax arises on taxable dispositions or services.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The VAT system credits tax paid on inputs against tax due on taxable outputs.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: VAT — Zero-Rated versus Effectively Zero-Rated Transactions
records.Essay Question:
For purposes of value-added tax, define, explain or distinguish the following terms:

(b) Zero-rated and effectively zero-rated transactions (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Both bear a zero VAT rate, but they differ in the legal source of that treatment.

Legal Basis: Sections 106(A)(2) and 108(B) of the NIRC and the doctrine discussed in Panasonic Communications, citing Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Seagate Technology (Philippines), Inc.

Application: Zero-rated transactions are principally exports or services expressly assigned a zero rate by the NIRC. Effectively zero-rated transactions are sales to persons or entities whose exemption under a special law or international agreement makes the seller’s transaction subject to a zero rate. In either case, no output VAT is charged and attributable input VAT may be creditable or refundable subject to statutory requirements.

Conclusion: The rate and practical VAT effect are the same; the source of zero-rating differs.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 106(A)(2) and 108(B); Panasonic Communications Imaging Corporation of the Philippines v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, citing Seagate Technology: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53572
records.Controlling Doctrine: Statutory zero-rating generally covers exports; effective zero-rating follows from the purchaser’s special-law or treaty exemption.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Panasonic Communications Imaging Corporation of the Philippines v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
For purposes of value-added tax, define, explain or distinguish the following terms:

(c) Destination principle (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: VAT is imposed where goods or services are consumed.

Legal Basis: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. American Express International, Inc. explains that the Philippine VAT system generally follows the destination principle and cross-border doctrine.

Application: Imports are ordinarily taxed because they are consumed in the Philippines, while exports are generally zero-rated because consumption occurs abroad. For services, the statutory place and use or consumption requirements must still be satisfied.

Conclusion: The destination principle allocates VAT to the jurisdiction of consumption, subject to the NIRC’s specific rules.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Under the destination principle, exports are generally zero-rated and imports are taxed because VAT follows consumption.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: VAT — Course of Trade or Business
records.Essay Question:
All the homeowners belonging to ABC Village Homeowners' Association elected a new set of members of the Board of Trustees for the Association effective January 2019. The first thing that the Board looked into is the need to increase the prevailing association dues. Mr. X, one of the trustees, proposed an increase of 100% to account for the payment of the 12% value-added tax (VAT) on the association dues which were being collected for services allegedly rendered "in the course of trade or business" by ABC Village Homeowners' Association.

(a) What constitutes transactions done "in the course of trade or business" for purposes of applying VAT?(2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The phrase covers the regular conduct or pursuit of a commercial or economic activity, including incidental transactions.

Legal Basis: Section 105 of the NIRC and Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and Commonwealth Management and Services Corporation (COMASERCO) provide that VAT may apply regardless of profit motive and may cover nonstock, nonprofit, or government entities.

Application: The character of the association, disposition of net income, or limitation of dealings to members does not by itself remove regularly conducted economic activity from Section 105. Philippine services by a nonresident foreign person are treated by statute as made in the course of trade or business despite irregularity.

Conclusion: Regular commercial or economic activity and its incidental transactions fall within the phrase, irrespective of organizational form or profit motive.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 105; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and COMASERCO: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53304
records.Controlling Doctrine: VAT’s “course of trade or business” test focuses on regular economic activity, not solely on profit motive or corporate form.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and Commonwealth Management and Services Corporation

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Due to rising liquidity problems and pressure from its concerned suppliers, P Corp. instituted a flash auction sale of its shares of stock. P Corp. was then able to sell its treasury shares to Z, Inc., an unrelated corporation, for Pl,000,000.00, which was only a little below the valuation of P Corp. 's shares based on its latest audited financial statements. In connection therewith, P Corp. sought a Bureau of Internal Revenue ruling to confirm that, notwithstanding the price difference between the selling price of the shares and their book value, the said transaction falls under one of the recognized exemptions to donor's tax under the Tax Code.

(a) Cite the instances under the Tax Code where gifts made are exempt from donor's tax.(3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The exempt gifts are those made to or for the use of the National Government, a nonprofit government-created entity, or a political subdivision, and qualifying gifts to specified nonprofit educational, charitable, religious, cultural, social-welfare, accredited nongovernment, philanthropic, or research institutions.

Legal Basis: Section 101(A) of the NIRC prescribes the exemptions and requires that no more than 30% of the gift be used for administration by the qualifying institutional donee. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and YMCA of the Philippines reiterates that a statutory tax exemption must be expressed in clear and unmistakable language.

Application: A donor must identify the donee and verify its nonprofit structure and statutory qualifications; a benevolent purpose alone is insufficient.

Conclusion: Only gifts falling within Section 101(A)’s governmental or qualified-institution categories are exempt.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Tax exemptions must be expressed in clear statutory language; donor-tax exemption depends on the identity and qualifications of the donee.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Donor’s Tax — Arm’s-Length Sale Without Donative Intent
records.Essay Question:
Due to rising liquidity problems and pressure from its concerned suppliers, P Corp. instituted a flash auction sale of its shares of stock. P Corp. was then able to sell its treasury shares to Z, Inc., an unrelated corporation, for Pl,000,000.00, which was only a little below the valuation of P Corp. 's shares based on its latest audited financial statements. In connection therewith, P Corp. sought a Bureau of Internal Revenue ruling to confirm that, notwithstanding the price difference between the selling price of the shares and their book value, the said transaction falls under one of the recognized exemptions to donor's tax under the Tax Code.

(b) Does the above transaction fall under any of the exemptions? Explain. (2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The transaction is not an enumerated exemption, but the facts indicate that it is not a taxable gift.

Legal Basis: Section 100 of the NIRC treats a bona fide, arm’s-length transfer in the ordinary course of business and free from donative intent as made for adequate and full consideration. The Philippine American Life and General Insurance Company v. Secretary of Finance recognizes that a bona fide business sale without donative intent falls outside Section 100.

Application: The flash sale addressed genuine liquidity needs, the buyer was unrelated, and the price was only slightly below book value. These facts negate donative intent and support arm’s-length dealing.

Conclusion: No donor’s tax should arise, although the reason is absence of a deemed gift rather than an exemption under Section 101.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A bona fide arm’s-length business transfer free from donative intent is treated as made for adequate consideration and is not a deemed gift.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Estate Tax — Family Home and Funeral Expenses
records.Essay Question:
A, a resident Filipino citizen, died in December 2018. A's only assets consist of a house and lot in Alabang, where his heirs currently reside, as well as a house in Los Angeles, California, USA. In computing A's taxable net estate, his heirs only deducted: 1. ₱10,000,000.00 constituting the value of their house in Alabang as their family home; and 2. ₱200,000.00 in funeral expenses because no other expenses could be substantiated.

(a) Are both deductions claimed by A's heirs correct? Explain.(2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The family-home deduction may be claimed up to ₱10,000,000.00, but funeral expenses are no longer a separate deduction under the TRAIN-amended estate-tax rules applicable to the death.

Legal Basis: Section 86(A)(7) of the NIRC, as amended by R.A. No. 10963, allows the family-home deduction up to the statutory ceiling. Dizon v. Court of Tax Appeals emphasizes that estate-tax deductions are statutory and must satisfy the governing law.

Application: The claimed family-home amount does not exceed the ceiling. The separate funeral-expense item is not among the post-TRAIN deductions for a 2018 death.

Conclusion: Allow the qualified family-home deduction; disallow the separate funeral-expense deduction.

Answer: Yes. The estate may claim the ₱5,000,000.00 standard deduction without itemized proof.

Legal Basis: Section 86(A)(1) of the NIRC, as amended by the TRAIN Law, grants the fixed standard deduction to the estate of a citizen or resident. Dizon v. Court of Tax Appeals confirms that estate deductions are governed by the statutory scheme.

Application: A was a resident Filipino citizen, and his death occurred after the TRAIN amendment took effect. The deduction is standard rather than reimbursement of a proved expense, so receipts or itemized substantiation are unnecessary.

Conclusion: The estate may deduct ₱5,000,000.00 without presenting proof of actual expenses.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
A, a resident Filipino citizen, died in December 2018. A's only assets consist of a house and lot in Alabang, where his heirs currently reside, as well as a house in Los Angeles, California, USA. In computing A's taxable net estate, his heirs only deducted: 1. ₱10,000,000.00 constituting the value of their house in Alabang as their family home; and 2. ₱200,000.00 in funeral expenses because no other expenses could be substantiated.

(c) In determining the gross estate of A, should the heirs include A's house in Los Angeles, California, USA? Explain.(2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes.

Legal Basis: Section 85 of the NIRC includes in the gross estate of a citizen or resident all property, real or personal, tangible or intangible, wherever situated. Dizon v. Court of Tax Appeals applies the NIRC’s estate-tax framework according to the decedent’s status and the statutory inclusions and deductions.

Application: A was both a citizen and a Philippine resident at death. The situs limitation for Philippine property applies to a nonresident decedent who was not a Philippine citizen, not to A.

Conclusion: The Los Angeles house forms part of A’s gross estate.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A citizen’s or resident’s gross estate generally includes property wherever situated; the situs limitation applies to a nonresident alien decedent.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Offline International Air Carrier
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Air, a 100% foreign-owned airline company based and registered in Netherlands, is engaged in the international airline business and is a member signatory of the International Air Transport Association. Its commercial airplanes neither operate within the Philippine territory nor are its service passengers embarking from Philippine airports. Nevertheless, XYZ Air is able to sell its airplane tickets in the Philippines through ABC Agency, its general agent in the Philippines. As XYZ Air's ticket sales, sold through ABC Agency for the year 2013, amounted to ₱5,000,000.00, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) assessed XYZ Air deficiency income taxes on the ground that the income from the said sales constituted income derived from sources within the Philippines.

Aggrieved, XYZ Air filed a protest, arguing that, as a non-resident foreign corporation, it should only be taxed for income derived from sources within the Philippines. However, since it only serviced passengers outside the Philippine territory, the situs of the income from its ticket sales should be considered outside the Philippines. Hence, no income tax should be imposed on the same.

Is XYZ Air's protest meritorious? Explain.(5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, subject to any applicable tax treaty.

Legal Basis: Section 28(A)(1) of the NIRC and Air Canada v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue hold that an offline international carrier selling tickets in the Philippines through a general sales agent is a resident foreign corporation doing business here.

Application: ABC Agency regularly sold XYZ Air’s passage tickets in the Philippines for the carrier. That local sales activity constitutes doing business and produces Philippine-source income even though the actual flights and passenger embarkation occur abroad.

Conclusion: XYZ Air is taxable as a resident foreign corporation on the Philippine ticket-sale income, subject to treaty limitations.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 28(A)(1); Air Canada v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61607
records.Controlling Doctrine: An offline foreign airline that continuously sells tickets locally through a general sales agent is doing business in the Philippines and earns Philippine-source income.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Air Canada v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question: Differentiate tax exclusions from tax deductions.(3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: An exclusion prevents an item from entering gross income; a deduction subtracts an authorized amount from gross income in computing taxable income.

Legal Basis: Sections 32 and 34 of the NIRC govern exclusions and deductions, respectively. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Airlines, Inc. explains that taxable income is gross income less deductions authorized by the NIRC or special law and that these terms have distinct technical meanings.

Application: An excluded item is omitted at the gross-income stage. A deductible item is first within the income computation but reduces the tax base only if the law expressly allows it and its conditions are met.

Conclusion: Exclusions define what is outside gross income; deductions reduce gross income to arrive at taxable income.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 32 and 34; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Airlines, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49399
records.Controlling Doctrine: Exclusions remove items from gross income, while statutory deductions are subtracted from gross income to determine taxable income.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Airlines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
B transferred his ownership over a 1,000-square meter commercial land and three-door apartment to ABC Corp., a family corporation of which B is a stockholder. The transfer was in exchange of 10,000 shares of stock of ABC Corp. As a result, B acquired 51 % ownership of ABC Corp., with all the shares of stock having the right to vote. B paid no tax on the exchange, maintaining that it is a tax avoidance scheme allowed under the law. The Bureau of Internal Revenue, on the other hand, insisted that B's alleged scheme amounted to tax evasion.

Should B pay taxes on the exchange? Explain.(3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Section 40(C)(2) and (6)(c) of the NIRC defer recognition when property is transferred to a corporation solely for its stock and the transferor or qualified transferor group gains control, defined as at least 51% of total voting power. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. HSBC Electronic Data Processing (Philippines), Inc. applies these requisites.

Application: B transferred property, received voting shares, and thereby gained 51% control of ABC Corporation. Nothing indicates that shares were issued for services or that disqualifying consideration was received.

Conclusion: The exchange is tax-free as to immediate gain or loss recognition; it is lawful tax avoidance, not tax evasion.

records.Controlling Doctrine: No gain or loss is immediately recognized on a qualifying property-for-shares exchange that gives the transferor statutory control of the transferee corporation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. HSBC Electronic Data Processing (Philippines), Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Sale of Machinery and Equipment
records.Essay Question:
GHI, Inc. is a corporation authorized to engage in the business of manufacturing ultra-high density microprocessor unit packages. After its registration on July 5, 2005, GHI, Inc. constructed buildings and purchased machineries and equipment. As of December 31, 2005, the total cost of the machineries and equipment amounted to ₱250,000,000.00. However, GHI, Inc. failed to commence operations. Its factory was temporarily closed effective September 15, 2010. On October 1, 2010, it sold its machineries and equipment to JKL Integrated for ₱300,000,000.00. Thereafter, GHI, Inc. was dissolved on November 30, 2010.

(a) Is the sale of the machineries and equipment to JKL Integrated subject to normal corporate income tax or capital gains tax? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The gain on the machinery and equipment is subject to normal corporate income tax, not the 6% capital-gains tax imposed on specified real property.

Legal Basis: Sections 27 and 39 of the NIRC and SMI-ED Philippines Technology, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue distinguish a corporation’s sale of machinery and equipment from a sale of land or buildings covered by the 6% capital-gains regime.

Application: The property sold consisted of machinery and equipment, not land or a building. The NIRC does not extend the 6% real-property capital-gains tax to those assets. Any taxable gain therefore enters the corporation’s regular income-tax computation.

Conclusion: Apply normal corporate income tax to the taxable gain on the machinery and equipment.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The 6% corporate capital-gains tax covers qualifying land and buildings, not machinery and equipment; gain on the latter is governed by regular corporate income tax.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: SMI-ED Philippines Technology, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Ordinary Asset versus Capital Asset
records.Essay Question:
GHI, Inc. is a corporation authorized to engage in the business of manufacturing ultra-high density microprocessor unit packages. After its registration on July 5, 2005, GHI, Inc. constructed buildings and purchased machineries and equipment. As of December 31, 2005, the total cost of the machineries and equipment amounted to ₱250,000,000.00. However, GHI, Inc. failed to commence operations. Its factory was temporarily closed effective September 15, 2010. On October 1, 2010, it sold its machineries and equipment to JKL Integrated for ₱300,000,000.00. Thereafter, GHI, Inc. was dissolved on November 30, 2010.

(b) Distinguish an ordinary asset from a capital asset.(2%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: An ordinary asset falls within the statutory exclusions from “capital asset”; a capital asset is the residual category.

Legal Basis: Section 39(A)(1) of the NIRC, applied in SMI-ED Philippines Technology, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, excludes inventory, property held primarily for sale to customers, depreciable property used in trade or business, and real property used in trade or business from capital-asset treatment.

Application: Classify the property according to its actual holding and use. If it belongs to any excluded business category, it is ordinary; if none applies, it is capital.

Conclusion: “Capital asset” is defined by exclusion, while ordinary assets are the business properties specifically removed from that category.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 39(A)(1); SMI-ED Philippines Technology, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/58727
records.Controlling Doctrine: Capital asset is a residual classification; inventory, customer-sale property, depreciable business property, and business realty are ordinary assets.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
City X amended its revenue code to tax every wholesale sale of merchandise based on the total selling price, inclusive of VAT. ABC Corporation argued that the local tax constituted prohibited double taxation because the National Government already imposed VAT.

Is the double-taxation objection correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not on that ground alone.

Legal Basis: Nursery Care Corporation v. Acevedo explains that direct duplicate taxation requires, among other elements, the same taxing authority and jurisdiction, as well as the same subject, purpose, period, and kind of tax.

Application: The challenged sales tax is imposed by City X, while VAT is imposed by the National Government. Because the taxing authorities and jurisdictions differ, the two exactions do not satisfy the test for direct duplicate taxation.

Conclusion: ABC Corporation’s first objection fails, without prejudice to the separate statutory limitation on an LGU’s power to impose a VAT-like tax.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code; Nursery Care Corporation v. Acevedo: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/57493
records.Controlling Doctrine: Direct duplicate taxation ordinarily requires two taxes imposed by the same authority in the same jurisdiction on the same subject for the same purpose, period, and character.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Local Taxation — Prohibition on VAT or Percentage Tax
records.Essay Question:
City X amended its revenue code to impose a tax on every wholesale sale of merchandise based on the total selling price, inclusive of VAT. ABC Corporation argued that the exaction was essentially VAT and exceeded the city’s taxing power.

Is the objection meritorious? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the local exaction is in substance a percentage or value-added tax on sales and no Local Government Code exception authorizes it.

Legal Basis: Section 133(i) of the Local Government Code withholds from local governments the power to levy percentage or VAT on sales, barters, exchanges, or similar transactions, except as otherwise provided. City of Manila v. Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines, Inc. enforces statutory limitations on local business taxation.

Application: The tax is measured as a percentage of the wholesale selling price and is described as akin to VAT. City X cannot evade Section 133(i) by changing the label of the exaction.

Conclusion: The VAT-like local levy is beyond the city’s authority unless a specific Code provision authorizes it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Section 133(i); City of Manila v. Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49595
records.Controlling Doctrine: An LGU may exercise only delegated taxing power and cannot impose a VAT or percentage tax on sales outside the Local Government Code’s express authority.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: City of Manila v. Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Nonresident Citizen and Worldwide Income
records.Essay Question:
JKL-Philippines is a domestic corporation affiliated with JKL-Japan, a Japan-based information technology company with affiliates across the world. Mr. F is a Filipino engineer employed by JKL-Philippines. In 2018, Mr. F was sent to the Tokyo branch of JKL-Japan based on a contract entered into between the two (2) companies. Under the said contract, Mr. F would be compensated by JKL-Philippines for the months spent in the Philippines, and by JKL-Japan for months spent in Japan. For the entirety of 2018, Mr. F spent ten (10) months in the Tokyo branch.

On the other hand, Mr. J, a Japanese engineer employed by JKL-Japan, was sent to Manila to work with JKL-Philippines as a technical consultant. Based on the contract between the two (2) companies, Mr. J's annual compensation would still be paid by JKL-Japan. However, he would be paid additional compensation by JKL-Philippines for the months spent working as a consultant. For 2018, Mr. J stayed in the Philippines for five (5) months.

In 2019, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) assessed JKL-Philippines for deficiency withholding taxes for both Mr. F and Mr. J for the year 2018. As to Mr. F, the BIR argued that he is a resident citizen; hence, his income tax should be based on his worldwide income. As to Mr. J, the BIR argued that he is a resident alien; hence, his income tax should be based on his income from sources within the Philippines at the schedular rate under Section 24 (A) (2) of the Tax Code, as amended by Republic Act No. 10963, or the "Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion" Law.

(a) ls the BIR correct in basing its income tax assessment on Mr. F's worldwide income? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Sections 22(E) and 23(B) of the NIRC classify as a nonresident citizen a Filipino who works and derives income abroad and is physically present abroad most of the taxable year; that taxpayer is taxable only on Philippine-source income. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Baier-Nickel explains that Philippine income taxation turns on taxpayer status and source.

Application: Mr. F spent ten months working in Tokyo, which is most of 2018. He therefore satisfies the statutory nonresident-citizen classification. His Japan-source compensation is outside the Philippine tax base for that year.

Conclusion: The BIR may not assess Mr. F on worldwide income.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A citizen working and physically present abroad most of the taxable year is a nonresident citizen taxable only on Philippine-source income.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Nonresident Alien Not Engaged in Business
records.Essay Question:
JKL-Philippines is a domestic corporation affiliated with JKL-Japan, a Japan-based information technology company with affiliates across the world. Mr. F is a Filipino engineer employed by JKL-Philippines. In 2018, Mr. F was sent to the Tokyo branch of JKL-Japan based on a contract entered into between the two (2) companies. Under the said contract, Mr. F would be compensated by JKL-Philippines for the months spent in the Philippines, and by JKL-Japan for months spent in Japan. For the entirety of 2018, Mr. F spent ten (10) months in the Tokyo branch.

On the other hand, Mr. J, a Japanese engineer employed by JKL-Japan, was sent to Manila to work with JKL-Philippines as a technical consultant. Based on the contract between the two (2) companies, Mr. J's annual compensation would still be paid by JKL-Japan. However, he would be paid additional compensation by JKL-Philippines for the months spent working as a consultant. For 2018, Mr. J stayed in the Philippines for five (5) months.

In 2019, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) assessed JKL-Philippines for deficiency withholding taxes for both Mr. F and Mr. J for the year 2018. As to Mr. F, the BIR argued that he is a resident citizen; hence, his income tax should be based on his worldwide income. As to Mr. J, the BIR argued that he is a resident alien; hence, his income tax should be based on his income from sources within the Philippines at the schedular rate under Section 24 (A) (2) of the Tax Code, as amended by Republic Act No. 10963, or the "Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion" Law.

(b) Is the BIR correct in basing its income tax assessment on Mr. J's income within the Philippines at the schedular rate? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Sections 22(G) and 25(B) of the NIRC treat a nonresident alien present for not more than 180 days as not engaged in trade or business and impose the applicable final tax on Philippine-source fixed or determinable income. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Baier-Nickel explains the controlling role of source and nonresident status.

Application: Mr. J is neither a citizen nor a Philippine resident and stayed only five months, which is not more than 180 days. His Philippine consulting compensation is Philippine-source income, but it is not taxed at the resident schedular rates.

Conclusion: Mr. J is a nonresident alien not engaged in trade or business and, under the law applicable to the 2019 examination, is subject to the 25% final tax on the Philippine-source compensation.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Vacation Stipend as Compensation
records.Essay Question:
As a way to augment the income of the employees of DEF, Inc., a private corporation, the management decided to grant a special stipend of ₱50,000.00 for the first vacation leave that any employee takes during a given calendar year. In addition, the senior engineers were also given housing inside the factory compound for the purpose of ensuring that there are available engineers within the premises every time there is a breakdown in the factory machineries and equipment.

(a) Is the special stipend part of the taxable income of the employees receiving the same? If so, what tax is applicable and what is the tax rate? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, subject to any specific exclusion or applicable statutory ceiling not established by the facts.

Legal Basis: Sections 24(A) and 32(A)(1) of the NIRC include compensation for services in whatever form in gross income. Confederation for Unity, Recognition and Advancement of Government Employees v. Abad explains that withholding on compensation is a method of collecting the employee’s income tax at source.

Application: The cash stipend is paid because of the employer-employee relationship and is not shown to be a reimbursement or a qualifying excluded benefit. It is therefore added to compensation income and subjected to the graduated individual income-tax rates, with withholding as required.

Conclusion: The ₱50,000.00 vacation stipend is taxable compensation under the law applicable to the 2019 examination.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Cash paid by reason of employment is compensation income unless a specific statutory exclusion applies; withholding collects the employee’s tax at source.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Confederation for Unity, Recognition and Advancement of Government Employees v. Abad

(b) Is the cash equivalent value of the housing facilities received by the senior engineers subject to fringe benefits tax? Explain. (3%)

Answer: No, if the stated operational necessity is substantiated.

Legal Basis: Section 33(A) of the NIRC excludes a fringe benefit required by the nature of or necessary to the employer’s trade or business, or furnished for the employer’s convenience or advantage. Conclusion: On the stated and adequately proved facts, the housing is not subject to fringe-benefits tax.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Real Property Tax — Beneficial Use by Taxable Lessee
records.Essay Question:
City R owns a piece of land which it leased to V Corp. In turn, V Corp. constructed a public market thereon and leased the stalls to vendors and small storeowners. The City Assessor then issued a notice of assessment against V Corp. for the payment of real property taxes (RPT) accruing on the public market building, as well as on the land where said market stands.

Is the City Assessor correct in including the land in its assessment of RPT against V Corp., even if the same is owned by City R? Explain. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes.

Legal Basis: Section 234(a) of the Local Government Code withdraws the exemption of real property owned by the Republic or a political subdivision when beneficial use is granted, for consideration or otherwise, to a taxable person. Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System v. Local Government of Pasay City reiterates that liability devolves on the taxable beneficial user.

Application: City R granted V Corporation, a taxable private corporation, beneficial use of the land through the lease. V Corporation used it for a market and further leased the stalls commercially.

Conclusion: The land loses the governmental real-property-tax exemption while its beneficial use is vested in V Corporation, and it may be assessed accordingly.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Government-owned real property becomes taxable when its beneficial use is granted to a taxable person; the tax liability rests on the taxable beneficial user.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System v. Local Government of Pasay City

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Calendar Year versus Fiscal Year
records.Essay Question: (a) Differentiate between a calendar year and a fiscal year. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A calendar year is the 12-month period ending December 31; a fiscal year is a 12-month accounting period ending on the last day of any month other than December.

Legal Basis: Sections 22(P) and 22(Q) of the NIRC define taxable year and fiscal year. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc. applies statutory filing periods by reference to the taxpayer’s prescribed taxable period.

Application: A taxpayer using January 1 through December 31 follows the calendar year. A corporation whose 12-month books close, for example, on June 30 uses a fiscal year.

Conclusion: Both cover 12 months, but only a calendar year ends on December 31.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 22(P) and 22(Q); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44251
records.Controlling Doctrine: A calendar year ends on December 31; a fiscal year is a 12-month accounting period ending on the last day of another month.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Income Tax — Corporate Final Adjustment Return Deadline
records.Essay Question: (b) When is the deadline for the filing of a corporation's final adjustment return for a calendar year? How about for a fiscal year? (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A calendar-year corporation files on or before April 15 of the succeeding year; a fiscal-year corporation files on or before the 15th day of the fourth month following the close of its fiscal year.

Legal Basis: Section 77(B) of the NIRC, as then applicable, prescribed those deadlines. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc. treats the statutory deadline as the starting point and applies the rule extending an act due on a holiday to the next working day.

Application: A December 31 close leads to April 15. A June 30 fiscal close leads to October 15, subject to the legal rule for weekends or holidays.

Conclusion: The deadlines are April 15 for a calendar year and the 15th day of the fourth following month for a fiscal year, under the 2019-examination law.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The corporate final return deadline is tied to the close of the corporation’s calendar or fiscal taxable year and moves to the next working day when legally due on a holiday.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Withholding Taxes — Identification of Withholding Agents
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Corp. is listed as a top 20,000 Philippine corporation by the Bureau of Internal Revenue. It secured a loan from ABC Bank with a 6% per annum interest. All interest payments made by XYZ Corp. to ABC Bank is subject to a 2% creditable withholding tax. At the same time, XYZ Corp. has a trust deposit with ABC Bank in the amount of ₱100,000,000.00, which earns 2% interest per annum, but is subject to a 20% final withholding tax on the interest income received by XYZ Corp.

(a) Who are the withholding agents in the case of: 1. the 20% final withholding tax; and 2. the 2% creditable withholding tax? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: ABC Bank is the withholding agent for the 20% final tax on deposit interest; XYZ Corporation is the withholding agent for the 2% creditable tax on loan interest it pays to the bank.

Legal Basis: Sections 57 and 58 of the NIRC impose withholding on the payor of covered income. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Smart Communications, Inc. explains that the withholding agent collects and remits tax for the government while the tax burden belongs to the income recipient.

Application: ABC Bank pays trust-deposit interest to XYZ Corporation, so the bank withholds the final tax. XYZ Corporation pays loan interest to ABC Bank, so the corporation withholds the creditable tax.

Conclusion: The payor in each payment stream is the corresponding withholding agent.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 57 and 58; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Smart Communications, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54268
records.Controlling Doctrine: The statutory withholding obligation generally rests on the payor of covered income, acting as the government’s collection agent.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Smart Communications, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Tax Refunds — Prescriptive Period for Withholding Taxes
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Corp. is listed as a top 20,000 Philippine corporation by the Bureau of Internal Revenue. It secured a loan from ABC Bank with a 6% per annum interest. All interest payments made by XYZ Corp. to ABC Bank is subject to a 2% creditable withholding tax. At the same time, XYZ Corp. has a trust deposit with ABC Bank in the amount of ₱100,000,000.00, which earns 2% interest per annum, but is subject to a 20% final withholding tax on the interest income received by XYZ Corp.

(a) When is the deadline for filing a judicial claim for refund for any excess or erroneous taxes paid in the case of: 1. the 20% final withholding tax; and 2. the 2% creditable withholding tax? (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Both are governed by the two-year limitation, but the legally relevant payment date differs.

Legal Basis: Sections 204(C) and 229 of the NIRC require both the administrative claim and judicial action within two years from payment. CBK Power Company Limited v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue reckons final-withholding-tax claims from remittance or payment. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Bank of Communications explains that for excess creditable withholding tax used as advance income-tax payment, the overpayment is ascertained upon the final adjustment return and final payment.

Application: For the 20% final tax, count from the date the withholding tax was remitted. For excess 2% creditable withholding tax claimed by the income taxpayer, count from filing the final adjustment return or final payment when the excess becomes determinable.

Conclusion: File both administrative and judicial claims within the applicable two-year period; filing an administrative claim alone does not suspend it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 204(C) and 229; CBK Power Company Limited v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/58996; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Bank of Communications: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29855
records.Controlling Doctrine: Final withholding-tax refunds are reckoned from remittance; excess creditable withholding-tax refunds are reckoned from the final adjustment return or final payment when the overpayment is ascertainable.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: CBK Power Company Limited v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine Bank of Communications

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
After a Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) audit, T Corp., a domestic corporation engaged in buying and selling of scrap metals, was found to have deficiency income tax of ₱25,000,000.00, including interests and penalties, for the year 2012. For 2012, T Corp. filed its income tax return (ITR) on April 15, 2013 because it used the calendar year for its accounting. The BIR sent the Preliminary Assessment Notice (PAN) on December 23, 2015, and eventually, the Final Assessment Notice (FAN) on April 11, 2016, which were received by T Corp. on the same dates that they were sent. Upon receipt of the FAN, T Corp. filed its protest letter on June 25, 2016.

Thereafter, and without action from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue (CIR), T Corp. filed a petition for review before the Court of Tax Appeals, alleging that the assessment has prescribed. For its part, the CIR moved to dismiss the case, pointing out that the assessment had already become final because the protest was filed beyond the allowable period.

(a) Is T Corp.'s contention regarding the prescription of the assessment meritorious? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Section 203 of the NIRC generally requires assessment within three years after the last day prescribed for filing the return. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Transitions Optical Philippines, Inc. explains that a valid assessment is embodied in the FAN, which states the tax due and demands payment.

Application: The three-year period ran from April 15, 2013 through April 15, 2016. The FAN was issued and received on April 11, 2016, four days before expiration. The earlier PAN was only preliminary and is not the controlling final assessment.

Conclusion: The deficiency assessment was timely.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 203; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Transitions Optical Philippines, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63727
records.Controlling Doctrine: A deficiency tax must generally be finally assessed within three years from the statutory filing date; the FAN, not merely the PAN, embodies the assessment.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Transitions Optical Philippines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
After a Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) audit, T Corp., a domestic corporation engaged in buying and selling of scrap metals, was found to have deficiency income tax of ₱25,000,000.00, including interests and penalties, for the year 2012. For 2012, T Corp. filed its income tax return (ITR) on April 15, 2013 because it used the calendar year for its accounting. The BIR sent the Preliminary Assessment Notice (PAN) on December 23, 2015, and eventually, the Final Assessment Notice (FAN) on April 11, 2016, which were received by T Corp. on the same dates that they were sent. Upon receipt of the FAN, T Corp. filed its protest letter on June 25, 2016.

Thereafter, and without action from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue (CIR), T Corp. filed a petition for review before the Court of Tax Appeals, alleging that the assessment has prescribed. For its part, the CIR moved to dismiss the case, pointing out that the assessment had already become final because the protest was filed beyond the allowable period.

(b) Should the CIR's motion to dismiss be granted? Explain. (2.5%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes.

Legal Basis: Section 228 of the NIRC requires a protest within 30 days from receipt of the FAN; otherwise, the assessment becomes final, executory, and demandable. Allied Banking Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue recognizes the administrative protest as the ordinary prerequisite to CTA review, subject only to exceptional circumstances not present here.

Application: June 25 was well beyond 30 days from April 11. Because T Corporation did not timely dispute the FAN, it became final before the CTA petition was filed.

Conclusion: The CTA cannot entertain the belated challenge, and the CIR’s motion to dismiss should be granted.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Failure to protest a FAN within 30 days generally makes the assessment final, executory, and demandable and forecloses ordinary CTA review.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Notarial Practice — Registers and Personal Appearance
records.Essay Question:
Atty. A, a duly licensed notary public, has maintained several notarial registers in his separate offices in order to cater to the needs of his clients and accommodate their growing number. Due to Atty. A's busy schedule, Atty. A's secretary would usually perform the notarial acts on his behalf.

Sometime in April 2017, Mrs. B, an Overseas Filipino Worker staying in Singapore, sought the legal services of Atty. A for the nullification of her marriage. Consequently, Atty. A drafted a petition with verification which was sent from his law office in Manila to Singapore for the signature of Mrs. B, who, after signing the same, sent it back to Atty. A. When the document arrived in Atty. A's office, his secretary, as per usual practice, notarized the signed document upon Atty. A's instruction.

(a) Name at least two (2) violations of the Rules on Notarial Practice committed by Atty. A. (3%)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Atty. A committed multiple violations.

Legal Basis: The 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice require a notary to keep only one active notarial register, personally perform the notarial act, and require the signatory's personal appearance. Boers v. Calubaquib enforces the personal-appearance and registry requirements.

Application: Atty. A kept several registers, delegated the notarial act to a non-notary secretary, and caused notarization although Mrs. B remained in Singapore and never personally appeared.

Conclusion: At least the multiple-register, unauthorized-delegation, and absent-signatory violations are established.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A notary must personally perform the act, require personal appearance, and keep the single active register required by the rules.
